title: KV Cache
content: KV CacheDuring LLM inference, computing attention scores in the attention layer requires taking the dot product of queries and keys, applying softmax normalization, and then computing a weighted sum with the values. Due to the autoregressive nature of generation, each new token must attend to all previous tokens, so the keys and values from prior steps must be cached for reuse. This caching technique is known as the KV cache and is widely used to accelerate inference. However, the KV cache consumes a substantial amount of GPU memory — especially for long-context inference, where it can account for more than 30% of total memory usage. This motivates research into compressing the KV cache to reduce memory footprint. KV Cache Compression and Computation OptimizationCompression and computation optimization are two distinct concepts: compression aims to reduce memory usage, while computation optimization aims to reduce FLOPs. They can be applied together or independently. There are many approaches to KV cache compression, broadly split into two categories: quantization (deserving its own post when I have a better handle on it) and pruning. Quantization converts floating-point values to lower-precision integers; pruning evicts unimportant tokens, channels, or layers, or allocates them a smaller cache budget. Let’s first look at the structure of the KV cache. where: B is the batch size N is the sequence length H is the number of attention heads L is the number of attention layers d is the embedding dimension Batch size is generally not amenable to optimization, so we focus on the four dimensions . We can compress along each of these four dimensions: N-dimension compression — compress along the sequence length by evicting unimportant tokens. Common strategies include: Random pruning: randomly select tokens to evict. Sliding window: retain only the most recent N tokens. H-dimension compression — compress along the head dimension by evicting unimportant heads. Some heads have little impact on the output, so they can be evicted or assigned a smaller cache budget. RazorAttention achieves >70% KV-cache reduction with no performance loss and no retraining by retaining the full cache only for a small set of retrieval heads, discarding remote tokens for the remaining heads, and recovering information through compensation tokens. It is compatible with FlashAttention. L-dimension compression — compress along the layer dimension by evicting unimportant layers. Some layers have little impact on the output and can be evicted or assigned a smaller cache budget. SqueezeAttention CAKE — CAKE frames KV cache eviction as a “cake-slicing” problem, combining per-layer spatial and temporal attention dynamics to allocate cache budgets in a cascaded, layer-aware fashion while introducing a new temporal eviction metric. It maintains performance using only 3.2% of the cache and significantly accelerates long-sequence inference. d-dimension compression — compress along the embedding dimension by removing less important dimensions. For example, a 256-dimensional embedding could be pruned to 128 dimensions by dropping the less salient ones. Low-rank projection — decompose the KV cache via low-rank factorization and cache only the low-rank representation, reconstructing the full-rank KV on the fly during attention computation. Palu — Palu applies low-rank decomposition to the projection layers that generate keys and values, caches only the low-rank intermediate representations, and dynamically reconstructs the full-dimensional KV at attention time, substantially reducing memory usage and improving inference efficiency. CPU offloading is another technique: evicted tokens’ KV cache entries are moved to CPU memory rather than discarded, reducing GPU memory pressure. KV Cache Computation OptimizationTopK selection: when computing attention scores, we can retain only the top-K scores, reducing the amount of computation needed for the weighted sum. The computational saving comes primarily from the weighted-sum step, since has a smaller effective dimension. The original cost is ; after selection it is , where is the sequence length, is the embedding dimension, and is the number of selected entries. (This counts the cost for a single token.) There are other selection strategies beyond top-K. For example, sampling-based approaches can preserve a statistical summary of the full context — MagicPIG uses LSH-based sampling together with CPU-offloaded heterogeneous execution to approximate attention with theoretical guarantees, providing an efficient, low-latency solution for very long-context LLM inference.

title: Patience Sorting
content: Patience SortingFrom Wikipedia: Patience sorting is a sorting algorithm, based on the card game “patience”, that sorts a list of elements by value according to the rules of the game. The goal of the game is to form as few piles as possible. Patience sorting can be used to solve the Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) problem. We can skip the proof here; for a detailed proof see the paper. All we need to know is that the number of piles equals the length of the longest increasing subsequence.

title: Segment Tree
content: A segment tree is a data structure commonly used to maintain range information. A segment tree can perform operations such as point update, range update, and range query (range sum, range max, range min) in time.

title: System Design Fundamentals
content: CAP TheoremThe CAP theorem, also known as Brewer’s theorem, states that a distributed database system can only guarantee two of the following three properties: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. A system that prioritizes availability over consistency may respond with stale data. Partition ToleranceIn CAP theory, Partition Tolerance refers to a system’s ability to continue serving requests even when a network partition occurs. A network partition is when the nodes in a system are split into two groups and the network communication between them is cut off. In this situation, a distributed system may exhibit one of two behaviors: Refuse to serve requests — the entire system becomes unavailable and invisible to users. Continue serving at the cost of consistency — the system remains visible to users but may return inconsistent data. Partition Tolerance means the system can tolerate network partitions and keep serving without completely breaking down. According to the CAP theorem, a system cannot simultaneously guarantee Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance — at most two can be satisfied at once. So a Partition-Tolerant system typically sacrifices data consistency to maintain service availability. This may mean allowing stale reads or tolerating conflicting data across partitions. This is an acceptable trade-off in many large-scale distributed systems. A classic example of Partition Tolerance is the DNS system. DNS uses a distributed tree structure where a single domain name is served by multiple DNS servers. When a network partition occurs, the following may happen: Users in certain regions cannot reach some DNS servers, but can still reach others and get a name resolution result. Different DNS servers return different resolution results (inconsistent IP addresses), but users still receive a response. This is the Partition Tolerance behavior DNS exhibits. When a network partition occurs, DNS chooses to accept the risk of returning inconsistent data rather than stopping all responses. Another example of Partition Tolerance is distributed caching systems like Memcached. When nodes lose contact with each other, data across different partitions may be inconsistent, but each partition can continue using its local cache — the overall system does not stop serving. These systems all adopt the design philosophy of “allow dirty reads” or “tolerate brief inconsistency” to achieve Partition Tolerance. For most applications, returning slightly stale or inconsistent data is still preferable to the entire system being completely unavailable. Modern Distributed System ComponentsLoad BalancerA load balancer is the entry point for web applications. It distributes incoming client traffic across different worker nodes/servers. It helps: Avoid overloading a single server Redirect requests to healthy servers when one is unavailable. Load balancers play an important role in enabling a system to scale horizontally. AWS provides the following load balancer services: Classic Load Balancer: primarily used to distribute traffic across EC2 instances Application Load Balancer: more flexible; the default choice. Network Load Balancer Gateway Load Balancer CDNA Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a fast file delivery service provided by a third party. By exposing a single endpoint, the CDN service automatically routes requests to the nearest server to fetch static files. It is mainly used to serve static assets such as HTML, JavaScript files, and images. It can also host other files like videos and archives. It can: Offload traffic from web servers Speed up file retrieval by fetching from the nearest server. CDNs require a TTL (Time to Live) to be configured. If the TTL is set too short, the cache will need to be refreshed from the origin frequently, increasing data transfer costs. If the TTL is set too long, clients may receive stale files. TTL should be set based on the system’s requirements. DNSThe Domain Name System (DNS) is a database that translates domain names into Internet Protocol (IP) addresses. DNS maps the names people use to locate websites to the IP addresses computers use to locate those websites. Web TierThe web tier primarily refers to web services. Web services mainly contain business logic — for example, fetching data from a database and returning it to the user, or submitting an order on behalf of a user. Ideally, the web tier should be stateless, as this makes it much easier to scale horizontally. Data TierThe data tier primarily refers to databases or persistent storage. “Persistent” means data is not lost even when the server goes down. In contrast, some in-memory caching systems will lose all data if the server restarts. As data has grown increasingly complex, a wide variety of database systems have been developed to accommodate different use cases. Relational databases NoSQL (Not Only SQL) Describing databases in full detail here would be too ambitious — we will cover them in a dedicated post. Cache TierThe cache tier exists because querying a database is an expensive operation. Some requests can also be expensive in other ways, such as running a model for computation. Thanks to the principle of locality, we know that processors tend to repeatedly access the same set of memory locations over a short period of time. This means the same data may be needed multiple times within a short window, making a cache tier very useful in production systems. The cache operates as middleware within the system and can be scaled independently. It also introduces its own set of challenges, such as cache stampede, cache misses, and data synchronization. Like the data tier, we will cover it in a dedicated post. Message QueueSometimes we may wonder about service call chains — how do these subsystems scale independently? For example, if Service A tries to call Service B and Service B is unavailable at the moment, Service A must wait, or the request from the client will be lost. We might want something that abstracts the input producers from the result consumers. This is where message queues come in. A message queue acts as a temporary storage service. Producers can publish messages to the MQ regardless of whether consumers are running. At the same time, consumers can consume messages from the MQ regardless of whether producers are running.

title: Union-Find (DSU)
content: Each set is represented by a tree, with its root as the representative. find walks up parent pointers to the root; union attaches one root under another. With path compression and union by rank, each operation is amortized — the inverse Ackermann function, practically , essentially . Intuition — one tree per setImagine a group of people, each pointing to their “boss”. To ask “are A and B in the same group?”, both climb up their boss pointers until they reach someone who points to themselves (the gang leader / root). Same root → same group. To merge two gangs, make one boss acknowledge the other as their new boss. The entire data structure is just one array: parent[i] = i's parent, where root nodes satisfy parent[i] == i. Two primitives: find(x): walk up parent pointers and return the root of x’s set. union(x, y): find both roots rx and ry; if they differ, set parent[rx] = ry. The naive version can degenerate into a chain, making find . Two optimizations fix this: Path compression: during find, on the way back up, attach every node on the path directly to the root — the tree gets flatter with use. Union by rank: attach the shorter tree under the taller one to prevent chaining. Used together, each operation is amortized . Animation — watch the tree grow, watch paths flattenThe animation below executes 5 union operations to connect 6 nodes (green = root), then click Run Find to watch path compression instantly pull all nodes directly under the root — the tree goes from having multiple levels to nearly flat in one shot. Watch carefully: before any union, every node is its own root; during union, root attaches to root; after Find, the whole tree is nearly just two levels deep. Template — path compression only (sufficient for 90% of problems) Three common mistakes: union must find both roots before merging — you can’t just do p[x] = y. That attaches a node directly, orphaning the rest of x’s original set. Only roots represent their entire set. Path compression goes inside find — don’t forget it. The recursive version is cleanest; the iterative version is slightly faster and doesn’t risk stack overflow. cnt decrements only when an actual merge occurs (rx != ry). Advanced — union by rank / weighted union-findUnion by rankTrack the “rank” (a rough measure of height) of each tree; attach the shorter tree under the taller one: In practice, path compression alone is enough. Only add union by rank when you need a rigorous complexity proof or the problem has tight constant-factor constraints. Weighted union-findEdges carry weights representing a relationship between two nodes (difference, ratio, distance, …). During find, accumulate edge weights along the path; during union, derive new edge weights from the known relationship. Classic problem: LC 399. Evaluate Division — a/b = 2, b/c = 3, deduce a/c. Use “ratio” as the edge weight and multiply during find. Three use cases — connectivity / component count / offline time-reversal1. Check connectivity: two nodes with the same root → connected. Redundant connection (LC 684): add edges one by one; the first one that hits two nodes with the same root is the redundant edge. 2. Count connected components: the final uf.cnt is the answer. Number of Provinces (LC 547) and Number of Islands (LC 200) are direct templates. 3. Offline “time-reversal”: Union-Find only supports merging, not splitting. Problem asks you to delete edges / remove nodes? Read all operations first, then add edges in reverse from the final state — deletions become additions. Classic problem: LC 803. Bricks Falling When Hit. The third use case is the key to “hard” interview problems — whenever you see “deletions in order”, immediately think about whether you can process it offline in reverse. Classic problemsWarm-up (nail one, know the whole category): LC 547. Number of Provinces — bare-bones component count LC 200. Number of Islands — 2D grid mapped to 1D id (i*n+j) LC 684. Redundant Connection — add edge, same root = answer LC 990. Satisfiability of Equality Equations — process == first, then != Advanced: LC 128. Longest Consecutive Sequence — union x with x+1 LC 399. Evaluate Division — weighted union-find template LC 721. Accounts Merge — use emails as nodes, union all emails within the same account LC 803. Bricks Falling When Hit — time-reversal classic LC 685. Redundant Connection II — directed graph variant, requires case analysis Memory aidOne sentence: Set is tree, root is representative; find finds the root, union joins roots. Three things to memorize: Item Key point Data parent[] one-dimensional array; root satisfies p[i]==i find Walk up parent pointers to root, attach to root on the way back (path compression) union Find both roots first, join root to root, cnt -= 1 Quick decision guide: “How many connected components / are these in the same group” → Union-Find “Add edges in order” → online Union-Find “Delete edges / nodes in order” → offline reverse + Union-Find Edge has weight (ratio, difference) → weighted Union-Find Get the template to the point where you can write it from memory in 30 seconds, and 90% of connectivity problems are just applying the template + figuring out “what are the nodes, and when do we union”.

title: Randomized Algorithms
content: Weighted random()random() is an important function that returns a random number with equal probability. Weighted random() asks us to generate random numbers with different weights. One naive approach is to create an array of elements, randomly set of them to , to , to , and to .We can then pick a random index from to and return the value at that index. However, this approach has an obvious drawback: it consumes a lot of memory and takes significant time to initialize. Can we compress this information instead of building the full array? Yes. Consider the prefix-sum array of a weight array of size (0-indexed): For the given array we have and . We can extract intervals from , each with length proportional to its weight. This means that if we pick a random index , the probability that falls into is . Fisher-Yates ShuffleThe Fisher–Yates shuffle algorithm generates a uniformly random permutation of an array. The key principle is that every pair of indices must have an equal probability of being swapped. In this implementation, for each we pick a random to swap with. Note that itself is included, since there is always a chance the element stays in place. By doing this, we cover all pairs , and as we iterate from down to , we cover every possible pair.

title: Docker Memo
content: DockerfileA Dockerfile is a text file containing the definition of a container image, which can be used to launch containers. This definition includes commands, a base image, configuration, and more. In this post we’ll walk through each component and discuss when to use each one. Let’s get started. Docker ImagesBefore diving into the individual components, you might want to know what a Docker image actually is. Reference: Structure of an Image An image is a read-only template with instructions for creating a Docker container. Often, an image is based on another image, with some additional customization. –Docker Official Docs A Docker image can contain many files. To get a closer look, let’s pull one. From the output above we can see that we pulled the python:alpine3.18 image from Docker Hub, and that this image has 5 layers. Base Image / Parent ImageIn most Dockerfiles, the first line you’ll see is FROM {base image}, for example FROM python:3.8. This line defines the base image for the image we’re building. A base image may itself consist of one or more layers. RUNThe RUN command can be used to execute commands such as installing packages, downloading files, and so on. One important thing to note is that each command adds a new layer on top of the existing image. Combining multiple commands into a single RUN instruction is a common trick to reduce image size and minimize the number of layers. CMDCMD describes the default parameters or command for the container. Users can easily override the default command at runtime. ENTRYPOINTENTRYPOINT also defines a command that always runs, meaning it cannot be overridden. ENTRYPOINT can be used to ensure that a specific command is always executed when the container starts, even if the user tries to override it. COPYCOPY can be used to copy local files into the container image, and nothing more. ADDThe ADD command also allows files/folders to be copied from the host into the image. It additionally supports tarball extraction and remote URL fetching. In general, ADD is preferred over COPY. Now let’s look at an example of using ADD in a Dockerfile. Suppose we are in a folder /tmp/app that contains the following files: And we write the following command in the Dockerfile: The command above copies the file /tmp/app/server.js (host path) to /tmp/server.js (container image path). Note that the first argument must be within the build context — the context can be understood as the path from which the docker build command is executed. VOLUMEA volume can be thought of as persistent data storage for a Docker container. The following command means that for any container started from this image, the /var/www/html directory on the host will be mounted to /var/www/html inside the container. Any changes made to that directory inside the container will be reflected on the host, and vice versa. DiveDive is a very useful tool for analyzing container images. It lets you see the commands for each layer and the corresponding changes reflected in the filesystem. References OCI Image Manifest Specification Docker FilesystemDocker supports many configurable filesystems; the most commonly used and recommended one today is overlay2, which offers good performance and stability. If you list Docker’s DataRoot directory, you’ll find many subdirectories, one of which is overlay2 — that’s where overlay2 stores its data. Inside you’ll find many subdirectories whose names are hash strings. These directories are the storage locations for the filesystems of individual images; each one is a layer, which could be a layer of an image, a layer of a currently running container, or a layer of a volume. The hash in each folder name is not the layer’s sha256; it’s a short ID — the diff directory name assigned by Overlay2 on disk for that layer. Key points of the Overlay2 storage structure: Image metadata & LayerDB /var/lib/docker/image/overlay2/imagedb/content/sha256/<digest> /var/lib/docker/image/overlay2/layerdb/sha256/<digest>/cache-idThe content of this file (a short ID such as 36849485abab637c0…) is the diff directory name that Overlay2 assigned on disk for that layer. Overlay2 working directories /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<cache-id>/diffStores the actual file contents for that layer. /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<cache-id>/mergedThe mount point when a container is running; on read, LowerDir + UpperDir are overlaid here.

title: Rate Limiting Algorithms
content: A rate limiter is a critical component in distributed systems, commonly used to guard against DDoS attacks or malicious requests.In this post we introduce several algorithms that can be used for rate limiting. Token BucketA token bucket is a container with a predefined capacity. Tokens are added to the bucket at a fixed rate. Once the bucket is full, no more tokens are added. As shown below, the token bucket has a capacity of 4 and the refiller adds 2 tokens per second. Once the bucket is full, excess tokens overflow and are discarded. The token bucket can handle burst traffic and ensures the rate never exceeds the preset capacity. Leaky BucketThe leaky bucket is similar to the token bucket, but it behaves like a FIFO queue. The leaky bucket has a processing rate that determines how many requests it can handle per second. When a request arrives, it first checks whether the queue is full; if not, the request is added to the queue, otherwise the request is dropped.Requests in the queue are drained and processed at a fixed time interval. One drawback of the leaky bucket is its FIFO processing order: if the queue is already filled with old requests, newly arriving requests will be rate-limited.

title: Backtracking Template
content: Backtracking = DFS on a decision tree: choose → recurse → undo. Every “enumerate all possibilities” problem uses the same template; the only difference is how you build the “choices list”. IntuitionImagine standing at every fork in a maze doing one thing: place a small stone to mark “I came from this path”, then walk forward; when you hit a dead end or find an answer, retrace your steps and pick up the stone. That stone-pickup step is “backtracking” — it lets you reuse the same path list over and over, instead of copying the state at every level. So backtracking has exactly three actions: Make a choice: path.append(c) Recurse: enter the next level Undo: path.pop() Step 3 is symmetric to step 1. Miss one, and the state gets dirty; add an extra one, and the result is wrong. The Decision Tree Is the CoreSubsets, permutations, combinations, partitions, N-queens, sudoku — they look very different, but once you draw the “decision tree”, you’ll see: backtracking is always DFS on a tree; only the shape of the tree differs. Subsets: each level decides “include/exclude the current element”; every node is an answer (leaves and internal nodes alike) Permutations: each level picks one from “what’s left unused”; collect only leaves, needs used[] Combinations: each level picks from start onward, avoiding duplicates; collect only leaves, needs start Click [Next Step] to watch how path evolves as the DFS advances: choose 1 → path=[1], then choose 2 → path=[1,2], hit the bottom → copy snapshot into ans, then pop back to [1], continue to the sibling node. The second animation places permutations and combinations side by side so you can visually see: permutations branch to “all remaining” at every internal node, combinations only branch to “elements further right”, so one tree is fat and full, the other narrow and lean. TemplateLock in this snippet — every variant just changes “choices” and the termination condition: Three pairs of operations that must be symmetric: path.append ↔ path.pop used[i] = True ↔ used[i] = False Any “mark dirty” state modification ↔ restore Three Problem Families Problem choices When to collect Count Subsets range(start, n) every node Permutations all + filter via used[] leaves (len==n) Combinations range(start, n) leaves (len==k) Quick mnemonic: subsets collect all nodes, permutations use leaves + used, combinations use leaves + start. Deduplication PatternWhen there are duplicate elements, sort first, then skip duplicate values at the same level: Why i > start and not i > 0? Because we want sibling deduplication, not parent-child deduplication — i == start is the first choice at this level; if it equals “the previous one”, that previous one is actually a parent node, not a sibling, so we must not skip it. Classic Problems 78. Subsets — bare subsets template 46. Permutations — permutations template, practice used[] 77. Combinations — combinations template, practice advancing start 39. Combination Sum — elements can be reused, recurse with i instead of i+1 90. Subsets II / 47. Permutations II — practice the i > start deduplication pattern 51. N-Queens / 37. Sudoku Solver — backtracking + complex pruning, state restoration becomes the main challenge 131. Palindrome Partitioning — choices are “split points” rather than elements, same template logic Approach: first figure out what the decision tree looks like, then apply the template. When stuck, hand-draw the first two levels. Common Pitfalls Forgetting path[:] — ans ends up full of references to the same list, which is empty after backtracking completes Asymmetric append/pop — missing one pop causes state contamination Using start for permutations or used for combinations — the decision tree shape is simply wrong Forgetting to sort before deduplication — i > start && nums[i]==nums[i-1] won’t work path.append before the recursive call but pop in the wrong position, corrupting state before recursion finishes ComplexityTime complexity = number of decision tree nodes × work per node. The worst case is determined by leaf count: permutations , subsets , combinations . The extra factor of or comes from the path[:] copy. One-sentence summary: Backtracking isn’t an algorithm — it’s the codification of “DFS on a decision tree while restoring state”. Draw the tree and the template snaps into place.

title: MLSys Study Notes 1
content: 1. GPU ECC (Error-Correcting Code) Principle: Generates redundant parity bits in VRAM for every N bits of data. The most common scheme is SECDED (Single-Error Correction, Double-Error Detection). Implementation: Enterprise-grade cards (Tesla/Quadro/A100, AMD Instinct) enable ECC by default; consumer cards mostly disable it or don’t support it. ECC logic is integrated in the memory controller and is transparent to user programs. Pros and cons: Pro: prevents silent data corruption from bit flips in VRAM; corrected/uncorrected error counts are monitorable. Con: roughly 12.5% VRAM overhead, 5–12% bandwidth and latency penalty. Enabling and monitoring (NVIDIA example): 2. NVIDIA Persistence Mode Purpose: Keeps the GPU context initialized even when no client is attached, reducing startup latency for short jobs and maintaining a stable P-state. Commands: Note: Slight increase in power consumption; pair with the nvidia-persistenced daemon to survive reboots. 3. Ring Reduce (All-Reduce) Algorithm Overview Segmentation (Scatter): Split the tensor evenly into N chunks; each round passes one chunk clockwise around the ring. Reduce-Scatter: After N–1 rounds, each chunk has been accumulated from all nodes and lands on exactly one owner node. All-Gather: Broadcast each chunk’s result back around the ring in the same fashion so every node holds the complete aggregated value. Communication cost: Reduce-Scatter: each node sends/receives data All-Gather: same Total for All-Reduce: 4. Reduce-Scatter Worked Example (4 Nodes, Vector Length 4) Initial data Segmentation rule: index 0 → Seg 0, 1 → Seg 1, …, 3 → Seg 3. 3 rounds of accumulation: Segment Round 1 result Round 2 result Round 3 result Owner node Global sum 0 5 + 1 = 6 9 + 6 = 15 13 + 15 = 28 Node 3 28 1 10 + 6 = 16 14 + 16 = 30 2 + 30 = 32 Node 0 32 2 15 + 11 = 26 3 + 26 = 29 7 + 29 = 36 Node 1 36 3 4 + 16 = 20 8 + 20 = 28 12 + 28 = 40 Node 2 40 Result: each node holds the global sum for its assigned segment, ready for the subsequent All-Gather phase.

title: Model Quantization
content: Model QuantizationQuantization is a technique used to reduce model size and speed up inference. The core idea is to convert model weights from a higher-precision data type such as FP32 to a lower-precision data type such as FP16/INT8.There are also more aggressive quantization approaches, like quantizing weights down to INT4, or even binarization — BitNet is a prime example of how far this can go. One thing worth noting: quantizing to INT8 and FP8 are not the same thing. INT8 is an integer type, while FP8 is a floating-point type; they have different representable ranges and precision. In general, INT8 offers better throughput — integer arithmetic is faster and more power-efficient than floating-point arithmetic — but its representable range is narrower. There are both upsides and downsides to quantizing a model. Benefits Reduced model size: A quantized model occupies less memory, loads faster, and has a smaller memory footprint. Faster inference: A quantized model can run on faster hardware. On a GPU, for example, quantized models can perform matrix multiplications more quickly. Lower power consumption: A quantized model can run on lower-power hardware, such as mobile devices, and can sustain longer operation. Drawbacks Accuracy loss: A quantized model may experience some accuracy degradation, especially when quantizing to INT8, where the loss can be significant. Added complexity: Quantization may introduce additional computation, such as the quantize and dequantize steps, which increases the overall complexity of the model. Quantization MethodsSymmetric QuantizationComputing the scale:Dequantization: Asymmetric QuantizationComputing the scale and zero_point, where the original tensor range is [x_min, x_max] and the quantized tensor range is [q_min, q_max]: Model Quantization Practice Here is some additional context on PTQ and QAT:Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) Definition: After training is complete, use a small calibration dataset (typically a few hundred to a few thousand samples) to compute quantization parameters (scale, zero-point) for each layer’s weights and activations, then convert the floating-point model to a low-bitwidth integer model. Pros: Fast, no retraining or fine-tuning required Straightforward to implement, suitable for resource-constrained scenarios Cons: Higher quantization error, especially noticeable for sensitive layers or small models Not robust to asymmetric or long-tail distributions The Role of the Calibration SetThe calibration set plays several key roles in static quantization: Estimating activation distributions: Run one forward pass of the model over the calibration set, letting Observers collect numerical statistics at each node. These statistics are used to compute optimal quantization parameters downstream. Determining quantization parameters: Use the collected statistics to compute scale and zero-point. Methods such as Min-Max or histogram-based approaches can be used to balance accuracy and dynamic range. Representative samples: The calibration set should cover typical inputs for the target application to ensure the quantized model performs well in real-world scenarios. Usually 100–1000 samples suffice, balancing statistical stability against calibration time. Static vs. dynamic quantization: Static quantization requires a calibration set but yields faster inference. Dynamic quantization requires no calibration, but must compute activation quantization parameters at each inference step. An example of dynamic quantization is shown below. Because scale and zero-point differ for each batch, they must be computed at inference time from the current batch. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) Definition: Introduce quantization simulation (FakeQuant) operators during training or fine-tuning so that the model simulates low-precision arithmetic in the forward pass while continuing to update parameters in the backward pass, allowing it to adapt to quantization-induced error. Pros: Can significantly recover or even exceed PTQ accuracy More friendly to complex distributions and custom strategies Cons: Requires additional training or fine-tuning overhead (1–5 epochs) More complex to implement, as it requires inserting FakeQuant layers into the training framework Current ResearchLLM-Specific PTQ Methods GPTQ performs one-shot weight quantization based on approximate second-order information, enabling 3–4-bit quantization of a 175B-parameter model on a single GPU with almost no accuracy loss. AWQ uses activation-aware per-channel scaling to protect only 1% of salient weights, dramatically reducing quantization error and enabling efficient 4-bit compression and acceleration on multimodal LLMs. SmoothQuant migrates activation outliers to weights offline to achieve W8A8 PTQ, delivering up to 1.56× speedup and 2× memory reduction on LLMs. The latest SmoothQuant+ pushes PTQ to 4-bit group-wise weight quantization for near-lossless LLM deployment. Model Export and Deploy Method Export Format / Tool Supported Hardware Pros Cons TorchScript .pt (TorchScript) CPU/GPU Native PyTorch support, no extra dependencies, easy to load in C++/Python Depends on libtorch; GPU performance lags behind dedicated inference frameworks ONNX + ONNX Runtime .onnx CPU/GPU (multi-platform) Cross-framework, multi-language deployment, mature ecosystem Limited custom-op support; performance depends on Runtime plugins ONNX + TensorRT .trt NVIDIA GPU Best-in-class GPU inference performance, automatic mixed-precision and quantization optimization NVIDIA only; export and deployment workflow is complex TensorFlow → TFLite .tflite Mobile/embedded devices Lightweight, low latency, small footprint; suitable for mobile and IoT Operator support is limited; requires calibration data and may degrade accuracy OpenVINO .xml + .bin Intel CPU/VPU Unified multi-hardware deployment, deep optimization for Intel hardware Intel only; steeper learning curve Apache TVM .so / .dll CPU/GPU/custom accelerators Highly customizable compilation pipeline, multi-platform and multi-backend support Complex to compile and tune; requires deep knowledge of the framework

title: Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning
content: LLM Training StagesCurrently the training of Large Language Models (LLMs) can be divided into three stages: Pre-trainingThe pre-training stage does one thing on a very large corpus of text: predict the next token. Fine-tuningFine-tuning is essentially the same as pre-training — predicting the next token on a specific dataset. The prompts are different though; they are structured around different tasks, such as conversational data or text-classification data.Examples: Conversational data: User: Hello, how are you? Assistant: I am fine, thank you! Text-classification data: Text: I love this movie. Label: Positive RLHFRLHF is a fine-tuning method that uses reinforcement learning to optimize the model’s generation quality. Anthropic’s approach is to train a reward model on a small amount of human-preference data; this reward model evaluates human feedback and scores the model’s outputs, which are then used to optimize the model. Parameter Efficient Fine-TuningParameter Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) targets the fine-tuning stage and is designed to address the problem of fine-tuning requiring too many trainable parameters. AdapterAn Adapter is a PEFT method that inserts a small network into each layer of the Transformer. The adapter itself can be a simple MLP or a more complex network. LoRALoRA is a PEFT method that approximates the parameters of each linear layer in the Transformer using a low-rank matrix decomposition. Here is a hyperparameter, typically set to a small value such as . This dramatically reduces the number of parameters in — from to . LoRA has spawned a large body of follow-on work focused on designing better structures for and , choosing better values of , and selecting which weight matrices to update. On the ML Systems side, a number of papers address how to efficiently serve multiple LoRA adapters simultaneously — for example in multi-tenant scenarios — and how to train LoRA adapters for multiple tasks jointly, as in Punica.

title: BFS (Breadth-First Search)
content: One sentence: BFS = treat the graph like a pond, drop a stone at the start, and watch the ripples expand outward ring by ring. The first ring that reaches the target is the shortest number of steps (unit edge weights). IntuitionImagine you’re standing at the entrance of a maze and shout into it. Sound doesn’t “pick one path and go deep” — it fills the current ring of air simultaneously, then the next ring. BFS is exactly this propagation process written as code: Current wavefront (nodes in the queue) = all nodes exactly steps from the start Next wavefront = all neighbors of the current wavefront (excluding already-visited ones) The at which the target first gets swept into the wavefront is the answer DFS is “go as deep as possible down one path before backtracking”; BFS is “march in step, advance simultaneously”. Whenever the question is “fewest steps”, it’s almost always BFS. The animation below draws these ripple layers. Click [Start] to watch how the queue swallows the grid layer by layer and which step it hits the target; switch to the second animation to see “multi-source BFS” — multiple stones dropped at once, ripples stop when they meet. Template (memorize this one) Three non-negotiable details (get any one wrong and you get WA or TLE): for _ in range(len(q)) — freeze len(q) first, then loop. Otherwise you’re dequeuing and enqueuing simultaneously and can’t tell which nodes belong to the current layer. visited.add(nxt) at enqueue time, not dequeue time. Marking at dequeue time means the same node gets pushed by all 4 neighbors, causing queue bloat (the animation makes this very visible: relax this constraint and the orange cells keep flashing repeatedly). step += 1 goes outside the for loop, not inside. step is a layer number, not a node number. VariantsGrid BFSThe most frequently tested form. Replace neighbors with a directions array: Multi-Source BFSMore than one starting point? Push all of them into the initial queue at once. This is equivalent to adding a virtual super-source outside that connects to every start with edge weight 0. The template doesn’t change at all — just change the initialization. Classic problems: Rotting Oranges (animation 2), 01 Matrix (distance to nearest 0). 0-1 BFSEdge weights are only 0 or 1. Replace the plain queue with a deque: weight-0 edges use appendleft, weight-1 edges use append. O(V+E) instead of Dijkstra’s O(E log V). Bidirectional BFSExpand from both start and end simultaneously; each round always expand the smaller frontier, return when the two sides meet. Search space drops from to — exponential halving. Requirements: target is known, neighbors can be reversed. Typical problems: 127 Word Ladder, 752 Open the Lock. BFS vs DFS — How to Choose Fewest steps / minimum operations → BFS All paths / permutations & combinations / connected component size → DFS Topological sort → either works (Kahn’s is BFS) Classic ProblemsWarm-up: 102. Binary Tree Level Order Traversal — the purest BFS; checks whether you’ve memorized the template 200. Number of Islands — grid BFS for connected components 994. Rotting Oranges — the canonical multi-source BFS problem Advanced: 127. Word Ladder — implicit graph BFS; bidirectional BFS for speedup 752. Open the Lock — state-space BFS 542. 01 Matrix — think in reverse: multi-source BFS starting from all 0s 1293. Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination — add one dimension to state: (r, c, remaining_eliminations) 847. Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes — bitmask state compression + BFS Memory Aid & Common PitfallsRemember three images: Pond ripples — the essence of BFS. The ripple radius at which the target is first reached = the answer. Frozen len(q) — the only way to distinguish “this layer” from “the next layer”. Mark at enqueue — not at dequeue, not at dequeue, not at dequeue. Common traps: Putting step += 1 inside the inner for loop → answer becomes “how many nodes were visited”, wildly wrong. Using BFS when edge weights aren’t 1 → wrong answer. Use Dijkstra or 0-1 BFS. Forgetting bounds checking in grid problems → IndexError or wrapping to the other side. Using BFS for “can we reach this node?” → not wrong, but wasteful; DFS is shorter to write. BFS is only mandatory when you need the shortest path. Exercises Why can BFS guarantee the shortest path (when edge weights are 1)? Layer-by-layer expansion ensures that nodes at layer are exactly distance from the start (no less: if they were closer, an earlier layer would have visited them; no more: adjacent layers differ by 1). The layer number when the target is first visited is the shortest distance. What's the difference between "mark at enqueue" vs "mark at dequeue"? Mark at enqueue: each node enters the queue at most once; queue size = O(V).Mark at dequeue: the same node can be pushed multiple times by different neighbors (in a grid, all 4 directions might push the same cell), bloating the queue to O(E), wasting both time and space. Both approaches produce correct results, but the latter frequently TLEs. When is bidirectional BFS applicable? Requirements: both start and end are known + neighbors can be traversed in reverse. Exponentially shrinks the search space ().Not applicable: target is unknown (e.g., “find the farthest node”), neighbors are one-directional (directed graph with no reverse graph available).

title: Bit Manipulation
content: Rarely shows up in interviews, but when it does, it’s pure memorization. Learn these cold and they’re free points. 5 Must-Know Operations Operation Meaning n & 1 Get the lowest bit (check odd/even) n >> 1 Right-shift by one (divide by 2) n & (n-1) Clear the lowest set bit n & -n Extract the lowest set bit (lowbit) n ^ n == 0 XOR of a number with itself is 0 Three Core Properties of XOR a ^ 0 = a — any number XOR 0 equals itself a ^ a = 0 — any number XOR itself equals 0 Commutative and associative — order doesn’t matter, grouping is flexible Put these three together: XOR a bunch of numbers and all pairs cancel out, leaving only the unpaired one. 6 Must-Memorize Tricks1. Check Power of Two A power of two has exactly one set bit. After n&(n-1) clears it, the result is 0. 2. Popcount (Count Set Bits) 3. Enumerate Subsets (bitmask) 4. Enumerate Subsets of a Subset Decrement by 1 then AND with mask — automatically jumps to the next valid subset. 5. Swap Two Numbers (trivia only — don’t use in interviews) 6. Find Two Numbers That Appear Only Once At the lowbit position, a and b must differ (otherwise XOR at that bit would not be 1), so they end up in different groups. State Compression DP Template (n<=20)Use an integer mask to represent which elements in a set have been selected. A 1 at bit i means element i is included. Time complexity is O(2^n * n) or O(3^n), so n is generally capped at 20. Animation: Bit Operation VisualizerUsing n = 13 (binary 1101) as an example, follow the animation to see two things: n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit entirely, while n & -n leaves only the lowest set bit. After watching, come back and re-read the 6 tricks above — muscle memory will kick in. Think-It-Through Questions Why does n&(n-1) clear the lowest set bit? Explain from a binary perspective. Say the lowest set bit of n is at position k. Then bits 0 through k-1 of n are all 0, and bit k is 1. What n-1 does: bit k becomes 0, and bits 0 through k-1 all become 1 (due to borrowing). So n & (n-1): bit k gives 1&0=0 (cleared!), bits 0 through k-1 give 0&1=0, and all higher bits are unchanged. Why is state compression DP only suitable for n The number of states is 2^n. At n=20 that’s 1 million states — just barely manageable. At n=25 it’s 33 million, at n=30 it’s 1 billion — both memory and time blow up. In practice, interview problems usually cap at n<=16; n=20 is the extreme limit. In "find two numbers that appear only once," why does lowbit split the two numbers into different groups? xor_all = a ^ b. The lowbit extracts the first bit where a and b differ. At that bit, a is 1 and b is 0 (or vice versa). Partitioning by that bit guarantees a and b end up in different groups. All the other paired numbers have both copies in the same group, so they XOR away. LeetCode ProblemsWarm-up: 136. Single Number, 191. Number of 1 Bits, 338. Counting Bits. Advanced: 137. Single Number II, 260. Single Number III, 421. Maximum XOR, 847. Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes, 698. Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets.

title: Difference Array and Prefix Sum
content: Difference array = the inverse of prefix sum. A range update [l, r] += k that would take with a loop becomes two single-point writes diff[l] += k; diff[r+1] -= k in . Finish with one prefix-sum pass to recover the array. Remember that one sentence and you’ll never write a loop for bulk range additions again. Intuition — The Inverse of Prefix SumThink of “prefix sum” and “difference” as a pair of functions: Operation Formula Analogy Prefix sum pre[i] = pre[i-1] + a[i] Integration ∫ Difference diff[i] = a[i] - a[i-1] Differentiation d/dx The two are mutual inverses: difference then prefix sum = original array. This isn’t a coincidence — it’s just the discrete version of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. So an immediate idea emerges: since modifying a range of the original array is expensive ( points to touch), operate on the difference array instead — the cost is just two endpoints. One final prefix-sum pass “materializes” all accumulated modifications at once. Why Two EndpointsLet the original array be and its difference be . After applying , the new differences are: changes: increases by while stays the same, so . changes: stays the same while increases by , so . Interior positions : both neighbors increased by , so the difference is unchanged. The entire range update leaves a mark at only two endpoints. That’s where the time savings come from. Animation — Follow the EndpointsThe animation below uses an array of length 8 to demonstrate three range additions: [1,4]+3, [2,6]+2, [5,7]+1. Each click of “Next” drops a pair of endpoints (green +, red -) onto diff; after all six drops, a single prefix-sum pass reconstructs the final result array. Key observation: during the modification phase, the middle elements are never touched — only positions l and r+1 change; the restoration phase finishes in a single linear scan. Template — Python Three easy mistakes: Allocate diff with n+1 elements to avoid the if r+1 < n guard. Closed interval [l, r] maps to diff[r+1] -= k; if the problem gives a half-open interval [l, r), use diff[r] -= k instead. If the original array is not all zeros, compute its difference array first to get the initial diff, then layer the operations on top. The Duality with Prefix Sum One is “read-only,” the other is “write-only.” The two are duals — choose based on whether the problem has more queries or more updates. When queries and updates alternate, reach for a segment tree. 2-D Difference Array — Bulk Update on RectanglesExtend the two-endpoint idea from one dimension to the four corners of a rectangle. To add to the sub-matrix : Recover with 2-D prefix sum: a[i][j] = a[i-1][j] + a[i][j-1] - a[i-1][j-1] + diff[i][j]. Template problem: LC 2536. Increment Submatrices by One. Mnemonic: top-left +, two outer sides of bottom-right -, outer corner of bottom-right +. This is the strict dual of the 2-D prefix sum inclusion-exclusion formula. Classic Problem — 1109. Corporate Flight Bookings There are n flights. bookings[i] = [first, last, seats] means seats seats are booked on each flight from first to last (inclusive). Return the total seats booked for each flight. Plug straight into the template; note that the problem uses 1-indexed flights: Time complexity where is the number of bookings. The brute-force approach is and will TLE on larger inputs. Other must-solve problems: LC 370. Range Addition — bare template LC 1094. Car Pooling — model pick-ups and drop-offs as ±, scan once to check capacity LC 1854. Maximum Population Year — 1-D sweep line is just a difference array LC 1674. Minimum Moves to Make Array Complementary — difference + enumeration; feel the power of “tracking changes” MnemonicsOne sentence: update the range’s two endpoints; recover with a prefix sum. Three contrasting pairs: Dimension Prefix Sum Difference Array Solves Range query Range update Operation Accumulate Take difference Calculus analogy Integration Differentiation Decision rules: Read-only (queries only) → prefix sum Write-then-read (updates then one final query, offline) → difference array Interleaved reads and writes (online) → segment tree Whenever you see “add/subtract a constant across a range” followed by “output or query the result once,” your reflex should be diff[l] += k; diff[r+1] -= k. Can’t go wrong.

title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
content: Dijkstra = BFS + greedy. Swap the FIFO queue for a priority queue, and at each step pick the unvisited node with the smallest known distance to relax its neighbors. One precondition: non-negative edge weights — because once a node’s distance is finalized, we never revisit it. Intuition — Why “BFS + Greedy”BFS is correct on unit-weight graphs: expand layer by layer from the source, and the first time you reach a node is the shortest path. This works because FIFO guarantees “earlier enqueued means smaller distance.” What about unequal edge weights? Upgrade the queue to a priority queue (min-heap) and still pull out the node with the smallest current distance each time. That node’s distance is then finalized forever — anyone trying to reach it via a detour can only be farther (since all edge weights ≥ 0). That’s where the greedy insight comes from. One-liner: “pick the nearest unfinalized node, relax its neighbors.” That’s the whole algorithm. Why Negative Edges Break ItThe greedy foundation is “finalized nodes are never updated again.” Once a negative edge exists, a longer-looking path might actually be shorter, and a distance we already finalized could be invalidated. Counter-example: Starting from A, Dijkstra pops B first and finalizes dist[B]=1, then never looks at B again. But the true shortest path is A→C→B = 5 + (-10) = -5. The algorithm has already moved on and can’t go back. All weights 1 → plain BFS. Weights 0/1 → 0-1 BFS (deque). Negative weights → Bellman-Ford / SPFA. Animation — Walk Through the Heap PopsThe animation below starts from node 0. Focus on two things: Which node is popped at each step — it is always the minimum in the current dist array among unfinalized nodes. Which cells turn yellow after relaxation — only when “new distance < old distance” is an update applied; updated nodes are pushed back into the heap. After watching once, compare it against “BFS expanding layer by layer”: Dijkstra does not go by layers — it finalizes nodes in ascending order of known distance. Template — Python with heapq Three key implementation details: Store (distance, node) in the heap — tuple comparison starts from the first element, so it automatically sorts by distance. if d > dist[u]: continue — the heap may contain multiple stale entries for the same node (Python’s heapq doesn’t support decrease-key, so we just push again). This line skips outdated entries; correctness holds without it, but skipping prevents a lot of wasted relaxation. Update dist[v] before pushing — don’t “push first, check later”; that causes the heap to blow up. Time complexity: . Variants — Different Skins, Same Skeleton Variant Change When to use A* Heap key becomes g(n) + h(n), where h is a heuristic estimate to the goal Single-source single-target with geometric/distance prior, e.g., game pathfinding Bidirectional Dijkstra Run Dijkstra from both source and target, meet in the middle Single-source single-target, prune large amounts of irrelevant search 0-1 BFS Weights only 0/1; replace heap with deque — weight-0 edges to front, weight-1 to back 0/1 weights, Layered graph / state expansion Nodes become (node, state), e.g., remaining free passes State affects transition cost Bellman-Ford No heap; V rounds of relaxing all edges Negative weights, SPFA Queue-based Bellman-Ford, faster on average Negative weights, sparse graphs Remember the skeleton: “what data structure maintains the frontier” — FIFO is BFS, min-heap is Dijkstra, deque is 0-1 BFS, scan-all is Bellman-Ford. Classic ProblemsWarm-up: 743. Network Delay Time — template 1631. Path With Minimum Effort — path weight becomes max rather than sum 787. Cheapest Flights Within K Stops — state expansion (node, stops) Advanced: 1514. Path with Maximum Probability — max-heap + log transform (product becomes sum) 1928. Minimum Cost to Reach Destination in Time — (cost, time, node) dual-dimension state 2045. Second Minimum Time to Reach Destination — maintain the two smallest distances 1976. Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination — Dijkstra while counting paths 407. Trapping Rain Water II — heap + “pour water inward” from the boundary Mnemonics / Common PitfallsMnemonic: one sentence — “pick the nearest unfinalized node, relax its neighbors.” Whenever you see “non-negative weights + single-source shortest path,” your reflex should be heapq. Common pitfalls: Not skipping stale entries: omitting if d > dist[u]: continue causes TLE. Negative weights: see a negative edge, switch to Bellman-Ford immediately — don’t force Dijkstra. Path weight is not a sum: for max-of-edges problems like 1631, use max(d, w) instead of d + w during relaxation. Keep the template flexible. State needs expansion: constraints like “K free passes” or “time limit” require nodes to become tuples. Max-heap: Python’s heapq is a min-heap; push negative values to simulate a max-heap. Exercises Why can't Dijkstra handle negative-weight edges? Give a counter-example. It greedily “finalizes” the node with the current minimum distance and never updates it again. If a subsequent negative edge could shorten an already-finalized node’s distance, there is no way to go back. Counter-example: A→B(1), A→C(5), C→B(-10); starting from A, the algorithm finalizes dist[B]=1 first, but the true shortest path A→C→B = -5 is never found. What happens if you omit if d > dist[u]: continue? The heap may contain multiple stale entries for the same node (because heapq doesn’t support decrease-key). Without skipping stale entries, correctness is unaffected, but the algorithm uses outdated distances to relax neighbors, doing a huge amount of wasted work, and complexity degrades. Why is 0-1 BFS faster than Dijkstra when edge weights are only 0 or 1? Using a deque: weight-0 edges go to the front, weight-1 edges go to the back. Each node is enqueued at most twice; no heap comparisons means no log factor — vs Dijkstra’s .

title: Dynamic Programming
content: DP = subproblems + no redundant computation. It compresses exponential search into polynomial time — all by “never recomputing what you’ve already computed.” Intuition — Non-overlapping SubproblemsDP really boils down to two steps. Memorize them: State definition: dp[i][j] represents some property of “the first i / first j” elements (length, count, feasibility, optimal value). Get the state right and the problem is halfway solved. Transition equation: how to build the current dp[i][j] from smaller subproblems. Two hallmarks of a DP problem: Optimal substructure: the optimal solution to the large problem is built from optimal solutions to smaller subproblems. No aftereffect: once the current state is determined, how you got there has no bearing on future decisions. Two equivalent implementations — pick whichever feels natural: Memoized recursion (top-down): looks like brute-force search; slap @cache on it and it becomes DP. No need to reason about traversal order; only computes visited subproblems. Iterative table-filling (bottom-up): compute small before large; loop order mirrors dependency order. No recursion stack, easier to optimize space. The animation below fills the LCS table cell by cell for "ABCDE" vs "ACE". Green is the current cell; semi-transparent green marks the three cells it depends on (left, above, upper-left). The lower half puts 0/1 knapsack (reverse order) and unbounded knapsack (forward order) side-by-side on the same data. Watch one thing: the value of the current cell always comes from cells that have already been filled — that is exactly “no aftereffect.” Three ParadigmsMaster three archetypal problems and 90% of DP questions are just variations of them. Linear DP — Climbing Stairs StyleState depends on only a fixed number of earlier positions. A one-dimensional array suffices. Same pattern: House Robber (dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]+nums[i])), Maximum Subarray, Minimum Path Sum. LIS — Picking a Subsequencedp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at nums[i]. Note it’s “ending at i,” not “among the first i” — otherwise you can’t write the transition. There is also an greedy + binary search solution (maintain a monotone tails array, binary-search insert). Know both for interviews. Knapsack — Multi-stage Decision Making“Include or not / include how many times” for each item — the highest-frequency DP paradigm. LCS / Edit Distance also fall here (“current characters match or not” is a two-way decision): 0/1 Knapsack: each item used at most once. 1-D optimization → reverse capacity order. Unbounded Knapsack: each item used any number of times. 1-D optimization → forward capacity order. Knapsack variant cheat sheet (the animation shows the difference between the two orderings): Problem Initialization Transition Max value dp = [0]*(W+1) dp[j] = max(dp[j], dp[j-w]+v) Count solutions dp[0]=1, rest 0 dp[j] += dp[j-w] Feasibility dp[0]=True dp[j] = dp[j] or dp[j-w] Combinations vs permutations — items outer loop = combinations; capacity outer loop = permutations Template — PythonMemoized recursion (least error-prone): Iterative table-filling (no stack risk, easy space optimization): Space Optimization — Rolling ArrayIf dp[i][...] depends only on dp[i-1][...], keep just two rows or even one. 2-D → two rows (depends on previous row): 2-D → one row (knapsack pattern, traversal order preserves semantics): 0/1 knapsack: j reverse order — dp[j-w] still holds the previous round’s value (“item i not yet selected”). Unbounded knapsack: j forward order — dp[j-w] already reflects the current round’s update (“item i can be selected repeatedly”). Get the order wrong and items are either selected multiple times or not at all. This is the most common knapsack bug. Mnemonics / Common PitfallsThree rules of thumb: Define the state first, then write the transition. Cover all base cases; get the traversal order right. Roll to one row: 0/1 goes reverse, unbounded goes forward. Common mistakes: Off-by-one: state dp[i] means “first i elements” → index into the array as s[i-1], not s[i]. Missing base cases: when counting solutions, dp[0]=1 (the empty set counts as one); when optimizing, initialize in the direction consistent with max/min. Wrong LIS state: must be “ending at i,” not “among first i” — otherwise the transition cannot be written. Knapsack order: reverse/forward order and which of items/capacity is the outer loop are two independent dimensions — don’t conflate them. Stale cache: @cache leaks data across multiple test cases; call cache_clear() before returning from the function. Exercises Q1: Why does 0/1 knapsack require reverse capacity order? What goes wrong with forward order? With forward order, dp[j-w[i]] may already have been updated in the current round, which means item i is used more than once — that is the unbounded knapsack. Reverse order ensures dp[j-w[i]] still holds the previous round’s value (item i not yet selected). Q2: When should you choose memoized recursion vs iterative DP? Afraid of getting it wrong → memoized recursion (no need to think about order; only computes needed subproblems). Need to save space / large input → iterative table-filling (no stack risk; rolling array is straightforward). Python’s default recursion limit is 1000; for deep state spaces, remember sys.setrecursionlimit. Q3: Why do "combinations" and "permutations" in knapsack require different traversal orders? Items as outer loop: each item is considered in a fixed order, so (1,2) and (2,1) count as one = combinations. Capacity as outer loop: every capacity scans all items, so the same set of items can appear in different orders = permutations. LeetCode PracticeWarm-up: 70. Climbing Stairs, 198. House Robber, 53. Maximum Subarray, 300. LIS, 322. Coin Change Advanced: 1143. LCS, 72. Edit Distance, 416. Partition Equal Subset Sum, 494. Target Sum, 518. Coin Change II

title: Greedy Algorithms
content: At each step, pick whatever looks locally optimal and hope it leads to a global optimum. The hard part isn’t writing the code — it’s proving that the greedy choice is actually correct. Greedy code is usually short, but correctness proof is the soul. Problems that look greedy are half the time actually DP. Intuition — Conditions for Local Optimum → Global OptimumGreedy works only when two hidden prerequisites are both satisfied: Greedy-choice property: The locally optimal choice at this step won’t ruin the globally optimal solution downstream. Optimal substructure: After making this step, the remaining subproblem is independent and can itself be solved greedily. The moment any “locally optimal” choice constrains future options, greedy will break down and you must fall back to DP. A quick rule of thumb: can you construct a counterexample? If you can’t think of one in a minute, greedy probably works; if you find one, switch to DP immediately. The animation below strings together the two most common greedy patterns — “interval scheduling sorted by end time” and “regret-based greedy for course scheduling” — watch it once before reading the code: Three Classic Patterns90% of greedy problems fall into one of the three patterns below. Recognize the pattern, apply the template. 1. Interval Scheduling — Sort by End Time Form: Given a collection of intervals/tasks, find the maximum number of non-overlapping ones you can select/complete. Key intuition: An interval that ends earlier leaves the most “room” for future intervals, so always greedily picking the earliest-ending one never hurts. The proof uses “greedy stays ahead” — by induction, after selecting k intervals, the greedy solution’s last end time is no later than that of any optimal solution. Variants: sort by start time (merge intervals), sort by right endpoint (minimum arrows to burst balloons), sort by left endpoint (merge/insert). Default: think right endpoint first. 2. Regret-Based Greedy — Use a Heap to Undo Previous Decisions Form: Maximize count or value subject to a budget/capacity constraint. Key intuition: Greedily pack everything in without thinking; once the budget is exceeded, kick out the “most expensive” item — the heap top. The ejected item is always ≥ the current one, so the total cost is non-increasing while the count is preserved. Classic problems: Course Schedule III, Minimum Number of Refueling Stops, IPO. Recognition signal: deadline/capacity constraint + maximize count. 3. Exchange Argument — Correctness of Sorting via “Swapping Adjacent Elements Doesn’t Make It Worse” Form: Find an ordering of a set of objects that optimizes some metric (e.g., total completion time, lexicographic order, minimum penalty). Key intuition: Assume the optimal solution has two adjacent elements in a different relative order than your sorting. Prove that swapping them doesn’t make the answer worse. By bubble-sorting all “greedy-violating” pairs, you still get an optimal solution — so the greedy ordering is correct. Typical problems: merging fruits (smallest first), queen game (sort by ), Huffman coding. Template — Interval Scheduling in Python Time complexity , bottleneck is sorting. Three variants require just one-line changes: Minimum arrows to burst balloons: change if s > last_end to >, depending on how the problem defines boundary conditions. Number of non-overlapping intervals: return n - count. Meeting Rooms II (max concurrency): different approach — use a min-heap to track end times of ongoing meetings. Regret-Based Greedy — Classic Pattern and CodeCourse Schedule III: each course has ; find the maximum number of courses you can take, starting from time 0. Three steps: sort by deadline → pack greedily → regret and eject the most expensive when over budget. The animation’s “regret phase” shows the moment the longest course in the heap gets replaced. Why it works: the ejected duration is the current one (otherwise it wouldn’t be the heap top), so total is non-increasing; and the heap size is preserved, so we never lose ground. Memory Aids / Common PitfallsOne-liner for the three patterns: sort by right endpoint (intervals) / max-heap regret (capacity) / pairwise swap (ordering). The three most common traps: Looks greedy, actually DP: The classic counterexample is the 0/1 knapsack — greedy by value/weight ratio doesn’t work, you need DP. Test: are subproblems independent? In a knapsack the remaining capacity changes with each choice → not independent → DP. Wrong sort key: Sorting by left endpoint is often wrong in interval problems; default to right endpoint. Watch for overflow in ratio-sort problems (e.g., IPO). Forgetting to maintain total in regret greedy: Every push/pop must be accompanied by a synchronized update to the resource used, otherwise the next iteration’s check will be wrong. Not sure if greedy applies? Three questions: (1) Is there a counterexample? (2) Are subproblems independent? (3) Can you write an exchange argument or a stays-ahead proof? All three pass → go ahead and be greedy; any one blocks you → write DP instead. Exercises When should you use "exchange argument" vs. "greedy stays ahead" as a proof technique? Exchange argument suits “permutation/ordering” problems — proving that a certain ordering is optimal (sort by deadline, by ratio, by ). Greedy stays ahead suits “selection” problems — picking one element per step and proving your set is never worse than the optimal at each step (interval scheduling, minimum spanning tree). Why does regret-based greedy use a max-heap? What goes wrong with a min-heap? When regretting, you eject the element with the highest cost so far, which frees up the most budget and drops the total cost the most. Using a min-heap means ejecting the cheapest element — you might still be over budget, and you’ve thrown away a “cheap choice” for nothing. The max-heap maximizes the marginal gain of each regret step. Why can't you solve the 0/1 knapsack greedily? Counterexample for greedy by value/weight: capacity 50, items (60,10), (100,20), (120,30) with ratios 6/5/4. Greedy picks the first two for a total of 160, but the optimal is the last two for 220. Reason: picking an item changes the remaining capacity, making subproblems non-independent — there is no “greedy-choice property”. This case requires DP to enumerate all states. LeetCode PracticeWarmup: 455. Assign Cookies, 122. Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II, 435. Non-overlapping Intervals, 55. Jump Game, 134. Gas Station Advanced: 630. Course Schedule III, 1024. Video Stitching, 763. Partition Labels, 502. IPO, 871. Minimum Number of Refueling Stops

title: Hash Table
content: A hash table isn’t really a data structure at its core — it’s an algorithmic pattern: trading O(1) lookups for O(N) scans. Any time you see “find two elements satisfying some relation,” your instinct should reach for a hash table. Intuition — O(1) Lookup in Place of O(N) ScanMost brute-force problems look like this: enumerate all (i, j) pairs and check whether they satisfy some condition. O(N²). What a hash table does is extremely simple: as you iterate, throw each “already-seen” element into the table; for every new element, ask the table whether there’s anything inside that can pair with it. One pass + O(1) lookup per step = O(N). Boiled down to one sentence: Turn an O(N²) “pair enumeration” into an O(N) “look up as you go.” When it applies: The problem asks for two elements satisfying f(a, b) = target (two-sum, 4Sum II, find pair with given difference/sum/product) The problem asks “did X appear before?” (longest substring without repeating characters, contains duplicate) The problem asks you to count “how many times does a certain value appear?” (counting, group anagrams) The problem wants to compress an O(N) range query into O(1) (prefix sum + hash, covered below) set vs. dict: use a set when you only care about whether something has been seen; use a dict when you need to store extra information (index, count, last-seen position). Two-sum needs to return indices, so it’s a dict; duplicate detection is a set. Don’t default to dict just to look fancy. Animation: “Look First, Then Store” for Two SumArray [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9. Pay attention to two things: For each new element x, query the table for target - x first, and only insert x afterward. The seen dict grows from empty; when the 2nd element 7 arrives, 2 is already in the table — immediate hit. Once you’ve watched the animation, go back and read the templates below — the pattern will be muscle memory. Templates — Two Sum, Subarray Sum Equals KPattern 1: Two Sum (look first, then store) Why must you always look first, then store? Consider nums = [3, 3], target = 6: if you store first, the first 3 goes in and immediately matches itself, returning [0, 0] — the same element paired with itself. Looking first keeps the current element out of the table. Pattern 2: Existence / Duplicate Check Notice the switch to a set here — no extra information needed. Pattern 3: Grouping / Counting (choosing the right key is everything) The criterion for a good key: hashable + uniquely represents the equivalence class. Prefix Sum + Hash CombinationThis is the hash trick that creates the biggest skill gap in algorithm problems. Subarray sum = prefix[j] - prefix[i], so “subarray sum equals k” is equivalent to “find two prefix sums whose difference is k” — which is just two-sum again. Two critical points: {0: 1} must not be omitted: it represents the “take nothing” empty prefix. Without it, any valid subarray starting at index 0 will be missed. “Look first, then store” still applies: use the old prefix counts to update count first, then write the current curr_sum into the table. Otherwise the current position will count itself as a “previous segment.” Once you internalize this combination, the following problems all collapse into the same one: Variant What to store as key Sum equals k prefix_sum Sum divisible by k prefix_sum % k Binary tree path sum (437) maintain prefix along the path Equal number of 0s and 1s in subarray treat 0 as -1, then find sum = 0 Classic ProblemsWarm-up (write from memory): Two Sum — template problem Contains Duplicate — set deduplication Group Anagrams — key selection Longest Consecutive Sequence — set + skip non-starting points, O(N) Subarray Sum Equals K — prefix sum template Advanced: 4Sum II — split into a+b and -(c+d), hash reduces O(N⁴) to O(N²) Subarray Sums Divisible by K — prefix sum mod K Path Sum III — prefix sum + backtracking, add on descent, remove before backtracking LRU Cache — dict + doubly linked list Design Twitter — hash nested with heap Python Quick Reference Counter subtraction is a powerful tool for sliding-window character frequency comparison and checking “can X be spelled from available letters.” Advanced: Rolling Hash / Rabin-KarpFor string matching, treat the window as a number in base base and update the hash in O(1) as the window slides: Even when hashes match, you still verify with an actual string comparison — standard practice in production. Mnemonics / Common Pitfalls See “pairing” → think hash: whenever the problem says “two numbers satisfying…”, “does there exist…”, “did it appear before…” — reflexively reach for a hash table. Look first, then store: never let the current element pair with itself. set vs. dict: only asking “seen?” → set; need to store index/count/position → dict. Prefix-sum hash must be initialized with {0: 1}: covers subarrays that start from index 0. Be careful modifying a dict during iteration: key changes can affect subsequent logic; copy or defer writes when necessary. Worried about collisions on large data: custom objects used as keys must implement both __hash__ and __eq__, and the two must be consistent. Only immutable objects can be keys: list no, tuple yes; set no, frozenset yes. Exercises Why must two-sum use "look first, then store"? Give an example where "store first, then look" produces a wrong answer. nums = [3, 3], target = 6. Store first: the first 3 is written as seen[3]=0, then immediately queried as 6-3=3 — found in the table, returns [0, 0] — the same element paired with itself. Wrong. Look first: when the first 3 arrives the table is empty, query misses, then it’s stored; when the second 3 arrives it finds the first 3 in the table and returns [0, 1]. Correct. In prefix sum + hash, what does {0: 1} initialization represent? What gets missed without it? It represents “the empty prefix that takes nothing, has sum 0, and has appeared once.” When some curr_sum exactly equals k (i.e., the subarray from index 0 up to the current position sums to k), the code looks up prefix[curr_sum - k] = prefix[0]. Without initialization, all such “starts-from-zero” subarrays are missed. Example: nums = [1, 2, 3], k = 3; the subarray [1, 2] is counted precisely because prefix[0]=1 is there. Why does Counter subtraction c1 - c2 keep only positive results? When is this useful? Counter is a multiset — element counts can’t go negative. Subtraction means “remove,” and removing more than you have clips to zero. Use cases: Check if word can be spelled from available letters: if Counter(word) - Counter(available) is empty, yes it can. Find missing letters: Counter(required) - Counter(have). Sliding-window character frequency comparison.

title: Heap / Priority Queue
content: In one sentence: a heap is a complete binary tree expressed implicitly via array indices. It looks like a tree; in memory it is flat. Each operation gets you the current min/max in O(log n); building the heap takes only O(n). Intuition — A Complete Binary Tree Expressed as an ArrayThe essence of a heap is not “a special kind of tree” — it is an array plus one index rule: The parent of node i is at (i-1)//2 The left and right children of node i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2 No pointers, no node objects. The tree structure is computed entirely from indices. The cost is that a heap must be a complete binary tree (packed tightly from left to right), so the array has no holes. This rule gives three properties that map directly to all heap operations: Operation How it works Complexity push Append to the end of the array, float up toward the parent (sift-up) O(log n) pop Remove heap[0], move the last element to position 0, sink down toward children (sift-down) O(log n) heapify sift-down from the last non-leaf node backward, Floyd’s algorithm O(n) not O(n log n) Min-heap invariant: every node ≤ its two children. Note this only orders parent–child pairs — siblings are unordered — so you cannot use a heap to retrieve the k-th element after sorting; you have to pop repeatedly. The animation below uses a Top-K scenario to demonstrate push / sift-up / pop / sift-down simultaneously. The left side shows the tree view; the right side shows the same data as an array. Focus on how both views stay in sync — that is the entirety of “array-simulated tree.” Template — Python heapq Basic OperationsPython’s standard library heapq is a min-heap only. Want a max-heap? Store -x. This is the most common gotcha in interview problems. If heap elements are tuples, they are compared lexicographically. For objects that are not directly comparable (e.g., linked-list nodes), add a monotonically increasing counter to break ties: (val, idx, node). 4 Canonical Use CasesHeaps in algorithm problems almost exclusively solve these four things. Recognizing the pattern matters more than writing the code. 1. Top-K — Min-Heap for Largest, Max-Heap for SmallestTo find the K largest elements, use a min-heap of size K; the heap top is the “threshold.” A new element enters only if it exceeds the threshold. Conversely, to find the K smallest, use a max-heap. Time O(n log k), space O(k). Better than sorting O(n log n) for data streams. 2. Streaming Median — Two Heaps Back to Backlo is a max-heap (holds the smaller half), hi is a min-heap (holds the larger half). Maintain |len(lo) - len(hi)| ≤ 1; the median is always at the two heap tops. Key trick: blindly push to lo first, then move one element to hi — this guarantees the invariant lo ≤ hi. 3. Merge K Sorted Lists — Store a Pointer per List in the HeapTake the smallest current element from each of the K lists/arrays and push them into the heap. Pop the minimum, then push the next element from that list. Each step is O(log K). Total time O(N log K), where N is the total number of elements. 4. Dijkstra — Heap-Optimized Shortest PathNaive Dijkstra is O(V²). Using a min-heap keyed by distance to pick the next node brings it down to O((V+E) log V).
