Store (dist, node) in the heap; when popping, skip the entry if dist > dist[node] (lazy deletion). Lazy deletion keeps the amortized complexity at O(log n): each element is pushed at most once and skipped at most once, each O(log n). Classic Problems 215. Kth Largest Element in an Array — Top-K template, min-heap of capacity K. 295. Find Median from Data Stream — Dual-heap back-to-back. 23. Merge K Sorted Lists — Push nodes into the heap, use a counter to break ties. 347. Top K Frequent Elements — Use Counter first, then a min-heap. 502. IPO — Dual heap: min-heap by capital, max-heap by profit. 857. Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers — Sort + max-heap to maintain the sum of current K wages. 703. Kth Largest Element in a Stream — Online Top-K. 1046. Last Stone Weight — Max-heap simulation. Memory AidsThink of a heap in two layers and you will never forget it: Physical layer: heap = array + index rule parent=(i-1)//2, children=2i+1, 2i+2. All “tree” operations ultimately reduce to arithmetic on array indices. Invariant layer: a min-heap only guarantees parent ≤ children — siblings are unordered. So a heap can only repeatedly give you the extremum; it cannot give you the “second largest.” Pattern layer: reflexively reach for a heap when you see these keywords: “Top K / K-th largest / K-th smallest” → Top-K (one heap) “Streaming median / sliding window median” → dual-heap back-to-back “K-way / K sorted” → K-way merge “Shortest path / minimum-cost expansion” → Dijkstra / weighted BFS variant On the Python side, just remember three calls: heappush / heappop / heap[0], negate for a max-heap, and heapify is O(n). Exercises Why does Top-K use a min-heap rather than a max-heap? A min-heap’s top is the minimum value, so you can quickly tell whether a new element is larger than the current K-th largest. With a max-heap the top is the maximum, and you have no efficient way to evict the smallest element. The min-heap guarantees the heap always contains the K largest elements, with the top acting as the “threshold.” In the dual-heap approach, why does "push to lo first, then move to hi" guarantee lo ≤ hi? We push to lo (max-heap) first, then move lo’s maximum to hi (min-heap). This guarantees the element transferred from lo to hi is greater than or equal to all remaining elements in lo. Therefore lo’s maximum ≤ hi’s minimum, i.e., every element in lo ≤ every element in hi. Why is Floyd heapify O(n) rather than O(n log n)? Pushing one by one is O(n log n): each sift-up is at most log n. Floyd heapify sifts down from the last non-leaf node backward. The leaf layer (n/2 nodes) does nothing; the second-to-last layer sinks at most 1 step; the layer above that at most 2 steps… Summing Σ (n/2^(h+1)) · h converges to O(n). Intuition: most nodes are near the bottom and barely need to move. Why doesn't "lazy deletion" in Dijkstra blow up the complexity? Each edge can push its target node into the heap at most once, so the heap holds at most O(E) entries. Each entry is either processed validly or skipped by the d > dist[u] check — both cases cost O(log E). Total complexity O((V+E) log V), consistent with the theoretical bound. LeetCode PracticeWarm-up: 215, 703, 347, 1046. Advanced: 23, 295, 378, 502, 857.

title: Interval DP
content: The state dp[i][j] is the optimal answer for a segment, and transitions enumerate a “split point” k inside the interval. The key isn’t the formula — it’s the enumeration order: you must go from shorter intervals to longer ones, because dp[i][j] needs dp[i][k] and dp[k+1][j] to already be computed. Remember that one sentence, and stone merging, burst balloons, and matrix chain multiplication all collapse into the same problem. Intuition — Interval State + Split Point + Enumeration OrderLinear DP states are “a single point” (dp[i]); interval DP states are “a range” (dp[i][j]). Whenever a problem asks for the optimal cost of some merge / split / matching operation over a contiguous sequence, it’s almost certainly interval DP. The standard transition: enumerate a split point k within [i, j], dividing the large interval in two, and recursively use the answers for the two sub-intervals. cost(i, k, j) is the cost of “joining the two halves together” — defined by the specific problem. For stone merging it is sum(a[i..j]), for matrix chain it is p[i-1] * p[k] * p[j], and for burst balloons it is nums[i-1] * nums[k] * nums[j+1]. Enumeration Order: Why Length Must Come Firstdp[i][j] depends on dp[i][k] and dp[k+1][j], both of which have lengths strictly less than [i, j]. So when filling the table you must ensure that all shorter intervals are already computed before you compute dp[i][j]. Three valid approaches, all equivalent in effect: Approach Outer loop Inner loop Notes By length (recommended) len from 2 to n Left endpoint i, j = i+len-1 Most intuitive, least error-prone i descending + j ascending i from n-1 to 0 j from i+1 to n-1 Exploits the “dependency has larger i, smaller j” property Memoized recursion — — No need to think about order; recursion guarantees topological order Incorrect approach: i ascending + j ascending — when computing dp[0][n-1], dp[1][n-1] (also a dependency) hasn’t been computed yet. Animation — Stone Merging Table FillArray [3, 1, 5, 2], find the minimum total cost to merge all stones into one pile (each merge combines two adjacent piles; cost = sum of the two piles). The animation below fills the dp table strictly in “length from small to large” order. Click “Next Step” and watch three things: The cell being filled (blue border) — which interval dp[i][j] is this. Yellow-highlighted cells — the two sub-interval cells dp[i][k] and dp[k+1][j] referenced in this step. They are always to the lower-left of the current cell, because they are shorter and already computed. The final dp[0][3] — that is the answer. The fill direction is always “short intervals already in place → long interval assembled from them.” That is the complete physical picture of interval DP. Template — Python (Loop by Length, Small to Large) Four-loop skeleton: len → i → (j derived from len and i) → k, time complexity , space . This skeleton stays the same for almost all interval DP problems; only the cost line changes. Memoized recursion version: More concise, and no need to worry about enumeration order. Trade-off: recursion stack depth ; for n in the thousands, switch to iteration. Three Paradigms — Stone Merging / Burst Balloons / Matrix ChainAll three problems use the template above; only cost differs. Memorize these three cost expressions and you’ve reduced half of all interval DP problems. 1. Stone Merging — cost = sum(a[i..j])LC 1000. The last merge combines piles [i,k] and [k+1,j]; the cost equals the total number of stones in those two piles = prefix[j+1] - prefix[i] (independent of k, so it can be hoisted out of the k loop). 2. Burst Balloons — reversed definition, dp[i][j] = max coins for popping everything inside open interval (i, j)LC 312. Intuitive trap: thinking forward about “which balloon to pop first” — after popping, left and right balloons become adjacent, contaminating the neighbor relationship and breaking sub-problem independence. When forward is hard, go backward: enumerate the balloon k inside interval (i, j) that is popped last. At the moment k is popped, all balloons in (i, k) and (k, j) are already gone, so k’s left neighbor is i and right neighbor is j — the coins nums[i] * nums[k] * nums[j] are fully determined. Note the split is written as dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] (k is excluded from both sub-intervals because k is popped last). 3. Matrix Chain Multiplication — cost = p[i-1] * p[k] * p[j]The classic “optimal parenthesization” problem. Matrix has dimensions ; dp[i][j] = minimum number of scalar multiplications to compute . The last multiplication joins the result of [i..k] (shape ) with the result of [k+1..j] (shape ); cost is p[i-1] * p[k] * p[j]. Nearly identical to stone merging — just a different cost shape. Mnemonics / Common PitfallsOne-line summary: state is an interval, transition finds a split point, enumerate from short to long. Four things that commonly trip people up: Base case dp[i][i]: the optimal value for a single-element interval. Sum-type (stone merging) → 0; product-type (burst balloons) → 0; count/matching-type (palindromic subsequence) → 1. Follow the problem definition; don’t blindly copy the template. Range of the split point: k in range(i, j) means both [i,k] and [k+1,j] are non-empty. The burst-balloons-style “k is the last operation” uses range(i+1, j) because k itself doesn’t belong to either sub-interval. Which one to use depends on how you define dp — don’t mix them up. Boundary sentinels: for burst-balloons-style problems and problems involving merging endpoints, it’s common to prepend and append a sentinel value (1 or 0) to the array, so that the “left/right neighbor of a split point” is always meaningful — saving a lot of if guards. The i-ascending + j-ascending trap: it looks natural but is wrong. Use either the length-based loop, or i descending / j ascending, or memoized recursion. When in doubt, use memoized recursion — it’s foolproof. Quick identification: Interval merge / split / optimal parenthesization / palindrome matching / “the last operation on an interval is …” → interval DP three-loop solution fits within time limits → n is typically ≤ 500 Too slow → look for quadrangle inequality optimization to bring it to , or rethink the approach LeetCode PracticeWarm-up (palindrome / symmetry): 5. Longest Palindromic Substring · 516. Longest Palindromic Subsequence · 647. Palindromic Substrings Advanced (merging / reverse enumeration): 312. Burst Balloons · 1000. Minimum Cost to Merge Stones · 664. Strange Printer · 546. Remove Boxes · 87. Scramble String By the third problem you’ll notice the differences between these problems come down to the shape of the cost function; the skeleton is always the same four-loop template. That’s all interval DP really is.

title: Core Linked List Operations
content: Every linked list bug traces back to one sentence: save cur.next before you overwrite it — otherwise you lose the rest of the chain forever. Remember that, add the dummy-node / two-pointer / head-insert-reversal trio, and 80% of linked list problems become template exercises. Intuition — Save next Before Breaking the LinkThe fundamental difference between linked lists and arrays: modify any element in an array and the other elements stay put; overwrite cur.next in a linked list and the original chain is instantly severed — there is no second path back. So the first line of every template is always nxt = cur.next. The three-step mantra: Save — nxt = cur.next (the lifeline) Redirect — cur.next = prev (perform the surgery) Advance — prev = cur; cur = nxt (move forward) The animation below walks through all three steps on a 5-node list. Keep your eyes on the three pointers: yellow cur, cyan prev, red nxt. Each time you click “Next Step,” see which arrow flips. The frame where red nxt appears is exactly where “Save” is saving your life. The Three Core Techniques — Dummy / Two Pointers / Head-Insert Reversal1. Dummy Head Node — Use It Whenever the Head Can ChangeAny problem where the head node might be deleted, swapped, or merged (reversal, merge, delete, group reorder) — open with dummy = ListNode(0, head) and return dummy.next at the end. Cost: one extra node. Benefit: no if head is None checks, no if node == head special cases. When to skip it: traversal only, value-only changes, no structural modifications (e.g., compute length, find midpoint). 2. Two Pointers — One Trick, Three Problems Scenario Recipe Find midpoint slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2; when fast reaches end → slow is at middle Detect cycle slow 1 step, fast 2 steps; meeting = cycle, never meeting = no cycle kth from end fast advances k steps first, then both move together; when fast reaches end → slow is at position k from end Why it works: the speed difference converts “distance” into a quantity you can exploit. Finding midpoint trades “2x speed to the end” for “1x speed to the halfway point”; kth from end trades “k steps of lead” for “k positions of lag.” 3. Head-Insert Reversal — Not Just for Reversing Lists Each iteration detaches the current node and prepends it to dummy, producing reverse order automatically. Reverse a subrange (LC 92) and reverse in k-groups (LC 25) are both variants of this head-insert pattern. Templates — PythonReverse an entire linked list: Merge two sorted linked lists: Detect cycle + find entry point (Floyd): The Math Behind Floyd’s Cycle DetectionWhy does “after meeting, send one pointer back to the start and walk both at the same speed — they’ll meet again exactly at the entry point” work? One diagram explains it: Let = distance from start to entry, = distance from entry to meeting point, = distance from meeting point back to entry (so cycle length ). At the meeting moment: slow has traveled fast has traveled (lapped the cycle times) fast moves twice as fast as slow: Simplifying: , i.e., . Translation: walking steps from start to entry is equivalent to walking steps from the meeting point plus full laps — which also lands at the entry. So a pointer from the start and a pointer from the meeting point, both moving at the same speed, must meet at the entry point. The one thing to remember: a = c (mod L). Everything else is muscle memory. Classic ProblemsWarm-up (pure templates): LC 206. Reverse Linked List — reversal template LC 21. Merge Two Sorted Lists — dummy + tail LC 876. Middle of the Linked List — fast/slow pointers LC 141. Linked List Cycle — Floyd cycle detection LC 83. Remove Duplicates from Sorted List — single pointer, one pass Advanced (combining techniques): LC 142. Linked List Cycle II — Floyd entry-point detection, direct application of the math above LC 19. Remove Nth Node From End — dummy + two pointers with n-step gap LC 92. Reverse Linked List II — head-insert reversal over a range LC 25. Reverse Nodes in k-Group — count k nodes first, then reverse; head-insert variant LC 143. Reorder List — find midpoint + reverse second half + merge LC 148. Sort List — find midpoint + merge sort LC 146. LRU Cache — doubly linked list + HashMap Palindrome check without extra array: find midpoint → reverse second half → compare with two pointers. All three core operations in a single problem. MnemonicsOne sentence: save next before touching pointers, use dummy whenever the head can change, open two pointers whenever you need to find a position. Three pairs: Problem Technique Head node might change dummy Need to find a position “midway” two pointers (speed gap or distance gap) Need to reverse / reverse a segment head-insert to after dummy For Floyd cycle detection, just remember: a = c (mod L) — distance from start to entry equals distance from meeting point to entry (modulo cycle length). Everything else follows from drawing the diagram. Never write linked list pointer code without drawing a diagram first — that rule is inviolable.

title: Monotonic Queue
content: The key to solving sliding window max/min in — discard elements that can never become the answer while they’re still in the window. One sentence summary: if a newcomer is larger than the tail, the tail should retire; when the left edge of the window slides past the head, the head expires. Each element enters and leaves the deque at most once, so the total cost is . Intuition — Discard “Elements That Can Never Be the Answer”Brute-force sliding window max: rescan k elements on every move, . The waste comes from repeatedly looking at numbers that are already “dominated” and will never get a turn. Consider [1, 3, -1, ...], window k=3. When the new element 3 arrives, does 1 still matter? While 3 is alive in the window, 1 is always smaller than 3 and will never be the maximum; once 3 expires, 1 will have expired long before. So 1 can be discarded immediately — the earlier the better. That’s the entire philosophy of the monotonic queue: Enqueue from the tail: when new element x arrives, pop all tail elements <= x (they’re permanently dominated by x). Read the answer from the head: after maintaining monotonicity, the head is always the current window maximum. Expire from the head: if the head’s index has slid out of the window, popleft. Since both ends need to be operated on, the underlying structure is a deque (double-ended queue), not a plain stack or queue. Each element enters once and leaves once, amortized , total . Key insight: the queue holds not “all elements in the window” but the candidates that may still become the maximum in the future — a strictly decreasing stack. Animation — Follow the Four StepsArray [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k=3. Click “Next Step” and watch the four colors: Green (current): the new element being visited Orange (cleaned): tail elements beaten by the newcomer and popped Red (expired): head index expired, popleft Cyan (in-queue): candidates currently in the deque Watch closely when 5 arrives: -3 and -1 at the tail get wiped out in one shot, because they can never beat 5. That’s the essence of amortized cost. Template — Python deque, Sliding Window Maximum Three common mistakes: Store indices, not values. The expiry check q[0] <= i - k requires the index. Order matters. Enqueue must come after tail cleanup (otherwise the new element might clean itself out); reading the answer must come after all cleanup. For minimum, change <= to >= — the queue becomes non-decreasing, everything else stays identical. Three-step mantra: ① clean the tail of defeated elements → ② enqueue → ③ clean the head of expired elements → ④ read answer from the head. Monotonic Stack vs. Monotonic Queue — One Word of DifferenceBoth use monotonicity to discard useless elements; the difference is whether there’s a window constraint. Dimension Monotonic Stack Monotonic Queue Structure Stack (one end) Deque (two ends) Solves Next greater/smaller element Sliding window extremum Scope Looks arbitrarily far ahead Fixed window k Head operation Not needed Expire outdated entries Answer location Determined at pop time Always at the head Complexity One line: a monotonic stack is a monotonic queue with infinite window size. The extra “head cleanup” step is the price paid for the window constraint. Classic Problem — 239. Sliding Window Maximum Given array nums and window size k, return the maximum of each sliding window. Drop the template in directly — max_sliding_window above is the AC solution. Complexity ; brute force TLEs at . Other must-solve problems: LC 1438. Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit — maintain two deques simultaneously, one for max and one for min. LC 862. Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K — prefix sum + monotonic queue, a classic combo. LC 918. Maximum Sum Circular Subarray — double the array, fix window to n. LC 1696. Jump Game VI — sliding window max inside a DP transition, reduces to . Recognition signal: the problem mentions “window size k”, “subarray of length at most k extremum”, or “DP transition depends on the max of the previous k terms” — reach for a monotonic queue. Memory AidOne sentence: those who can outshine you will never let you shine; those who wait for you will have already expired. Three standard moves: New element enters from the tail; pop all smaller tail elements (tail fights) If the head’s index is expired, popleft (head retires) Head is the window extremum (head collects the prize) Quick lookup: Only asking “next greater element” → monotonic stack Windowed extremum → monotonic queue Mixed updates / arbitrary range extremum → segment tree or sparse table One image to remember: a strictly decreasing lineup of candidate kings stands in the deque; the head wears the crown — expire to yield, overpower to enter.

title: Monotonic Stack
content: Keep only the candidates still waiting for their next greater element. When a new value arrives, pop every stack top that is — each one’s “next greater” is exactly . Every element is pushed once and popped once: total. Intuition — “pop stack tops that can no longer be the answer”Thinking forward — “for each , find the first element to the right that’s larger” — is . Flip the perspective: instead, each new element actively claims whose answer it is. The stack maintains a list of indices of candidates that haven’t yet found their next greater element, strictly decreasing from bottom to top (earlier arrivals are larger). When arrives: Stack top ? Then is the stack top’s “next greater”. Pop it and record the answer. Keep comparing the next stack top, until the top is or the stack is empty. Push onto the stack and wait for its own “next greater”. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once — 2n total operations, amortized . In one line: the stack and the target are opposite. To find something larger, the stack holds candidates sorted large-to-small. Animation — watch the color of the stack topThe animation below runs through array [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] finding “next greater element”. Step through it one click at a time, keeping an eye on three things: Green is the current nums[i] being visited. Cyan are the candidates still in the stack, waiting for their answer. Red is the stack top being popped by x — the →x floating above it is the recorded answer. Pay special attention when 5 arrives and pops both 1 and 2 in one go, and when 6 pops 5 too — that’s the true face of “ amortized”: paying off multiple old debts at once. After watching the animation, the stack’s shape is always a decreasing staircase of cyan columns. That picture is the core mental image for monotonic stacks. One template, four variantsThere’s just one template; change two things to get any variant. The stack’s monotonicity is the opposite of the target — that’s the core. Target Stack monotonicity (bottom→top) while condition Traversal direction Next greater Decreasing nums[top] <= x Left to right Next smaller Increasing nums[top] >= x Left to right Previous greater Decreasing nums[top] <= x Right to left Previous smaller Increasing nums[top] >= x Right to left Mnemonic: “Greater uses decreasing; smaller uses increasing. Looking left means traverse right, looking right means traverse left.” As for whether to include the equality in the comparison, it depends on whether equal elements can serve as each other’s answer — including it is usually the safer default. Template code — Daily Temperatures (LC 739)Return how many days you have to wait for a warmer day. Just change the “next greater” answer from a value to an index difference: Why store indices, not values: you also need to compute distances, widths, and window ranges. Storing values loses position information. For all monotonic stack problems, default to storing indices. Advanced — Largest Rectangle in Histogram (LC 84)Idea: enumerate “use this bar as the height” for the maximum rectangle. To determine the width, you need to know the first shorter bar on the left and right. That’s exactly the “previous smaller + next smaller” two variants — handled in a single pass with the same stack. What the two sentinel 0s do: The trailing 0 forces all real bars to be flushed from the stack, handled uniformly inside the loop. The leading 0 acts as the left boundary, ensuring stack[-1] never goes out of bounds on a pop. Trapping Rain Water (LC 42) follows the same pattern: when popping the top mid, the left boundary is the new stack top, the right boundary is i, and the water trapped at this level is . “Pop and settle immediately” is the unified technique for solving geometry-style problems with a monotonic stack. Memory aidOne sentence: “When the stack top is beaten by , is the stack top’s answer.” Three steps: Recognize the problem type: “next/previous greater/smaller”, “first bar to the right shorter/taller than …”, “histogram / rain water” → reflexively write a monotonic stack. Pick the direction: looking for “greater” → decreasing stack; looking for “smaller” → increasing stack. Stack and target are opposites. Pop and settle immediately: inside the while loop when you pop the top, the current i and the new top are its right and left boundaries respectively — distance, width, and contribution are all computed in that instant. Quick decision guide: Single point + “next X” → monotonic stack Sliding window + “interval extremum” → monotonic deque (add an expiry check) Offline + “comparison queries” → offline scan + monotonic stack Essential LeetCode problems: 496, 739, 503 (warm-up); 84, 42, 85, 907, 316 (advanced).

title: Quickselect
content: Finding the K-th element doesn’t require sorting the whole array. One partition call places the pivot at its final position, then you recurse only into the half where K lies. Expected — thoroughly beats sorting’s . Intuition — Partition Is Enough; No Full Sort NeededSorting is because every level of recursion has to fully sort both halves. But finding the K-th element doesn’t care about the relative order of anything else — it only cares about one thing: Whose final position is exactly K? That’s precisely what partition produces. After one partition call, the pivot lands at its “correct sorted position” p, with everything to the left pivot and everything to the right pivot. Three cases: p == k — return nums[p] immediately. Done. p < k — the K-th element is in the right half; recurse there. p > k — the K-th element is in the left half; recurse there. Only one side is recursed, which is the fundamental reason quickselect beats quicksort by a log factor. The expected problem size halves each time: — a geometric series that converges. The worst case (always picking an extreme value as pivot) degrades to , but randomizing the pivot makes this statistically negligible. Animation — Tracing the i/j Pointers Through PartitionThe animation below runs on the array [3, 6, 2, 8, 1, 5, 4] with the last element 4 as pivot. Step through the Lomuto partition and watch two pointers: Pointer i (green): marks “where the next element smaller than pivot should go” — everything left of i is < pivot. Pointer j (cyan): the scanning pointer, inspects each element in turn. The rule is just one line: if nums[j] < pivot, do swap(i, j); i++; otherwise just j++. After the scan, swap the pivot into position i and the partition is complete. Read the template after watching the animation and every step will match up. Template — Python (randomized pivot) Three common mistakes: You must randomize the pivot. Without it, a sorted input causes every call to eliminate only one element, degrading to . k is 0-indexed. To find the K-th largest, convert with k = n - K; for the K-th smallest, use k = K - 1. Write it as while True + iteration, not recursion. Recursion can blow the stack in the worst case. Three-Way Partition — Handling Many Duplicate ElementsIf the array contains many elements equal to the pivot, Lomuto partition keeps cutting between them and degrades. Three-way partition (Dutch National Flag) splits the array into < pivot, == pivot, and > pivot segments; the equal segment is skipped entirely. Determine which segment K falls in: k < lt → go left; k > gt → go right; otherwise nums[k] is the answer. Quickselect vs. Heap for Top-K — ComparisonTwo common misconceptions: “use a heap to find the K-th element” and “quickselect is always faster.” Neither is right. It depends on the situation: Dimension Quickselect Heap Time (expected) Time (worst case) Space in-place Original array gets shuffled untouched Data model offline (all data must be available) online / streaming Multiple queries each time maintain one heap, per query How to choose: One-shot, offline, enough memory, large data → quickselect. Streaming data, cannot modify the original array, need guaranteed worst-case complexity, → heap. Extreme cases ( or ): a single linear scan beats everything. Note that when , is practically (log k is a tiny constant), the heap code is also shorter, and in an interview setting writing the heap solution is usually the safer choice. Classic Problems LC 215. Kth Largest Element in an Array — pure template. Note: “K-th largest” → k = n - K. LC 347. Top K Frequent Elements — count frequencies first, then quickselect (or heap) on the frequencies. LC 973. K Closest Points to Origin — partition by squared distance; a standard application. LC 324. Wiggle Sort II — quickselect for the median, then three-way partition + index mapping. Hard. LC 462. Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements II — median = element at index ; pull it out with quickselect, no sorting needed. Memory Aid / Common MistakesOne sentence: one partition places the pivot; only recurse into the side containing K. Three-way comparison: Problem Algorithm Complexity Full sort quicksort (recurse both sides) Find K-th element quickselect (recurse one side) expected Maintain Top-K heap (min-heap of size K) Checklist of common mistakes: K’s index: 0-indexed or 1-indexed, “K-th largest” or “K-th smallest” — sort this out before writing. Pivot must be randomized, or sorted input immediately gives . Partition returns pivot position p, not the value. You compare the indices p and k. Many duplicate elements → use three-way partition, otherwise it degrades. Don’t recurse — use while True + adjust lo/hi to avoid stack overflow. The original array gets shuffled. If the caller can’t tolerate that, copy it first.

title: Sliding Window
content: Two pointers l and r: r keeps expanding to the right; when the window becomes “invalid”, l shrinks from the right; once valid again, update the answer. Each pointer moves at most N steps, so crushes the brute-force enumeration. Intuition — Monotonic Advancement of Two PointersThink of brute-force enumeration of all subarrays as a 2D grid with cells. Sliding window only walks one monotone path: r only ever increases, l only ever increases. Together the two pointers take at most steps, giving . Why doesn’t l retreat? Because moving r one step to the right only makes the window “more invalid” (more elements, larger sum, more duplicates). An l that has already been moved right to restore validity has no reason to go left again — that would only make the window invalid again. When Can You Use Sliding WindowKey criterion: monotonicity. You must have: Window expands → condition moves in one direction (more invalid / more valid) Window shrinks → condition moves in the opposite direction For example, “subarray sum target”: adding elements only increases the sum, removing them only decreases it — the validity is monotone, sliding works. For “exactly K distinct characters”: expanding or shrinking can both break the “exactly K” condition, there is no monotonicity, so you can’t slide directly (convert to “at most K minus at most K-1”, see below). Get this wrong and you’re stuck: when you see a problem, ask first — “does expanding the window push the condition in only one direction?” Yes → you can slide. Animation — Two Templates Side by SideThe animation below has two parts. Top half demonstrates “longest substring without repeating characters” ("abcabcbb"): watch how l shrinks when r encounters a duplicate, and ans is updated outside the while loop. Bottom half compares the same pointer logic side by side for two ans update positions: left side shows “longest valid” (shrink while invalid, update outside while), right side shows “shortest cover” (record while valid, update inside while). Focus on two things: (1) l never retreats; (2) the position of the ans update determines whether you’re computing longest or shortest. Two Templates — Longest Valid vs. Shortest CoverTemplate A: Longest Valid Window (shrink while invalid) Intuition: exiting the while loop means the window just became valid again — this is the largest valid window with right as the right endpoint, so record it. Template B: Shortest Cover Window (record while valid) Intuition: entering the while loop means the window is already valid; every step of shrinking is a valid window, so greedily record the shortest. Once l has shrunk to the point where going further would make it invalid, exit and wait for r to expand more. Mapping to Problem Types Problem characteristic Which template ans update position Find longest X subarray A: longest valid outside while Find shortest X subarray B: shortest cover inside while Count how many X subarrays Variant of A: ans += right - left + 1 outside while The third variant is a high-frequency trick: after exiting the while loop, [left..right] is the largest valid window ending at right, so there are exactly right - left + 1 valid subarrays ending at right. Classic ProblemsLC 3. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (Template A) Small optimization: the window becomes invalid only when the newly added c is a duplicate, so while window[c] > 1 is faster than scanning the entire window. LC 209. Minimum Size Subarray Sum (Template B) LC 76. Minimum Window Substring (Template B + counter) Key: use have to track the number of satisfied character types, avoiding a full Counter scan each time for validity — making validity checks truly . “Exactly K” = “At Most K” - “At Most K-1” (LC 992)“Exactly K” has no monotonicity → convert to two “at most” problems that do: Three Rules to Write It Right Symmetric enter/exit: whatever operation right does entering the window, left must undo on exit. Don’t forget to del from Counter when it reaches zero, otherwise len(cnt) will be wrong. left only moves inside while: moving left outside the while breaks the amortized analysis. ans position = problem intent: outside while → longest / count; inside while → shortest. Memory AidOne sentence: r expands until invalid → l shrinks until valid. Three-question checklist: Does expanding the window push the condition in one direction (monotone)? No → can’t slide directly (or convert). Looking for longest or shortest? Longest → shrink while invalid, update outside while; Shortest → record while valid, update inside while. Are enter/exit operations symmetric? Counter zeroed out → delete; sum added → subtract. When you see “contiguous subarray/substring + longest/shortest/count”, reflexively write two pointers with a while loop. You won’t go wrong. Exercises Why does the left pointer only move right and never retreat? What complexity does this guarantee? After r moves right, the window can only become “more invalid”. An l that has already been moved right to restore validity has no reason to go left again — that would only make the window invalid again. Each of the two pointers moves at most steps, for a total of . This is a classic example of amortized analysis: even though there are two loops (for + while), the total number of while iterations is bounded by the total displacement of l. Why can't "exactly K distinct characters" be solved with a direct sliding window? How do you convert it? With exactly K, expanding can jump to K+1 (invalid) and shrinking can jump to K-1 (also invalid) — neither direction has monotonicity, so the while loop can’t maintain a clean invariant. Conversion: exactly K = at most K minus at most (K-1). “At most K” is monotone (the larger the window, the more likely it exceeds K), so standard sliding window applies. In Template A, why must be updated outside the while loop? Inside the while loop, the window is in the middle of “shrinking from invalid back to valid” — intermediate states are all invalid. Exiting the while loop guarantees that [left..right] is a valid window, and specifically the largest valid window with right as the right endpoint. Updating ans while invalid would corrupt the answer. LeetCode PracticeWarmup: 3. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters — Template A bare problem 209. Minimum Size Subarray Sum — Template B bare problem 438. Find All Anagrams in a String — fixed-length window variant 1004. Max Consecutive Ones III — Template A, “invalid = count of 0s > K” Advanced: 76. Minimum Window Substring — Template B + have counter optimization 992. Subarrays with K Different Integers — exactly K = at most K minus at most K-1 239. Sliding Window Maximum — fixed-length + monotone deque, a clever variation 395. Longest Substring with At Least K Repeating Characters — no monotonicity, requires divide-and-conquer or enumerate distinct character counts

title: Topological Sort
content: Order all nodes in a DAG so that every edge points from an earlier node to a later one. Know both implementations by heart: Kahn’s algorithm (BFS in-degree method) and DFS post-order reversal. Cycle detection comes for free. Intuition — “First Come First Served” on a DAGTopological sort solves exactly one problem: given a bunch of tasks with dependencies, find an order that lets you complete them one by one. More formally: given a directed acyclic graph (DAG), arrange all nodes in a line so that for every edge u → v, u appears before v. Analogies: Course prerequisites: prerequisite courses come before the courses that depend on them. make build system: targets that are depended on get compiled first. Task scheduling: predecessor tasks execute first. The critical requirement is no cycles. With a cycle it’s impossible to say who comes first, which is why topological sort naturally doubles as a DAG validator. The animation below uses a 6-node DAG 0→2, 0→3, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4, 3→5 to walk through Kahn’s algorithm. Focus on two things: how the in-degree array changes on the right, and the order in which nodes are enqueued in the output sequence. Read the template after watching — the code is just the animation’s moves translated into Python. Two Implementations — Kahn (BFS) and DFS Post-OrderKahn’s Algorithm — Push Zero-In-Degree Nodes Into the QueueOne sentence: count in-degrees; push all nodes with in-degree 0 into the queue; each time you pop a node, decrement its neighbors’ in-degrees, and re-enqueue any that hit 0. Intuitive, controllable, easy to adapt. To get the lexicographically smallest topological order, swap deque for a min-heap (heapq). DFS Post-Order Reversal — Stack-Exit Order Is Topological OrderOne sentence: once DFS finishes a node, push it onto a stack; reversing at the end gives topological order. Why does reversing post-order give topological order? Because before node u exits the stack, all of its successors have already exited. Nodes that exit later must come earlier in the final order, so we flip at the end. Which One to Choose Scenario Choose Stable, controllable, layer-by-layer processing Kahn Lexicographically smallest order Kahn + min-heap Shorter code / also need SCC DFS Reverse topological order (DAG DP from sinks) DFS (post-order is already reverse topo) Very large graph, worried about recursion stack overflow Kahn Free Cycle Detection — Using Topological Sort to Validate a DAGCycle detection is a byproduct of topological sort — both implementations include it for free, no separate algorithm needed. Kahn’s method: after the run, check len(order). If < n, some nodes have an in-degree that never reached 0 — they’re stuck in a cycle → cycle exists. DFS method: gray meets gray means a cycle in three-color marking. Gray means “currently on the DFS path”; encountering a gray node again means we’ve walked back to ourselves, forming a back edge. Two reminders: You can’t use topological sort to detect cycles in an undirected graph (undirected graphs have no “in-degree” concept). Use union-find or DFS checking for non-parent visits instead. If you only need to detect a cycle without outputting the order, Kahn’s method can just keep a counter instead of storing order, saving some memory. Classic Problems — Course Schedule / Task SchedulingLC 207. Course Schedule: given numCourses and prerequisites [[a, b], ...] (you must take b before a), determine whether you can finish all courses. This is essentially just validating a DAG. LC 210. Course Schedule II: same graph, output the course order. Replace done += 1 with order.append(u), then return order if len(order) == n else []. Classic trap: edge direction. The problem says “you must take b before a”, meaning b is the prerequisite for a, so the graph edge should be b → a (b before a). Reversing the direction and getting WA is a rite of passage. Other must-solve problems: LC 802. Find Eventual Safe States — reverse graph + topological sort; safe = all paths terminate LC 269. Alien Dictionary — build edges from the first differing character of adjacent words, run topo sort LC 310. Minimum Height Trees — topo-sort-like, peel leaf nodes (degree=1) each round; the last 1–2 nodes are the answer LC 329. Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix — DP on a DAG, can use memoized DFS or topological DP LC 2192. All Ancestors of a Node in a Directed Acyclic Graph — merge ancestor sets in topological order LC 1857. Largest Color Value in a Directed Graph — topological order + color-count DP, cycle detection included Memory AidOne sentence: zero in-degree goes first; each departure trims one edge. Three contrasts: Dimension Kahn (BFS) DFS Post-Order Entry Nodes with in-degree 0 enqueued Any unvisited node, DFS Progress Dequeue → decrement neighbor in-degrees Recurse to bottom → exit stack Cycle detection Output count < n Gray meets gray Order Topological order falls out naturally Reverse the post-order array Recognition cheat sheet: See “prerequisite”, “dependency”, “predecessor task” → topological sort. Problem asks “can you finish?” → cycle check is enough; use Kahn’s counter. Problem asks “output the order” → Kahn storing order, or DFS post-order reversed. Requires “lexicographically smallest” → swap Kahn’s deque for heapq. DP on a DAG → iterate in topological order; predecessors are already computed, just transition. One thing to remember: topological sort is not a sorting algorithm — it’s a dependency resolution algorithm. The “order” it produces is one valid execution sequence and may not be unique.

title: Tree DP
content: One sentence: one DFS pass, and each node’s answer = subtree aggregate + its own contribution. At its core it’s post-order traversal + state propagated on nodes, returning bottom-up. Intuition — Post-order DFS + Subtree AggregationLinear DP reads state from the left; tree DP reads state from the subtree below. In other words, trees don’t need a new algorithm — you just replace “the previous state” with “the return values of all child nodes.” The core pattern boils down to one sentence: Write a dfs(node) that recursively post-orders both children, combines their return values, then returns the result to the parent. When we reach node u, we already have the results of dfs(u.left) and dfs(u.right). We need to decide two things: What does the current node contribute (update the global answer, or fold it into its own state) What does it return upward (what information about my subtree does the parent need to continue) These two things are often different. The animation below demonstrates this most clearly with the binary tree diameter (LC 543): the “path through me” that updates the global answer is left-chain + right-chain, but the “chain extending upward” that gets returned can only go one way — because a path can’t branch at the parent. Follow the post-order in the animation: leaf 4 → leaf 6 → node 5 → node 2 → leaf 3 → root 1. Each time a node is visited, the blue ↑ is the depth it returns to its parent, green is the longest path passing through it, and the red global ans is only refreshed when needed. Once you’ve watched this, every template below is just the same skeleton. Template — Python (dfs returns a tuple)The skeleton looks like this; almost every tree DP problem is a variant of it: Three things you must think through before writing a single line: What does an empty node return — this is the base case. Usually 0 or (0, 0), but some problems (like maximum path sum) need -inf. How many states go in the return tuple — single state (depth) / two states (take vs. skip) / more (binary tree cameras uses 3). Is this node’s contribution local or global — “the path passing through me” updates the global ans; “the chain extending to me” is what gets returned upward. Never mix the two. Two Classic FlavorsSubtree Aggregation — Binary Tree Diameter (LC 543)Diameter = the longest path between any two nodes. Key distinction: a path may “bend” at some node, but the bent segment cannot be passed upward. The same skeleton applies directly to: LC 124 Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (empty node returns 0, negative contributions clipped with max(L, 0)); LC 687 Longest Univalue Path (only extend to a child if its value matches). Take/Skip — House Robber III (LC 337)Each node is either robbed or not; if you rob it, its children cannot be robbed. Return (max value robbing me, max value skipping me): Note that skip_me uses max(L), not L[1] — when you skip the current node, children are free to be robbed or not, so take the better option. Extensions using this same skeleton: LC 968 Binary Tree Cameras — 3 states per node (place camera / covered / not covered), returns a 3-tuple. Maximum independent set / minimum vertex cover on trees — all follow this “take vs. skip” pattern. Advanced: Rerooting DP (Two-Pass DFS)The templates above assume a fixed root. If the problem asks for “the answer when each node is the root” (e.g. LC 834 Sum of Distances in Tree), brute-forcing a DFS from every node is . Rerooting DP uses two DFS passes: First DFS (post-order): fix node 0 as the root and compute dp[0]. Second DFS (pre-order): propagate downward, incrementally updating dp[child] = dp[parent] + delta. The key insight is figuring out “when we reroot from parent to child, what is the incremental change?” It’s generally an formula, giving total time. Memory Aid / Common MistakesOne-sentence mantra: post-order recurse both children, pack results into a tuple and return upward, update global answer along the way. Three points people get wrong repeatedly: Updating the global answer vs. returning to the parent are two separate operations — in diameter / maximum path sum problems, if you return the “bent path” upward, the parent sees a fork and everything goes wrong. The identity element for empty nodes — when maximizing and node values can be negative, don’t reflexively return 0; see LC 124 for negative-contribution clipping. The skip case — when skipping the current node, children can be taken or skipped freely, so use max(L), not L[1]. Nearly everyone steps on this bug the first time they write House Robber III. Decision cheat sheet: “Longest path / diameter on a tree” → subtree aggregation, return one extending chain. “Select nodes with no parent-child pair” → take/skip, return a tuple. “Answer for each node as root” → rerooting DP, two DFS passes. Exercises 1. Why does tree DP use post-order traversal? Can pre-order work? Post-order means “process children before processing the current node.” A node’s answer depends on its children’s return values, so post-order is required. In pre-order the children haven’t been computed yet, so there’s nothing to combine. The one exception is the second DFS in rerooting DP, which propagates the parent’s information down incrementally — that pass uses pre-order. 2. Why can't you mix "the path passing through me" with "the chain extending to me"? “Path through me” = left chain + me + right chain — an upside-down V that can be the global optimum. “Chain extending to me” = max(left, right) + me — a straight line. The difference is that a path can bend at me, but what I pass to my parent cannot bend, otherwise the parent sees a fork, and the grandparent gets even more confused. 3. Why does rerooting DP only need two DFS passes? The first DFS establishes the baseline “rooted at node 0.” Rerooting from parent to child involves exactly one topological change: the child’s subtree moves from “below the parent” to “above the parent.” The delta is computable, and we propagate it top-down in pre-order, for total work. LeetCode PracticeWarm-up: 104 Maximum Depth · 543 Diameter · 110 Balanced Binary Tree · 687 Longest Univalue Path Advanced: 124 Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum · 337 House Robber III · 968 Binary Tree Cameras · 834 Sum of Distances in Tree · 310 Minimum Height Trees

title: Trie (Prefix Tree)
content: Each node stores one character, and the path from root to leaf spells out a complete string. Strings with a common prefix share the leading nodes — that’s why it’s called a “prefix tree.” Both insert and lookup run in , independent of how many words are in the dictionary. Intuition — Shared Prefix, Shared NodesA hash set can look up a single word in , but it can’t answer “give me all words that start with app.” A trie spreads characters across a tree: strings that share a prefix follow the same path, and branching only happens at the first position where characters differ. After inserting apple, app, ant, bee: apple and app share the three nodes a -> p -> p; ant branches off after a; bee starts an entirely separate subtree. Three things to internalize at once: Each edge represents one character; each node represents the prefix accumulated so far. Nodes don’t store the whole string. is_end (shown as # in the diagram) is mandatory. Without it you can’t tell “app was explicitly inserted” from “app is just a waypoint on the path to apple.” Query cost is , where is the length of the query string. Whether the dictionary has ten thousand or a hundred million words is completely irrelevant. Comparison: Operation HashSet Trie Exact lookup Prefix query Not supported List all words starting with P full scan Walk to P, DFS subtree Memory Each word stored independently Shared prefixes; denser dictionary = more savings A trie isn’t about looking up a single word faster — it’s about batch operations over prefixes. That’s the only reason it exists. Animation — Watching Characters LandThe animation below inserts apple, app, ant, bee one by one, then demonstrates search("app") and search("ap"). Focus on three things: Shared prefix: apple already built the three nodes a-p-p; inserting app creates no new nodes, it just stamps a # on the last p. The # marker: once app‘s # is placed, search("app") returns True; but search("ap") — even though the path exists — returns False because p has no #. It’s a prefix, not a word that was actually inserted. Node count ≠ total character count: the four words have 13 characters in total, but the tree has only 11 nodes (the a-p-p segment is shared). The denser the dictionary, the greater the savings. Template — Python class TrieDictionary-based implementation; works with any character set; the preferred Python approach: Three implementation details: search and starts_with both call _walk. The only difference is whether the endpoint needs a # check. Any key outside the character set works as the end marker — # is just a convention. node.is_end = True is equally valid. Don’t write _walk recursively. Python recursion is slow and will blow the stack; use a plain for loop. Array-Based Variant (common in competitive programming / C++)When the character set is fixed, pre-allocate a node pool and use integer IDs instead of dict references — compact memory, cache-friendly: Which to pick: use the dict version for LeetCode in Python; switch to the array version when the character set is only lowercase letters, you’re chasing constant-factor speed, or you want to land in the top 5% of submissions. Advanced — 01-Trie for Maximum XOR LC 421. Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array: given an array of integers, find . The naive approach is . A 01-Trie brings it down to . The core idea in one sentence: treat each integer as a 30-bit binary string and insert it into a trie — the character set is just {0, 1}, hence “01-Trie.” Why does this solve maximum XOR? XOR’s defining property: bits that differ contribute 1. Starting from the most significant bit, greedily try to take the branch that is the opposite of the current bit — if that branch exists, this bit contributes 1; otherwise fall back. Because high bits outweigh all lower bits combined, the greedy is optimal. This problem is the signature 01-Trie application. Memorize the pattern — “from high bit to low bit + greedy take the opposite branch” — and every variant (count pairs whose XOR falls in a range, maximum XOR subarray, etc.) is just a twist on this same template. ApplicationsTries aren’t just interview fodder — they show up throughout production systems: Autocomplete / search-box suggestions: type a prefix, walk to its subtree, DFS to collect all words, rank by popularity. Longest-prefix matching in IP routing: a routing table is essentially a binary trie; an incoming packet walks from root to leaf, matching the longest prefix it finds. Spell-checking / fuzzy matching: DFS on the trie while allowing a small number of substitutions/insertions/deletions (edit distance) — much faster than scanning the full word list. Sensitive-word filtering (Aho-Corasick): multi-pattern string matching; add failure pointers to a trie and scan a text once to find all patterns. String XOR / bitwise extrema: see 01-Trie above. Suffix tree / suffix array family: index all suffixes of a string for fast substring queries. When to reach for a trie: any time a problem mentions “prefix,” “dictionary,” or “multi-pattern,” think trie first. Memory AidOne sentence: characters on the edges, prefixes on the paths, # at word endings. Three things to burn into muscle memory: Point Detail Node design children: dict[char, Node] + is_end: bool Time complexity Insert/lookup both , independent of dictionary size Common mistake End marker # is non-negotiable; omitting it makes prefixes and full words indistinguishable Decision cheat sheet: See “prefix” → Trie See “multiple strings queried together” → Trie See “maximum/minimum XOR” → 01-Trie See “sensitive words / multi-pattern matching” → Aho-Corasick (Trie + failure pointers) When writing the template, recite mentally: allocate node → walk to it → stamp the end marker. Three steps, never get it wrong. Exercises What specifically goes wrong without #? After inserting apple, search("app") would return True — because the path a-p-p does exist. But app was never actually inserted, so this is a false positive. The role of # is to distinguish “a node that lies on some path” from “the endpoint of a word that was explicitly inserted.” Why does the 01-Trie start from the high bit instead of the low bit? The XOR result is a binary number, and the highest bit’s weight exceeds the sum of all lower bits (). So if you can secure a 1 in the high bit, you should always do so, even at the cost of all lower bits. Greedy from the low bit can be overturned by a single high bit. How does a trie's memory footprint compare to a HashSet? Each trie node must store a dict (or a length-26 array), which isn’t cheap. But the denser the dictionary (more shared prefixes), the more memory is saved: ten thousand English words share so many prefixes that the node count is far smaller than the total character count. A sparse dictionary (every word has a unique prefix) actually costs more memory than a HashSet. LeetCode PracticeWarm-up: 208. Implement Trie (Prefix Tree) — pure template 1268. Search Suggestions System — autocomplete 648. Replace Words — shortest prefix matching Advanced: 212. Word Search II — Trie + grid DFS pruning 421. Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array — signature 01-Trie problem 336. Palindrome Pairs — reverse insertion + palindrome check 677. Map Sum Pairs — attach weights to nodes 745. Prefix and Suffix Search — two tries or suffix concatenation

title: Two-Pointer Techniques
content: One-liner: use the relative motion of two pointers to compress an brute force down to . This works because the problem hides a monotonicity — moving one pointer makes the “target” change monotonically, so there’s never any reason to backtrack. Intuition — Monotone Motion of Two PointersThe reason a brute-force double loop wastes time is that the inner loop rescans from the start every iteration, retrying combinations that are already known to be wrong. Two pointers are different: every step is informed by what the previous step revealed, so we never backtrack. Why can we get away with never backtracking? Because the problem has monotonicity: Opposing pointers: the array is sorted → moving left always increases sum, moving right always decreases it. Fast/slow pointers: the speed difference is constant → relative displacement grows monotonically over time; if they’re supposed to collide, they will. Two pointers, each walking at most N steps, combined: . In the animation below, watch how the green / red pointers “close in” and “give chase”: Read the three patterns below while keeping the animation in mind — the ideas will stick twice as well. Three Patterns — Opposing / Fast-Slow / Floyd Pattern Starting positions Motion Monotonicity exploited Classic problems Opposing Both ends Converge inward Array is sorted; sum changes monotonically with each move Two Sum II, 3Sum, Valid Palindrome Fast/Slow Same start / offset Same direction, different speeds Constant speed gap → relative displacement is monotone Linked list midpoint, in-place dedup Floyd Same start Same direction, fast takes 2 steps Cycle guarantees a catch-up (mod-L period) 141 Linked List Cycle, 142 Cycle Entry Memory hook: opposing pointers watch the sum, fast/slow watch the distance gap, Floyd watches the period. Why Opposing Pointers Can Discard an Entire ColumnWhen the array is sorted, if nums[left] + nums[right] < target, then pairing left with any value smaller than nums[right] will still be too small — the entire column is eliminated at once → we must left++. Symmetrically for right--. Each step eliminates a whole row or column, so N steps finish the job. Why “Container with Most Water” Always Moves the Shorter Line (LeetCode 11) Given a height array height, the -th vertical line runs from to . Pick two lines together with the x-axis to form a container; find the maximum water it can hold. Capacity depends on width and the shorter line: Two pointers start from both ends, and each step moves the shorter line. Why can’t this miss the optimal pair? Key lemma: suppose (left is the shorter line). Fix and move the right pointer to any ; capacity strictly decreases: (Step one: height ; step two: width .) Width: , strictly smaller. Height: height is locked by the short side ; no matter how tall is, we can only take , and if it’s shorter it’s even worse, so . Implication: the short line paired with any line to its right has at most — its potential is exhausted, and leaving it in can only shrink things further. So we safely discard it with left++. Symmetrically, when we discard the right side with right--. short i j water level = min(h[i], h[j]) = h[i] move short Moving the taller line: width shrinks, water level is still capped by the short side → pure loss; only moving the short side can unlock a higher water level. Loop invariant: the globally optimal pair always lies within the current window. Every discarded pair (short line paired with anything inside the window) has capacity the already-recorded , so the optimum is never discarded; the window shrinks by 1 each step, and steps close it completely → . 💡 What is a loop invariant? (click for a refresher) A loop invariant is a statement that remains true at the start of every iteration. It’s not code — it’s a promise about “where we are right now”; when the loop terminates, that promise directly becomes your answer. Proving “the entire loop is correct” head-on is hard, but you only need to verify three small things, and that’s equivalent to proving the loop is correct no matter how many iterations it runs (it’s essentially mathematical induction): Initialization: Does the statement hold before the loop begins? (The base case of induction.) Maintenance: Assuming it holds at the start of some iteration, does it still hold after that iteration completes? (The inductive step.) Termination: When the loop stops, does the invariant plus the fact that “the loop has ended” directly yield the answer? Applied to the container problem, the invariant is: “the globally optimal pair always lies within the current [left, right] window”: Initialization: the window starts as the entire array, so the optimal pair is certainly in it. Maintenance: each iteration only discards the short-side line, and the lemma guarantees every discarded pair doesn’t exceed the already-recorded value → the optimal pair is never discarded and remains in the shrunken window. Termination: when left == right the window closes and the loop stops; the maximum recorded during the process is the answer. With the invariant in hand, you never need to worry about “accidentally discarding the optimal pair in some step” — the maintenance clause has permanently closed off that possibility. This is exactly why two pointers can “never backtrack” with confidence: backtracking is unnecessary because everything discarded is genuinely useless. How to find your own invariant: ask yourself “At the start of this iteration, what have I already accomplished? What do each of my variables represent right now?” For example, slow = “the next position to write a result” ⟹ invariant: “[0, slow) is already the finished answer.” A good invariant often simultaneously explains why a variable has its name and why it points where it does. This is structurally identical to “discarding an entire column” above: there we discard a row/column of a sorted array; here we discard all pairs the short line can form. Why Fast/Slow Pointers Find the Midpointslow moves 1 step, fast moves 2. When fast reaches the tail, slow is exactly halfway — the distance gap grows at a rate of 1 per step, and that “time gap” is the answer. Templates — One Python Version EachOpposing pointers: Two Sum II Fast/slow pointers: Linked list midpoint Fast/slow pointers: In-place dedup (mnemonic: slow points to “the next position to write”) Floyd: Cycle detection + finding the cycle entry Why Floyd Works — Breaking Down the MathPin down the notation first (refer to the animation’s tail + cycle): : distance from head to the cycle entry, i.e., the tail length. : distance from the cycle entry to the meeting point, measured in the forward direction. : cycle length. Phase One: Why They Must Meet, and Why slow Hasn’t Completed a Full LapOnce both pointers are inside the cycle, slow moves 1 step per turn and fast moves 2 — fast gains exactly 1 step on slow per turn. Let denote the distance fast still needs to cover along the cycle to catch slow (measured in the forward direction). It obeys two iron rules: : purely because the cycle has length ; the distance between any two points on a cycle cannot be , regardless of where they entered. decreases by exactly 1 each step: fast closes the gap by 1 per turn; and because the relative step size is exactly 1, fast can’t “jump over” slow — it will land precisely on the cell where (so they must meet, not pass each other). cycle length = L forward D ≤ L-1 S slow F fast D decreases by 1 each step and never overshoots 0 ⇒ they meet at D=0 in at most L-1 steps. Putting it together: starting from and decreasing by 1 each step, they meet at in at most steps. In those steps slow has walked the same number of steps — less than one full lap ( steps). This is what justifies the next section’s claim that “slow’s total distance is exactly with no full-lap term.” How Far Has Each Pointer Traveled at the Meeting Point? slow: from the previous section, slow is caught before completing one lap (those steps are exactly ), so its total distance is . fast: double the speed means double the distance: . But fast’s distance can also be counted another way: travel to the entry, then loop full times around the cycle, then travel more to the meeting point, giving ( is the number of extra laps, ). Two expressions for the same distance, set equal: Subtract from both sides: Phase Two: Why Walking from the Meeting Point Locates the Cycle Entry in plain English: walking more steps from the meeting point = going around the cycle full times and then retreating , landing exactly at the cycle entry. Meanwhile, starting from head and walking steps also arrives at the entry. That’s why the template’s phase two is written the way it is: reset one pointer to head, set both pointers to 1 step per move and start simultaneously — after steps both land at the entry. This is a consequence forced by , not a coincidence. In the animation, the cell where green slow and red fast meet inside the cycle is exactly steps away from the cycle entry. Classic ProblemsWarm-up — one problem per pattern to build muscle memory: 167. Two Sum II — opposing pointers, bare template 11. Container With Most Water — opposing pointers + greedy (move the short line) 283. Move Zeroes — fast/slow; slow points to “next non-zero slot” 876. Middle of the Linked List — fast/slow standard 141. Linked List Cycle — Floyd intro Advanced — all about “figuring out where the monotonicity lives”: 15. 3Sum — sort + fix one element + opposing pointers; watch out for deduplication 42. Trapping Rain Water — opposing pointers + maintain left/right max; short side determines contribution 142. Linked List Cycle II — Floyd phase two, apply the template 287. Find the Duplicate Number — treat the array as a linked list, Floyd to find entry 75. Sort Colors — three pointers, Dutch national flag Practice Problems Why do opposing pointers require a sorted array? What if it's unsorted? Sorted → monotonicity → every move definitively shrinks the search space. Without sorting, that guarantee breaks. Two fallbacks: a hash table ( time + space), or sort first then use opposing pointers ( time, extra space). Which trade-off the problem calls for depends on the constraints. In Floyd's algorithm, after slow returns to head, why do two pointers moving at the same speed meet at the cycle entry? Because . Walking steps from the meeting point = going around the cycle times and retreating = the cycle entry. Walking steps from head also reaches the entry. Same speed, same time — they must meet at the entry. That’s all the magic in Floyd’s phase two. How do you modify in-place dedup to allow at most 2 duplicates? Look one position further back in the comparison: nums[fast] != nums[slow - 1]. That is, slow checks “the value written two writes ago”; a new element is allowed to be written only if it differs from that. To allow up to duplicates, compare against nums[slow - (k-1)]. The pattern generalizes. Memory AidOne-liner: two pointers moving in a consistent direction, making the target change monotonically, never backtracking. Three patterns + keywords: Pattern Keywords Trigger signal Opposing sorted + sum “two-sum / container / palindrome” Fast/Slow speed gap “midpoint / dedup / move zeroes” Floyd period “does the linked list have a cycle / find the entry / duplicate number” When you see a problem, ask first: is there monotonicity? Along which dimension? Once you answer that, two pointers follow naturally.

title: Advanced Optimization Techniques for Large-Scale ML Systems
content: This chapter covers cutting-edge optimization techniques in large-scale ML systems: from Zero-Overhead scheduling, DP Attention, and online weight updates, to FP8/INT4 training, speculative decoding, long-context optimization, and Diffusion LLMs. The body is markdown; key mechanisms are accompanied by interactive animations. 6.1 Zero-Overhead Batch SchedulingCore IdeaIn LLM inference, the CPU overhead of batch scheduling causes idle bubbles on the GPU. Zero-Overhead Scheduling achieves zero scheduling cost through CPU-GPU overlap: while the GPU executes the forward pass of the current batch, the CPU concurrently completes scheduling decisions and data preparation for the next batch. Key Technical Components1. Placeholder Buffering: Pre-allocate placeholder slots to avoid the overhead of dynamic memory allocation. When a new request arrives, only the placeholder needs to be filled — no tensor resizing required. 2. Async Scheduling: The scheduling logic runs in a separate thread and fully overlaps with GPU kernel execution via a double-buffering mechanism. 3. CPU-S and CPU-L Separation: CPU operations are split into short-latency (CPU-S) and long-latency (CPU-L) categories. CPU-S covers lightweight operations like token sampling and detokenization; CPU-L covers heavier operations like the scheduling policy and radix tree updates. Both are pipelined independently. The animation below illustrates the pipeline overlap between CPU-S, CPU-L, and the GPU, comparing “no overlap” versus “pipelined” execution modes: Overlap Scheduler Pseudocode Performance AnalysisLet GPU forward time be , CPU-S time be , and CPU-L time be : Without overlap: per-step latency With overlap: per-step latency When (usually the case), speedup . In a typical scenario where and , the speedup is about 1.29x. 6.2 DP Attention for MoEBackgroundIn Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, traditional Tensor Parallelism (TP) requires every GPU to hold a full copy of the KV cache. For models like DeepSeek-V3 (236B parameters, 128 experts), this leads to enormous memory waste. The Core Idea of DP AttentionUse Data Parallelism for the Attention layer (each GPU handles different requests and maintains its own KV cache), and Tensor/Expert Parallelism for the MLP/Expert layers. This means: KV cache does not need to be replicated across GPUs, greatly improving memory efficiency Attention computation requires no all-reduce, reducing communication volume Expert layers still use EP/TP to distribute parameters Communication PatternAn All-to-All communication is needed between Attention and MLP: each GPU sends its token hidden states to the GPU responsible for the corresponding expert. This is similar to MoE routing communication, but in the opposite direction. The interactive diagram below lets you adjust Num Heads, TP Degree, and Seq Length to compare the KV cache, communication, and compute costs of TP Attention versus DP Attention: DP Attention Configuration Example 6.3 Online Weight UpdatesMotivation and ChallengesIn RLHF/Online RL training, the policy model must be updated continuously. The traditional approach — saving and reloading checkpoints — introduces: High latency: Saving and loading a checkpoint can take tens of seconds to minutes Resource waste: The inference engine sits idle during training, and the training cluster sits idle during inference Staleness: The model version used for rollout lags behind the latest policy NCCL Broadcast ApproachLeveraging NCCL’s cross-node communication, weights are broadcast directly from training nodes to inference nodes: After completing a training step/epoch, the trainer triggers a weight broadcast Weights are synchronized to inference workers via NCCL all-gather or broadcast The inference engine atomically updates model weights (using double buffering) In-flight inference requests are unaffected (they complete using the old weights) Latency Optimization TechniquesChunked Transfer: Transfer the model layer-by-layer; update on the fly without waiting for all layers to finish. Priority Scheduling: Transfer embeddings and the last few layers first (they have the largest impact on outputs); transfer remaining layers asynchronously. Delta Compression: Transmit only the weight delta () and exploit sparsity to compress the transfer volume. Online Weight Update Code Architecture 6.4 FP8/INT4 Training for RLWhy Unified Precision MattersIn RL-for-LLM scenarios, using different precisions for training and inference leads to: Reward hacking: Quantization error introduces bias in the reward signal Train-inference gap: Training in BF16 but inferring in INT4/FP8 causes behavioral inconsistency Precision conversion overhead: Frequent quantize/dequantize cycles consume compute FP8 E4M3 FormatFP8 E4M3 uses 1 sign bit + 4 exponent bits + 3 mantissa bits, with a dynamic range of , making it well-suited for forward computation. E5M2 uses 5 exponent bits + 2 mantissa bits, offering a wider dynamic range, which makes it suitable for gradients. Dynamic ScalingTo maximize the effective utilization of FP8, a per-tensor or per-channel dynamic scaling factor is applied: Quantization: Dequantization: The interactive diagram below shows how a floating-point number is encoded into the sign/exponent/mantissa bits of FP8 E4M3, and computes the quantization error and dynamic scale factor: FP8 Quantization with Dynamic Scaling 6.5 Speculative Decoding in RLThe Rollout BottleneckIn RL training (e.g., PPO, GRPO), rollout (generating trajectories) accounts for 60–80% of total training time. Speculative Decoding uses a small draft model to accelerate generation: Basic Flow Draft: Use a small model (e.g., 1.5B) to quickly generate K tokens Verify: The large model (e.g., 70B) verifies the probability of all K tokens in a single pass Accept/Reject: Accept or reject draft tokens according to rejection sampling Correction: If a token is rejected, resample from the large model RL-Specific ConsiderationsOnline SFT for the Draft Model: During RL training, the policy model changes continuously. If the draft model is frozen, its acceptance rate will decline over time. Solutions: Every N RL steps, use the policy model’s rollout data to SFT-update the draft model Apply a knowledge distillation loss to keep the draft model tracking the policy distribution The training cost for the draft model is low (fewer parameters, data already available) Speedup AnalysisLet the acceptance rate be , draft length , and the draft-to-verify time ratio be : At , , , the speedup is approximately 2.5x. 6.6 Long-Context OptimizationDuoAttention: Retrieval vs Streaming HeadsA key observation: in multi-head attention, different heads serve different roles: Retrieval Heads (~25%): Responsible for retrieving information from the long context; their attention patterns are sparse and long-range. These heads require the full KV cache. Streaming Heads (~75%): Primarily attend to recent tokens and special positions (e.g., sink tokens); their patterns exhibit strong locality. These heads only need to retain the KV cache for a recent window plus sink tokens. Memory SavingsAssuming 75% of heads are streaming heads and only the most recent 1024 tokens’ KV is retained: At seq_len = 128K, this saves approximately 74.4% of KV cache memory. StreamingLLMStreamingLLM observes the “sink” phenomenon in attention: the first few tokens always receive high attention scores regardless of their content. Therefore, only the following need to be retained: Sink tokens (KV cache for the first 4 tokens) Recent window (KV cache for the most recent N tokens) This allows LLMs to handle streaming input of unlimited length with a constant KV cache size. 6.7 Diffusion LLMsFrom Autoregressive to Non-AutoregressiveTraditional LLMs are autoregressive: they generate one token at a time, with total latency scaling linearly with sequence length. Diffusion LLMs (such as LLaDA — Large Language Diffusion with mAsking) adopt a different generation paradigm: How LLaDA Works Forward Process (training): Randomly mask input tokens (similar to BERT’s MLM, but with the mask ratio varying continuously from 0 to 1) Reverse Process (inference): Starting from all-masked, progressively “denoise” to recover tokens Block-wise Decoding: Multiple tokens can be recovered simultaneously at each step (confidence-based unmasking) Advantages and Challenges Parallel generation: Multiple tokens are recovered per step, reducing the total number of steps (e.g., 128 tokens in only 8–16 steps) Global consistency: Each step can “see” the current state of all positions, avoiding the local decisions inherent in AR generation Speed vs. quality trade-off: More diffusion steps = higher quality; fewer steps = faster generation Challenge: Current quality is still slightly behind same-scale AR models, though the gap is narrowing The animation below shows how tokens are progressively “denoised” from random masks into coherent text (block-parallel decoding, multiple tokens recovered per step): Exercises Exercise 1: Computing the Theoretical Speedup of Overlap Scheduling Given the following parameters: GPU forward pass time: = 20ms CPU-S (sampling + detokenize) time: = 1.2ms CPU-L (scheduling + radix tree) time: = 5.8ms Compute: (a) per-step latency without overlap; (b) per-step latency with overlap; (c) speedup; (d) if increases to 25ms (exceeding ), how does the speedup change? Key formulas: Without overlap: With overlap: Note that overlap can fully hide CPU-L cost only when . When , the GPU incurs idle time. Solution: (a) Without overlap: ms (b) With overlap: ms (CPU-L fully overlapped within GPU forward) (c) Speedup: latency reduction (d) When = 25ms: Without overlap: ms With overlap: ms Speedup When CPU-L is large, the benefit of overlap is more pronounced, but the GPU now has a 5ms idle bubble (ms). Consider optimizing CPU-L or increasing batch size to raise . Exercise 2: DP Attention Memory Savings Calculation Given the following MoE model configuration: Num KV heads (GQA): 8 Head dimension: 128 Sequence length: 32768 Total batch size: 128 requests TP/DP degree: 8 GPUs Precision: FP16 (2 bytes per element) Compute: (a) KV cache size per GPU in TP Attention mode; (b) KV cache size per GPU in DP Attention mode; (c) memory savings percentage; (d) if batch size doubles to 256, how does the savings ratio change? KV cache size formula: Solution: (a) TP Attention — KV cache per GPU: Each GPU needs the full batch’s KV cache (GQA heads are not split): (b) DP Attention — KV cache per GPU: Each GPU handles only requests: (c) Memory savings: , i.e., (d) With batch_size = 256: TP: GB DP: GB (256/8=32) Savings ratio is still (independent of batch size!) The savings ratio depends on the DP degree, not on batch size. This is the elegance of DP Attention. Exercise 3: FP8 Quantization Error Analysis Assume a weight tensor follows a normal distribution with (typical LLM initialization). Tensor size: elements Using FP8 E4M3 (max representable = 448) Per-tensor dynamic scaling Compute: (a) expected tensor max (); (b) scale factor; (c) effective precision after quantization (minimum distinguishable step); (d) approximate quantization MSE. Quantization error can be approximated as uniform over , with variance . For a typical value (): scales to , step , original step . (d) Approximate quantization MSE: Simplified estimate : , relative to the ratio is . Exercise 4 (Bonus): Speculative Decoding Acceptance Rate Given per-token acceptance rate and draft length : Compute: (a) expected number of accepted tokens per verify call; (b) if the draft model is 10x faster than the target model, what is the end-to-end speedup? Coding Exercise A: Implementing FP8 Quantization and Dequantization Implement per-tensor dynamic-scaling FP8 E4M3 quantization/dequantization with error analysis and visualization.
