Per-AllReduce communication volume (ring): bytes 25 KB/token. (b) What DP Attention replaces it with: Zero AllReduces for the Attention portion! Each GPU independently computes the complete attention for its own batch subset (since the KV cache is also DP-distributed). The Expert portion still uses 2 All-to-Alls (dispatch + combine), present in both schemes. (c) Total communication volume per token: Traditional TP+EP: AllReduce: MB/token All-to-All (EP): MB/token Total MB/token DP Attention+EP: AllReduce: 0 (no communication needed for attention!) All-to-All (EP): MB/token Total MB/token Savings: 3 MB/token of AllReduce bandwidth eliminated, reducing communication volume by approximately 64%. This is the core value of DP Attention for MoE models: it eliminates all collective communication overhead from the attention layers. Exercise 6: Loss Scaling Design for FP8 Training FP8 E4M3 has a representable range of . In RL training, gradients can have outliers exceeding 1000: FP8 E4M3 max = 448 RL training gradient variance is 3–5x higher than SFT Policy exploration leads to wider activation ranges Answer: (a) What happens to gradient outliers without loss scaling? (b) Design a dynamic loss scaling strategy; (c) Why is FP8 training harder in RL settings than in supervised training? Solution: (a) Consequences without loss scaling: Gradient values > 448 overflow to NaN or Inf → parameter updates become NaN → training diverges completely. Even a single overflowing element will “infect” all GPUs’ gradients during AllReduce. (b) Dynamic Loss Scaling Strategy: Advanced optimization: use per-tensor scaling (different scales for different layers), since gradient magnitudes for attention layers and FFN layers can differ substantially. (c) Why FP8 is harder in RL: Higher gradient variance: RL reward signals are noisy (from a reward model or rule-based verification), unlike the clean labels in SFT, resulting in 3–5x higher gradient variance Policy exploration: RL encourages the model to explore diverse outputs, widening the range of activation values and increasing overflow risk Non-stationarity: RL data distribution shifts as the policy changes (on-policy), making gradient statistics unstable and requiring more frequent dynamic scaling adjustments More frequent outliers: When the model produces very good or very bad outputs, reward differences are large → large advantage → large gradients → high overflow risk Mitigations: more conservative initial scale, shorter growth interval, per-tensor scaling + delayed scaling (using amax statistics from prior steps to pre-set the scale). Exercise 7: Speculative Decoding in RL Rollout Using speculative decoding to accelerate generation in GRPO rollout: Draft model: 1B parameters Target model (Actor): 70B parameters Draft length Per-token acceptance rate Each sequence generates 512 tokens Compute: (a) expected output tokens per verify step; (b) how many target model forward passes are needed to generate 512 tokens? (c) As RL training progresses, does the draft model’s distribution remain close enough to the actor’s? What happens? Solution: (a) Expected output tokens per verify step: Accounting for the bonus token guaranteed by rejection sampling, in practice tokens/step. (b) Required target model forward passes: verify passes. Compare with 512 passes required without speculative decoding. Speedup (draft cost is negligible; 1B vs 70B cost ratio is roughly 1:70). (c) Draft model distribution drift: As RL training proceeds, the actor (70B) distribution drifts away from the initial policy. If the draft model (1B) is frozen, its distribution will increasingly mismatch: Acceptance rate drops: may fall from 0.7 to 0.4–0.5, significantly reducing speedup Early training: actor changes little, draft still works → high speedup Late training: actor has drifted substantially → draft becomes nearly useless Solutions: Periodically use the actor’s outputs to online SFT the draft model (SFT is cheap for a 1B model) Use an earlier checkpoint of the actor as the draft (update draft = actor[step-N] every N steps) Adaptive K: when acceptance rate drops, reduce draft length K to minimize wasted compute Chapter SummaryThis chapter covered cutting-edge optimization techniques in ML systems: Zero-Overhead Scheduling: Eliminate scheduling overhead via CPU-GPU overlap and double-buffering DP Attention: Optimize memory efficiency for MoE models, reducing KV cache demand by a factor of DP_degree Online Weight Updates: Use NCCL broadcast for seamless weight synchronization between training and inference FP8 Training: Unify training and inference precision, eliminating the train-inference gap Speculative Decoding: Accelerate RL rollout with a draft model + online SFT Long Context: DuoAttention exploits head functional specialization to save KV cache Diffusion LLMs: Non-autoregressive generation; block-parallel decoding breaks sequential dependencies This post is Chapter 6 of the ML Systems series. title: CUDA Graph: A Deep Dive
content: An interactive visualization guide to understanding GPU execution optimization. Every GPU kernel launch carries CPU overhead; CUDA Graph records an entire kernel sequence into a graph and replays it with a single launch. This post is written in Markdown, with interactive animations illustrating the key mechanisms. 1. The Problem: Death by a Thousand Kernel LaunchesEvery GPU kernel launch carries CPU overhead. For large kernels this is negligible, but modern deep learning runs hundreds of small kernels per step. The animation below compares the CPU/GPU timeline with and without Graph. Without it, the CPU spends most of its time on driver overhead (red gaps) while the GPU idles waiting for the next launch instruction. With Graph, a single launch triggers the entire kernel sequence. 2. How CUDA Graph Works: Three PhasesCUDA Graph operates in three phases: Capture: All GPU operations are recorded into a graph structure. No actual computation happens during this phase. Instantiate: The graph is compiled into an executable form. Dependencies are validated and resources are allocated. This usually happens automatically when capture ends. Replay: The entire graph is executed via a single CPU launch. This is the fast path. The captured graph records all operations and their dependencies as a DAG — for example: Input Buffer → {LayerNorm, Attention} → MatMul → GELU → Output Buffer. 3. Graph-Friendly vs. Non-Graph-Friendly CodeThe basic rule: everything captured must be identical on every replay — same operations, same shapes, same memory addresses. The interactive checker below lets you click each line of code to determine whether it is Graph-Friendly: Operations That Break Graph Capture Graph-Friendly Patterns Data-dependent control flow Fixed-shape tensor ops (matmul, conv) Dynamic tensor shapes In-place buffer updates (.copy_()) Memory allocation / deallocation Static control flow (no runtime branches) CPU-GPU sync (.item(), .cpu()) Pre-allocated memory pools print on GPU tensors Fixed kernel grid dimensions Variable-length loops cuDNN/cuBLAS with fixed parameters cudaMalloc / cudaFree Pad to max shape + masking cudaStreamSynchronize Condition checks performed outside the graph 4. Memory Model: Why Addresses MatterDuring Capture the GPU memory layout is recorded: During Replay the same addresses must be used — only the data can change. If a tensor gets reallocated to a new address (e.g., 0x7f02_0000 → new_alloc [8, 512]), the replay will fail. Key rule: You can modify the data at a recorded address (via .copy_()), but you cannot change the address itself. This means: no reallocating memory, no changing shapes, no creating new tensors during replay. 5. Strategies for Efficient UseStrategy 1: Graph Pool / CacheCache graphs for known batch sizes: Strategy 2: Segmented PipelineOnly use Graph for the static, repeated core; let dynamic pre/post-processing run normally: Strategy 3: LLM Decode Mode (Best Use Case) Why this scenario works so well: Every decode step executes exactly the same operations and shapes (1 token). The only thing that changes is the data content. This is the perfect use case for CUDA Graph. 6. When Does CUDA Graph Actually Help? Scenario Without Graph With Graph Speedup LLM Decode (small model) ~2.1ms/token ~0.7ms/token 3x ResNet-50 inference ~4.2ms ~2.8ms 1.5x Large matmul (4096×4096) ~12ms ~11.5ms 1.04x Training step (many small kernels) ~8ms ~5ms 1.6x Rules of thumb: Many small kernels (each <100μs) → huge gains (2–5x) Medium kernels (100μs – 1ms) → moderate gains (1.3–2x) Few large kernels (each >10ms) → almost no gain (<1.1x) 7. Refactoring Patterns: Before & AfterPattern 1: Dynamic Shapes → Padded Static Shapes Pattern 2: Conditional Logic → Multiple Graphs Pattern 3: Internal Allocation → Pre-allocated Pool 8. Decision Flowchart: Should You Use CUDA Graph?Answer each question in order; all must be “yes” to recommend it: Does the workload execute repeatedly with the same shapes? (No → skip) Are the kernels small (each <1ms)? (No → probably not worth it) Can all memory be pre-allocated? (No → refactor first) No data-dependent branches inside? (No → split into multiple segments) Will it be replayed many times (>100)? (No → skip) All satisfied → Use CUDA Graph! Expect 1.5–5x speedup. 9. Common Pitfalls and SolutionsPitfall: Forgetting to Warm Up Before Capture. CUDA lazily initializes its context, cuDNN algorithm selection, and JIT compilation. If you capture before warming up, these one-time operations get baked into the graph. Pitfall: Forgetting .clone() When Using Graph Output. The output tensor is a fixed buffer; if you don’t clone it before the next replay, the data will be overwritten. Pitfall: cuDNN Benchmark Mode. cuDNN benchmark mode selects different algorithms across runs; the graph may capture a suboptimal one. Pitfall: Graph Pool Memory Fragmentation. Each graph captures its own memory pool; too many graphs leads to GPU memory fragmentation. Use a shared pool instead. Pitfall: Gradient Accumulation Inside a Graph. If you graph a training step, gradients accumulate in the same buffer — be careful about where you zero gradients (inside or outside the graph). 10. Quick Reference Card Pre-graph Checklist: All tensor shapes are fixed No .item() / .cpu() / print inside No dynamic memory allocation inside No data-dependent branches Warmup iterations completed cudnn.benchmark disabled or stabilized Outputs cloned before next replay Will replay >100 times This post’s body is rendered Markdown, with 2 interactive animations embedded as isolated iframes via the custom {% anim %} tag, sourced from the Arkive tutorial.

title: DP Attention: Eliminating KV Cache Duplication
content: In MoE large-model inference, the conventional TP + EP approach causes every GPU to hold a complete copy of the KV Cache, leading to severe memory redundancy. DP Attention eliminates this redundancy entirely by having each GPU handle only its own requests. This post compares the two approaches (4 GPU, 8 Expert example) with interactive animations. Conventional approach: TP (Attention) + EP (Experts)In the conventional approach, Attention uses Tensor Parallelism (each GPU computes 1/N of the heads), and Experts use Expert Parallelism (each GPU holds a subset of Experts). The problem: every GPU must hold a complete KV Cache for all requests — N-fold redundancy. The animation below shows the full flow for one layer in the conventional approach: initial KV Cache redundancy → Attention (TP) + AllReduce → All-to-All dispatch → Expert computation → All-to-All combine: Communication overhead per layer: Attention communication: AllReduce (2× per layer, merging partial head results) Expert communication: All-to-All (2× per layer, dispatch + combine) KV Cache: every GPU stores KV for all requests → EP/TP redundant copies DP Attention: DP (Attention) + EP (Experts)DP Attention switches Attention to Data Parallel: each GPU handles one request and independently computes the full Attention (all heads) by itself. The Attention parameters are replicated on every GPU, but Attention parameters are very small (~1% of the model), so the cost of replication is negligible. Key benefit: each GPU only stores the KV Cache for its own request — zero redundancy — and the Attention phase requires zero cross-GPU communication. The animation below shows the DP Attention approach: initial zero-redundancy KV Cache → Attention (DP, zero communication!) → All-to-All dispatch → Expert computation → All-to-All combine: Notice the contrast: compared to the conventional approach, DP Attention has no communication at all during the entire Attention phase — one layer is left with only the 2× All-to-All for Experts, and no AllReduce whatsoever. Dataflow diagram: how a batch flows through one layer (step by step)Just looking at “compute + communication” isn’t intuitive enough. The step-by-step animation below traces the data itself: a batch of 4 sequences (1 per GPU) enters, then walks through Attention (DP, zero communication) → Router → All-to-All dispatch → Expert → All-to-All combine. Click Next → one step at a time; pay attention to: during Attention, each sequence is computed locally, while in MoE, sequences are broken into tokens and scattered by All-to-All to different experts, then reassembled. Comparison summary Metric ❌ Conventional TP + EP ✓ DP Attention + EP Attention communication AllReduce (2× per layer) Zero! (each GPU computes independently) Expert communication All-to-All (2× per layer) All-to-All (2× per layer) KV Cache copies EP/TP copies (redundant!) 1 copy (zero redundancy) Total KV Cache size × EP/TP factor Minimized Attention parameters Sharded by TP Replicated per GPU (~1% of params) Core trade-off: DP Attention trades “replicating a small slice of Attention parameters” for “eliminating KV Cache redundancy + eliminating Attention communication”. In MoE models, the KV Cache is typically the dominant memory cost during inference, making this trade-off extremely worthwhile — which is why models like DeepSeek-V2/V3 use DP Attention at inference time. This post renders as markdown with 2 interactive animations embedded via the custom {% anim %} tag in isolated iframes, sourced from the Arkive tutorial.

title: Distributed Training and Communication Primitives
content: As model scale grows exponentially, a single GPU can no longer hold an entire model. This post systematically covers data/tensor/pipeline/sequence/expert parallelism, NCCL collective communication primitives, Ring AllReduce, FSDP/ZeRO, and communication–computation overlap — the core mechanisms of distributed training. The body is markdown, with interactive animations for key mechanisms (step through with buttons). 3.0 Why Do We Need Distributed Training?As model scale grows exponentially (GPT-3: 175B, PaLM: 540B, Llama 3: 405B), a single GPU can no longer hold an entire model’s parameters, gradients, and optimizer states. Distributed training spreads computation and storage across multiple devices, making it possible to train truly massive models. Core challenge: Minimize communication overhead and maximize GPU utilization while preserving mathematical training equivalence. Three fundamental parallelism strategies can be combined (called 3D Parallelism): Strategy What Gets Split Communication Pattern When to Use Data Parallelism (DP) Data (batch) AllReduce gradients Model fits on a single GPU Tensor Parallelism (TP) Per-layer parameters AllReduce / AllGather A single layer is too large Pipeline Parallelism (PP) Layer-wise split Point-to-point Send/Recv Model has many layers 3.1 Parallelism Strategy ComparisonData ParallelismCore idea: Each GPU holds a complete replica of the model. A mini-batch is evenly divided into micro-batches; each GPU independently runs forward and backward passes, then gradients are synchronized via AllReduce. A Mini-Batch (B=32) is distributed to 4 GPUs, each holding a complete model replica. After independent computation, gradients are synchronized through AllReduce — after synchronization all GPUs hold identical gradients, and parameters stay consistent after the update. Advantages and limitations Simple to implement; PyTorch’s DistributedDataParallel works out of the box Communication volume: each iteration requires AllReducing all gradients (2M bytes, where M = parameter count) Limitation: model must fit in a single GPU’s memory Limitation: communication overhead grows linearly with GPU count (though Ring AllReduce mitigates this) The animation below steps through the Data Parallelism training flow (data splitting → Forward/Backward → AllReduce → parameter update): Tensor ParallelismCore idea: Split a single layer’s weight matrix across multiple GPUs; each GPU computes a partial result, then communicate to merge. Megatron-LM first proposed this approach systematically. Column Parallel: , each GPU gets , Y = [Y₁, Y₂] (concat); no communication needed in the forward pass. Row Parallel: , requires AllReduce to sum partial results . Megatron-LM’s MLP sharding strategy In the Transformer MLP, the first linear layer uses column parallelism and the second uses row parallelism, so the forward pass only needs one AllReduce and the backward pass also only needs one AllReduce: The animation below steps through the Tensor Parallel MLP compute flow (column parallel → GeLU → row parallel → AllReduce): Pipeline ParallelismCore idea: Split the model into stages by layer, placing each stage on a different GPU. Data flows between stages as micro-batches. For example: Stage 0 (Layers 0–5) on GPU 0, Stage 1 (Layers 6–11) on GPU 1, and so on. Bubble Ratio The central problem with pipeline parallelism is the pipeline bubble — time GPUs spend idle waiting. where = number of pipeline stages and = number of micro-batches. Increasing the number of micro-batches reduces the bubble ratio. Common scheduling strategies GPipe: Complete all forward micro-batches first, then all backward passes 1F1B: Interleave forward and backward passes to reduce peak memory Interleaved 1F1B: Each GPU holds multiple non-contiguous stages, further reducing bubbles The animation below can be toggled between GPipe and 1F1B schedules, letting you step through the Forward/Backward data flow and bubbles time-step by time-step: 3D Parallelism (Hybrid Parallelism)When training truly large models in practice, DP + TP + PP are typically used simultaneously. For example, Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) uses (2048 GPUs): Dimension Degree Notes Tensor Parallelism 8 8 GPUs within a single node (NVLink high bandwidth) Pipeline Parallelism 8 Cross-node; small communication volume (only activations) Data Parallelism 32 2048 / (8×8) = 32-way data parallelism Total GPUs — 8 × 8 × 32 = 2048 Design principles TP stays intra-node: leverages NVLink/NVSwitch high bandwidth (900 GB/s on H100) PP crosses nodes: point-to-point communication volume is small, lower bandwidth requirement DP scales across the remaining dimension: use gradient accumulation to further hide communication Sequence ParallelismWhen sequence lengths are long (e.g., 128K+ tokens), even the activations for a single layer can blow up memory. Sequence parallelism shards the sequence dimension across multiple GPUs. The animation below shows the switch between TP regions and SP regions (4 GPUs): Core idea: shard along the sequence dimension in non-TP regions. Tensor Parallelism already shards Attention and FFN across cards. But operations like LayerNorm and Dropout still keep the full-sequence activation on every card — which is redundant. TP region (already sharded): QKV Proj → Attention → O Proj → FFN SP region (sequence-sharded): LayerNorm, Dropout, Residual Add TP-to-SP transition: AllReduce → ReduceScatter (forward) / AllGather (backward) Benefit Notes Memory savings Activation memory reduced to 1/TP_size (e.g., TP=8 → 87.5% activation savings) Communication overhead No extra communication! The existing AllReduce is split into ReduceScatter + AllGather Megatron-SP code sketch Activation shapes at the same layer: Normal vs TP vs TP+SP comparisonWalking through every intermediate tensor in one transformer block, comparing three columns: Left NORMAL: single GPU retains all activations, this is the baseline Middle TP only: TP=8 shards along hidden / heads, but LN i/o and residuals are rows TP cannot shard (still full (b,s,h)) Right TP+SP: SP layered on top of TP, shards along seq the parts TP cannot touch — compressing the residual/LN region down to 1/T as well Config: 70B (h=8192, n_h=64, d_k=128), b=1, s=2048, FP16, T=8. Click [Next] to add one row at a time; pay close attention to Steps 6/7/11: in the two TP columns x_attn/LN2/x_out are a stubborn 32 MB — SP rescues them down to 4 MB. The final frame gives the formal Korthikanti formula: NORMAL 1850 MB → TP 373 MB (5×) → TP+SP 224 MB (8.3×), the extra ~1.7× SP saves on top of TP comes entirely from those residual/LN i/o rows. ★ marks the big-ticket items — O(s²) at s=8192 is a single 17 GB/layer term; it’s exactly what FlashAttention targets. Three region types, three sharding dimensions — understood in one row Region Sharding dim Per-GPU shape Who shards it SP region (LN i/o, residual) along seq (b, s/T, h) SP TP region, attention (Q, K, V, scores, softmax, ctx) along heads (b, n_h/T, s, d_k) etc. TP TP region, MLP (up, GeLU) along hidden (b, s, 4h/T) TP Boundary transients (x1, x2 at TP region entry; attn_out, down at TP region exit) Full (b, s, h), but partial sum, immediately reduced by communication — (none, intermediate state) Boundary transients look like they save nothing — but they are ephemeral states that computation flows through, immediately consumed by reduce-scatter or @ matmul as soon as they’re computed, and never live in memory simultaneously. In the peak memory accounting they count as one copy, not all transients at once. Why ~8× savings SP region (LN i/o, residual): largest contributor (6+ copies of (b,s,h) per layer), sharded along seq → 1/T TP region attention: O(s²) term sharded by heads → 1/T TP region MLP: 4× fat tensors (up + GeLU) sharded along hidden → 1/T Boundary transients: not sharded, but only alive momentarily, counted as one copy in peak Full formula (Korthikanti et al. 2022): activation per layer goes from 34·s·b·h + 5·a·s²·b → (34·s·b·h + 5·a·s²·b) / T, a full 1/T saving. Paired with selective recomputation to cut ~80% of O(s²) → in 70B training, per-GPU per-layer activation drops from 1.85 GB to ~50 MB. For a detailed dissection of activation shapes at each position in the Transformer (x_in/Q/K/V/scores/MLP up and the three orders of magnitude, which tier FlashAttention eliminates, why output logits are 524 MB), see LLM Inference §4.1 “Where Activations Actually Live in the Transformer”. Expert ParallelismIn Mixture of Experts (MoE) models, different experts are distributed across different GPUs. Each token is routed to top-k experts by a router. The animation below shows token routing and All-to-All (4 GPUs, 8 Experts, top-1): MoE + Expert Parallelism execution flow: Input Tokens [B, S, H] → Router (softmax → top-k) → All-to-All (dispatch tokens) → Expert FFN (local compute) → All-to-All (combine results) → Output [B, S, H]. GPU distribution example (8 Experts, EP=4): GPU 0 holds E0, E1; GPU 1 holds E2, E3; GPU 2 holds E4, E5; GPU 3 holds E6, E7. Advantages Challenges Parameter count can scale 10×, compute only ~2× (each token activates only top-k experts) All-to-All communication: each token must be sent to the GPU holding its target expert Each GPU only stores a subset of expert parameters Load imbalance: popular experts may receive too many tokens (requires a load balancing loss) Orthogonally composable with DP/TP/PP Token dropping: tokens are dropped when an expert’s buffer is full DeepSeek-V3’s EP in practice 3.2 NCCL Collective Communication PrimitivesNVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) provides the low-level communication operations needed for distributed training. Understanding these primitives is foundational. Operation Description Input → Output Comm volume (N GPUs, M bytes) Broadcast Send one GPU’s data to all GPUs 1 copy → N identical copies Reduce Reduce data from all GPUs to one GPU N copies → 1 aggregated copy AllReduce Reduce data from all GPUs; result goes to all GPUs N copies → N identical aggregated copies AllGather Gather data from all GPUs to all GPUs ReduceScatter Reduce, then scatter shards to each GPU Key insight: AllReduce = ReduceScatter + AllGather. This decomposition is the heart of the Ring AllReduce algorithm. Select different primitives and watch how data flows among 4 GPUs. Each GPU initially holds a differently colored data block: Communication Volume ComparisonThe chart below shows per-primitive communication volume with 4 GPUs and 1 GB of parameters (AllReduce comm volume = ; others = . N=4, M=1GB): 3.3 Ring AllReduce Algorithm Deep DiveRing AllReduce is one of the most classic AllReduce implementations, introduced into deep learning training by Baidu in 2017. Its core advantage is that communication volume is independent of GPU count (per-GPU bandwidth utilization stays constant). Algorithm steps — Ring AllReduce has two phases, each with N-1 steps (N = number of GPUs): Phase 1: Reduce-Scatter — after N-1 steps, each GPU holds 1/N of the final result Phase 2: AllGather — after another N-1 steps, each GPU holds the complete final result The animation below walks through each GPU’s chunk contents step by step with concrete values (ring topology; each GPU only sends to its right neighbor): Ring AllReduce pseudocode Communication Volume DerivationSetup: = number of GPUs, = gradient size per GPU (bytes). Each GPU splits its gradients into chunks, each of size . Phase 1: Reduce-Scatter — each step, every GPU sends 1 chunk to its right neighbor; N-1 steps total (so each chunk passes through all N GPUs and gets accumulated). Phase 2: AllGather — each step, every GPU sends 1 fully-reduced chunk to its right neighbor; again N-1 steps. Total communication volume: Key property: communication volume is almost independent of GPU count! When is large, , so per-GPU communication approaches . Whether you have 4 GPUs or 4096, the total data each card sends is essentially the same. Comparison: Naive AllReduce (tree-based) Method Per-GPU sent N=4 N=64 N=1024 Naive (one-to-all) 3M 63M 1023M Ring AllReduce 1.5M 1.97M 1.998M Bandwidth utilization: In Ring AllReduce, every step has every GPU simultaneously sending and receiving data (full duplex), giving bandwidth utilization of . In the naive approach, most of the time only the root node is communicating while other GPUs sit idle. 3.4 FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel) / ZeROMicrosoft’s ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) and PyTorch’s FSDP break through data parallelism’s memory limits by sharding optimizer states, gradients, and parameters. Memory Breakdown (Mixed Precision Training)For a model with parameters, training with Adam + mixed precision, per-GPU memory usage is: Component Precision Memory (bytes) Parameters (FP16) FP16 Gradients (FP16) FP16 Parameter master copy (FP32) FP32 Adam momentum (FP32) FP32 Adam variance (FP32) FP32 Total ZeRO’s Three Stages Stage What Gets Sharded Memory Comm Volume Stage 1 Optimizer States Same as DP Stage 2 Optimizer + Gradients Same as DP Stage 3 Everything (including Parameters) 1.5× increase FSDP Memory CalculatorDrag the sliders to adjust parameter count, GPU count, and per-GPU memory capacity; compare DDP vs. the three ZeRO stages’ per-GPU memory usage: FSDP execution flow (Gather-Compute-Scatter) 3.5 torch.distributed API in PracticeInitializing the Process Group AllReduce Example AllGather Example ReduceScatter Example Point-to-Point Communication with Send/Recv 3.6 Communication Strategy Overhead ComparisonCommunication patterns and overhead differ dramatically across parallelism strategies. The table below compares per-iteration communication volume under different configurations: Strategy Primitive Per-GPU comm volume per iteration Frequency DDP AllReduce Every backward step FSDP (ZeRO-3) AllGather + ReduceScatter Every layer forward + backward Tensor Parallel AllReduce per layer Every layer forward + backward Pipeline Parallel P2P Send/Recv Every micro-batch Trade-off: FSDP Stage 3 has 50% more communication volume than DDP, but the memory savings let you train models N times larger or use much bigger batch sizes. What Is a CUDA Stream?A CUDA Stream is an ordered command queue on the GPU. Think of it as a conveyor belt: Operations within the same stream execute strictly in order (FIFO) Operations across different streams can run in parallel — the GPU hardware schedules them automatically By default, all operations go to stream 0 (the default stream), making everything serial Single stream (serial): total time = A + copy + B. Multiple streams (parallel): total time = max(A+B, copy). Key hardware basis: The GPU has independent hardware engines: SMs (Streaming Multiprocessors) for compute, Copy Engines (CE) for data movement, NVLink/PCIe DMA for cross-GPU communication. Multi-stream parallelism works because these engines are physically independent — it’s real hardware parallelism, not software-simulated concurrency. Communication–Computation OverlapThe performance bottleneck in distributed training is often not communication itself but communication blocking computation. The core idea: keep the GPU doing useful work while waiting for data transfer, effectively “hiding” communication latency. Why can they overlap? With the concept of multiple CUDA streams, the answer is natural: put communication and computation on different streams and the hardware runs them in parallel. No overlap (naive): communication and computation are serial, Total = T_compute + T_comm With overlap: communication and computation run in parallel, Total = max(T_compute, T_comm) Technique 1: Gradient Bucketing (DDP) DDP doesn’t fire off a communication for every individual gradient; instead it packs multiple gradients into a “bucket” (default 25 MB), starting from the last layer: Backward computes gradient for Layer N → placed into Bucket 1 Bucket 1 is full → triggers async AllReduce (on the communication stream) Meanwhile, the compute stream keeps computing gradients for Layers N-1, N-2, … By the time all backward passes are done, the earlier AllReduces have long since completed Technique 2: FSDP Prefetching FSDP AllGathers the next layer’s parameters while computing the current layer. Both forward and backward passes use prefetching. During the forward pass, a layer’s parameters are freed immediately after computation to save memory. During the backward pass, three streams work simultaneously: compute current layer’s gradients | prefetch next layer’s parameters | send previous layer’s gradients (async ReduceScatter). Technique 3: Async Communication (manual control) The low-level API allows manually implementing overlap: GPU hardware perspective: why overlap works Compute stream: kernels execute on SMs, consuming CUDA Cores / Tensor Cores Comm stream: NCCL moves data via the Copy Engine, not occupying SMs — completely independent hardware Key insight: both sets of hardware can run at full capacity simultaneously; software just needs to place them on different CUDA streams When does overlap break down? Communication far exceeds compute: small models + many GPUs → AllReduce time >> single-layer backward time; can’t fully hide it Insufficient bandwidth: multi-node setups connected by PCIe; the communication bottleneck is too large Bubble phases: the warmup/cooldown phases of Pipeline Parallelism have no computation to overlap with Single-stream implementation: if communication and computation are on the same CUDA stream, hardware cannot parallelize them Overlap effectiveness comparison across three scenarios: ideal case (communication fully hidden, effective time = ); partial overlap (after compute finishes, still waiting for communication to complete, producing an idle bubble); no overlap (same stream or synchronous communication, Total = T_compute + T_comm). Rule of thumb: When communication time / compute time ≤ 1, overlap can almost completely hide communication overhead. During real-world tuning, use torch.profiler‘s trace view to verify that the two streams are truly running in parallel. 3.7 Exercises Exercise 1: Compute Ring AllReduce Communication Volume Suppose you have N GPUs, each with gradients of size M bytes. Derive the total bytes sent and received per GPU in the Ring AllReduce algorithm. Specific question: When N=8 and M=2 GB (FP32 gradients for a 500M-parameter model), how much data does each GPU send and receive? Complete solution: Data is split into N chunks, each of size M/N Reduce-Scatter phase: N-1 steps, each step sends M/N bytes AllGather phase: N-1 steps, each step sends M/N bytes Total sent = 2(N-1) × M/N = 2M(N-1)/N Total received is identical = 2M(N-1)/N Plugging in N=8, M=2 GB: per-GPU communication = 2 × 2 GB × 7/8 = 3.5 GB. Note: compared to naive AllReduce (send to a root then broadcast) of 2M(N-1) = 14 GB, the ring approach dramatically reduces per-GPU bandwidth requirements. Exercise 2: Design a Parallelism Strategy You need to train a 70B-parameter model on 64 A100 80GB GPUs (8 nodes, 8 GPUs per node, NVLink interconnect). Given: training memory requirement (including optimizer) ~16 bytes/param = 1120 GB; NVLink bandwidth 600 GB/s (intra-node); InfiniBand bandwidth 50 GB/s (inter-node). Question: Design the DP/TP/PP combination and justify your choices. Recommended setup: TP=8, PP=2, DP=4 (verify: 8 × 2 × 4 = 64 GPUs) TP=8 (intra-node): 70B / 8 TP = ~8.75B parameters stored per GPU; including activations ~35 GB, fits in 80 GB. TP communication is frequent (two AllReduces per layer), so NVLink high bandwidth is essential. PP=2 (cross-node): Split model into 2 stages, each ~35B parameters. PP only transmits activations (relatively small), suitable for InfiniBand bandwidth. Use enough micro-batches to reduce bubble ratio. DP=4: 64 / (8 × 2) = 4-way data parallelism. Can pair with ZeRO Stage 1 to further reduce optimizer state memory. Gradient AllReduce can be overlapped with backward computation. Alternative: Using FSDP Stage 3 instead of TP+DP → PP=8, FSDP=8, but with higher communication overhead. Per-GPU memory breakdown (A100 80GB) — 70B model, TP=8 shards hidden dim, PP=2 shards layers, each GPU holds 35B/8 ≈ 4.375B parameters: Component Precision Calculation Memory Model parameters (FP16) FP16 4.375B × 2 bytes 8.75 GB Gradients (FP16) FP16 4.375B × 2 bytes 8.75 GB Parameter master copy (FP32) FP32 4.375B × 4 bytes 17.5 GB Adam momentum (FP32) FP32 4.375B × 4 bytes 17.5 GB Adam variance (FP32) FP32 4.375B × 4 bytes 17.5 GB Activations (+ checkpointing) Mixed b=1, s=2048, full ckpt ~1.3 GB Total ~71.3 GB Further optimization with ZeRO Stage 1: optimizer states (master + momentum + variance = 52.5 GB) are sharded across the DP=4 group, so per-GPU optimizer usage = 52.5/4 = 13.1 GB, total memory ≈ 32 GB with comfortable headroom. How to estimate activation memory? Per-layer total activation (Megatron paper formula): $$\text{Act\_per\layer} = sbh \times \left(34 + \frac{5 \cdot s \cdot n{head}}{h}\right) \approx 34,sbh$$ where s=seq_len, b=micro_batch_size, h=hidden_dim, n_head=number of attention heads; 34 is the sum of per-component coefficients (FP16, 2 bytes per element), for the case without activation checkpointing. Plugging in 70B (h=8192, n_head=64, this GPU’s 40 layers, s=2048, b=1): activation per layer = 2048×1×8192×34 = 544 MB/layer. TP=8 can shard ~65% (22/34) of activations (QKV/attn_out/FFN); LayerNorm inputs and similar ~12bsh terms cannot be sharded. Actual per-GPU per layer ≈ 247 MB, 40 layers ≈ 10 GB/GPU (without checkpointing). In the 1F1B schedule, the number of in-flight micro-batches equals the number of PP stages; peak ≈ 2 × 10 = 20 GB. In practice, activation checkpointing is mandatory: full checkpointing only stores each layer’s input (2bsh = 32 MB/layer), 40 layers ≈ 1.3 GB (at the cost of 33% extra compute); selective checkpointing only recomputes attention scores, ≈ 3–4 GB (10% extra compute). Key factors affecting activation size: seq_len (linear + attention scores are ), micro_batch (linear), hidden_dim (linear), layer count (PP layer sharding reduces it), TP degree (some can be sharded), checkpointing (~33% extra compute for ~90% activation savings). Programming Exercise A: Ring AllReduce (Full Implementation) Implement Ring AllReduce from scratch using torch.distributed‘s isend/irecv primitives. Requirements: implement Reduce-Scatter + AllGather and verify with 4 processes that results match dist.all_reduce. Index calculation pattern: In Reduce-Scatter, send_idx = (rank - step) % N, recv_idx = (rank - step - 1) % N. In AllGather, send_idx = (rank - step + 1) % N, recv_idx = (rank - step) % N. Intuition: the received data should be accumulated into the “next” chunk that is about to be sent. Programming Exercise B: Pipeline Schedule Simulator (GPipe vs 1F1B) Simulate both schedules and compare bubble ratio and peak activation memory. 3.8 Chapter Summary Concept Key Points Data Parallelism Replicate model, split data, AllReduce gradients; simple but has memory bottleneck Tensor Parallelism Split intra-layer weights (column/row split); requires high-bandwidth interconnect Pipeline Parallelism Split model by layers; bubble ratio = (p-1)/(p-1+m) Ring AllReduce Comm volume O(M), independent of GPU count; bandwidth-optimal FSDP / ZeRO Shard optimizer states/gradients/parameters; Stage 3 gives linear memory reduction 3D Parallelism TP (intra-node) + PP (cross-node) + DP (scale-out); standard paradigm for training very large models Next chapter preview: Chapter 4 will dive deep into GPU memory management and efficient attention implementations (FlashAttention, PagedAttention), for a hardware-level understanding of training and inference efficiency. This post is Chapter 3 of the ML Systems series. Body is rendered as markdown, with 9 interactive animations embedded as isolated iframes via the custom {% anim %} tag, sourced from the Arkive tutorial.

title: GEMM Tiling: How Matrix Multiplication Maps to Tensor Cores
content: Matrix multiplication (GEMM) is the operator that consumes the vast majority of compute in deep learning. This post starts from a concrete C[64, 24576] = A[64, 8192] × B[8192, 24576], and walks through how it maps layer by layer onto the GPU’s Grid / Block / Warp / Tensor Core hierarchy — and why the Decode phase wastes compute. The main text is Markdown; key mechanisms have interactive animations. 1. The Big Picture: Why TilingConsider a typical LLM forward GEMM: where (batch), (hidden), (output). The full matrix cannot fit in any level of on-chip storage, so it must be cut into small tiles, with each compute unit handling only one tile at a time. The core idea is output-stationary tiling: partition the output into tiles, assign each tile to an independent thread block, and accumulate along the dimension in a loop. The animation below uses a scaled-down 8×8 = 8×8 × 8×8 example with block size 2×2×2 to step through this tiling schedule: each program (thread block) owns one output tile of , loops over loading tiles of and from Global Memory into registers to accumulate, and only writes back the accumulated result after the K-loop ends: Corresponding Triton-style pseudocode: Key point: the accumulator acc stays in registers for the entire K-loop — no write-back to Global Memory until the final tl.store. This reduces the number of writes to from down to 1. 2. Hierarchical Breakdown: From Grid to Tensor CoreBack to the real-scale GEMM, the GPU splits it across four levels. The animation below steps through the full hierarchy: Grid partitions the output space → Block slices K and loads SRAM → Warp issues instructions → Tensor Core computes 16×16×16 — and finally shows the memory hierarchy and the Decode/Prefill difference. ① Grid Level: Slice Output Space into BlocksSplit the output along into 192 Blocks, each . Each Block needs all rows of — — and the corresponding 128 columns of — . These 192 Blocks are distributed across 132 SMs (H100 example) for parallel execution; Blocks communicate zero. ② Block Level: Load SRAM + K LoopEach Block is executed by 256 threads (= 8 Warps) on one SM. The 256 threads cooperate to move one tile (2 KB) and (4 KB) from HBM into SRAM (Shared Memory), shared across all 8 Warps. They then loop 512 times () along , with a step size of — the reason it is 16 is that the Tensor Core’s mma.K = 16. ③ Warp → Register → Tensor CoreEach Warp uses wmma::load_matrix_sync to load the SRAM tile into 16×16 fragments in registers, then feeds them to the Tensor Core via wmma::mma_sync. The result accumulates into a register-resident accumulator , which never leaves the registers. ④ Tensor Core: 16×16×16 = 8192 FLOPsOne MMA instruction on a Tensor Core computes , i.e., FLOPs in just 1–2 cycles. Physically this is a 4×4 FMA array × 4 TCs, internally split into 64 sub-operations, but the ISA wraps it as 16×16 — transparent to the programmer. Inputs are FP16; accumulation is FP32. 3. Memory Hierarchy: HBM Is the Sole BottleneckData flows HBM → SRAM → Register → Tensor Core — each level is faster and smaller: Level Capacity Bandwidth What it holds HBM 80 GB 3.35 TB/s All weights (e.g., 384 MB) SRAM (Shared Memory) 228 KB/SM ~30 TB/s A_tile + B_tile Register 256 KB/SM ~60 TB/s 16×16 fragments Tensor Core — 989 TFLOPS 8192 FLOPs/instruction Arithmetic Intensity determines where the bottleneck is: In other words, for every byte read from HBM you need to perform at least 295 floating-point operations to keep the Tensor Core fed. Bottleneck: HBM → SRAM. The GEMV in the Decode phase has an arithmetic intensity of only ~1 FLOP/Byte, far below 295, so the Tensor Core spends 99% of its time waiting for data. Solution: increase batch size. With batch=1, weights are read once and used once; with batch=64, each read is reused 64 times, lifting TC utilization from ~6% to near 100%. 4. Why Decode Is Slow: the Fragment Padding ProblemThe minimum granularity of a Tensor Core is 16×16. When , the missing rows are zero-padded. The hardware still executes all 8192 FLOPs — most of them are wasted work. Scenario Effective rows Efficiency Decode: batch=1 1 / 16 rows have data ~6% Prefill: batch=64 16 / 16 rows all have data 100% With batch=1, 15/16 fragment rows are zeros; ~94% of TC work is wasted. Increasing batch fills those 16 rows, making every FLOP count. The essence of Continuous Batching: pack enough requests to fill all 16 rows of a fragment — this is exactly why LLM serving concatenates tokens from multiple requests into one large GEMM, converting memory-bound Decode into compute-bound efficient computation. 5. Summary Tiling cuts a matrix that is too large for on-chip storage into tiles that fit. The output-stationary scheme keeps the accumulator in registers throughout, writing back only once. The GPU decomposes GEMM across four levels: Grid (partition output space) → Block (slice K, load SRAM) → Warp (issue MMA instructions) → Tensor Core (16×16×16). Data flows HBM → SRAM → Register → TC; HBM bandwidth is the sole bottleneck, with a machine balance point of ~295 FLOP/Byte. Increasing batch size raises both data reuse and fragment fill rate — the key to pulling Decode from memory-bound back to compute-bound, and the core motivation for Continuous Batching. title: GPU Computing & CUDA Fundamentals
content: From hardware architecture to programming model — a deep dive into the core concepts of GPU parallel computing. This post is written in Markdown, with key mechanisms illustrated by interactive animations (click, hover, or step through them). 2.1 GPU Architecture: SMs, Warps, and the Thread HierarchyThe Core Idea Behind GPU ParallelismThe fundamental difference between GPUs and CPUs lies in their design philosophy: CPUs optimize for low latency (a small number of powerful cores + large caches + complex control logic), while GPUs optimize for high throughput (thousands of simple cores + massive concurrency to hide latency). Streaming Multiprocessor (SM): The basic compute unit of a GPU. Each SM contains multiple CUDA Cores, Tensor Cores, Load/Store units, and Shared Memory. Warp: 32 threads form one warp — the smallest scheduling unit on the GPU. All threads in a warp execute the same instruction (SIMT). Thread Hierarchy: Thread → Warp → Thread Block → Grid, forming a multi-level parallel structure. Full GPU Architecture Overview (Blackwell Architecture)The diagram below shows the complete hardware layout of a modern GPU, from the chip level down to the internals of a single SM, covering all key compute and memory units: Component Count / Spec Function Peak Performance CUDA Cores 24,064 (128/SM × 188 SMs) Scalar FP/integer ops (FP32, FP64, INT32) 125 TFLOPS (FP32) Tensor Cores 752 (4/SM × 188 SMs), 5th Gen Matrix FMA: D = A×B + C (supports FP4/FP8/BF16/TF32) 4000 TOPS (FP4) / ~500 TFLOPS (BF16) RT Cores 188 (1/SM), 4th Gen Hardware ray tracing (BVH traversal, triangle intersection) 380 TFLOPS SRAM (Shared/L1) 228 KB/SM (configurable split) High-speed scratchpad shared among threads in a block; manually managed ~19 TB/s aggregate bandwidth L2 Cache 96 MB Shared across the full GPU; hardware-managed; reduces HBM traffic ~12 TB/s HBM (GDDR7) 96 GB, 512-bit interface Global device memory; holds model weights, activations, KV cache 1792 GB/s Register File 256 KB/SM (65536 × 32-bit) Per-thread private storage; the fastest memory tier ~20 TB/s Data flow path through a single GEMM: Performance key: maximize data reuse in SRAM (Shared Memory + Registers) and minimize HBM accesses — this is the central idea behind tiling. Interactive GPU Architecture Diagram (click an SM to see its internals) Thread Hierarchy in Detail Level Size Hardware Mapping Available Memory Communication Thread 1 CUDA Core / Tensor Core Registers (~255 per thread) — Warp 32 threads SM scheduling unit + Tensor Core MMA Register File (shared) Warp shuffle, Tensor Core cooperation Thread Block up to 1024 threads Single SM Shared Memory (up to 228 KB) Shared Memory reads/writes Grid multiple blocks Entire GPU (all SMs) Global Memory (HBM) Global Memory / Atomics Where Tensor Cores Fit in the Thread HierarchyTensor Cores are warp-level compute units. Each MMA (Matrix Multiply-Accumulate) operation is completed cooperatively by an entire warp (32 threads): Key properties of Tensor Cores: Warp cooperation: Each of the 32 threads holds a different fragment of the A/B/C matrices. A single mma.sync instruction is executed cooperatively by the whole warp. Data distribution: A/B fragments live in the registers of the 32 threads — they do not pass through Shared Memory. Mixed precision: FP16/BF16/FP8 inputs, FP32 accumulator — balancing speed and numerical precision. Throughput (H100): Each SM has 4 Tensor Cores, each capable of one MMA per cycle → single-SM peak ~200 TFLOPS (FP8). Programming Model Mapping 2.2 Memory Hierarchy: From Registers to HBMThe GPU memory hierarchy forms a pyramid — the closer to the compute units, the smaller the capacity but the higher the bandwidth and the lower the latency. Hover over each level to see its bandwidth. Bandwidth Comparison (H100 SXM) Level Bandwidth Registers ~20 TB/s Shared Memory ~19 TB/s L2 Cache ~12 TB/s HBM3 3.35 TB/s PCIe 5.0 (Host ↔ Device) 64 GB/s Key Design Principles Data reuse: Keep data in Shared Memory as long as possible to reduce HBM traffic. Coalesced access: Threads in the same warp should access consecutive memory addresses so their requests can be merged into a single transaction. Avoiding bank conflicts: Shared Memory is divided into 32 banks; avoid having multiple threads in the same warp access the same bank. Occupancy tuning: Balance Shared Memory and register usage to maximize the number of active warps per SM. 2.3 GEMM and Tensor CoresWhy Is GEMM So Important?The core operations in deep learning — fully-connected layers, convolutions, and the and products in attention — are all fundamentally matrix multiplications (General Matrix Multiply, GEMM). Optimizing GEMM means optimizing the entire training and inference pipeline. A computation C[M,N] = A[M,K] × B[K,N] requires FLOPs (counting multiply and add separately). For the matrix sizes typical in LLMs (e.g., 4096×4096), this means billions of operations. GEMM Tiling Animation (click “Start” to watch the tiled computation) Hierarchical Tiling Strategy 2.4 CUDA Graphs: Eliminating Kernel Launch OverheadThe Problem: Kernel Launch OverheadEvery time the CPU submits a kernel to the GPU, there is roughly 5–10 microseconds of launch overhead. For a single large kernel this is negligible, but in the decode phase of LLM inference dozens to hundreds of small kernels execute sequentially: A single Transformer layer may involve 20+ kernels (LayerNorm, QKV projection, Attention, FFN, …). If each kernel’s compute time is only 10–20 µs, launch overhead can account for 30–50% of total time. The CPU becomes the bottleneck — the GPU sits idle waiting for the next kernel to be dispatched. CUDA Graph Timeline Comparison (animation) The CUDA Graph Three-Step Flow: Capture → Instantiate → Replay CUDA Graph Limitations Static shapes: Tensor shapes at capture time are fixed — dynamic shapes are not allowed. No CPU dependencies: The graph cannot contain if/else branches, Python control flow, or CPU synchronization. Fixed memory addresses: Input/output addresses are fixed at capture; only in-place writes are permitted afterward. No dynamic allocation: torch.empty() and similar calls cannot appear inside a graph. Best use case: the decode phase (inference loops with fixed batch size and sequence length). 2.5 Memory Management and ProfilingPyTorch CUDA Memory AllocatorPyTorch uses its own caching memory allocator to avoid frequent calls to cudaMalloc/cudaFree (each call requires a full GPU synchronization, which is very slow). Block pool: Freed memory is returned to a pool rather than given back to CUDA, ready for reuse. Fragmentation: After long training runs, the pool fills with small fragments that cannot be coalesced into large contiguous blocks. Expandable segments (PyTorch 2.0+): Uses cudaMallocAsync or the virtual memory API to grow allocations on demand rather than all at once. Memory Profiling in Practice Enabling Expandable Segments Common OOM Debugging Checklist Check memory_reserved vs memory_allocated — a large gap indicates severe fragmentation. Call torch.cuda.empty_cache() to release cached memory (note: does not affect tensors still in use). Enable expandable_segments to reduce external fragmentation. Use gradient_checkpointing to trade compute for memory. Check for tensors being accidentally kept alive (a common culprit is a list accumulating loss values). 2.6 CUDA Programming ModelGrid / Block / Thread MappingThe heart of CUDA programming is mapping a computation onto the GPU’s thread hierarchy: Writing a GEMM Kernel with Triton (Python-style) Kernel Launch and OccupancyChoosing the right block size is critical for performance: Block too small (e.g., 32 threads): cannot fully utilize SM resources; occupancy is low. Block too large (e.g., 1024 threads): each block demands more resources, so fewer blocks fit on an SM. Rule of thumb: 128 or 256 threads/block is usually a good starting point. Use torch.cuda.get_device_properties() to query hardware parameters and guide your configuration. 2.7 Exercises Exercise 1: Computing GPU Arithmetic Utilization (calculation) Given: GPU: NVIDIA H100 SXM, FP16 Tensor Core peak throughput = 989.5 TFLOPS Your GEMM kernel processes C[4096, 4096] = A[4096, 4096] × B[4096, 4096] Kernel execution time = 0.35 ms (measured by NSight) Question: What is the Model FLOP Utilization (MFU) of this kernel? Hint: GEMM FLOPs = 2 × M × N × K; MFU = actual TFLOPS / peak TFLOPS; actual TFLOPS = FLOPs / execution time. Solution: Answer: MFU ≈ 39.7%. Note: a well-optimized GEMM (e.g., cuBLAS) can reach 70–80% MFU at this size. 39.7% indicates room for improvement — possibly suboptimal tiling or poor memory access patterns. Exercise 2: Determining Whether a Kernel Is Compute-Bound or Memory-Bound (analysis) Given (H100 SXM): peak throughput 989.5 TFLOPS (FP16); HBM bandwidth 3.35 TB/s; machine arithmetic intensity ridge point = 989.5 / 3.35 ≈ 295 FLOPs/Byte. Two kernels: Kernel A (Vector Add): element-wise addition of N=1M FP16 elements. Read 2N elements + write N elements = 6 MB data transferred, total compute = N = 1M FLOPs. Kernel B (GEMM 4096×4096×4096): as in Exercise 1, 137.4 GFLOPs; data read/written = (4096×4096 + 4096×4096 + 4096×4096) × 2 bytes = 96 MB. Question: Classify each kernel as compute-bound or memory-bound, and walk through the Roofline Model analysis. Solution: Conclusion: Kernel A (Vector Add) is memory-bound: optimize by reducing memory traffic, leveraging caches, and kernel fusion. Kernel B (GEMM) is compute-bound: optimize by using Tensor Cores, improving occupancy, and tuning instruction scheduling. This is exactly why operator fusion matters so much in LLM inference — fusing multiple memory-bound micro-kernels (e.g., bias add + activation + dropout) into one eliminates the intermediate HBM round-trips. Exercise 3: CUDA Graph Applicability (true/false with explanation) For each scenario below, decide whether CUDA Graph can be used and explain why: Scenario A: LLM decode phase, batch_size=8, seq_len grows by 1 each step (KV cache grows), but using paged attention. Scenario B: Fixed-batch-size image classification inference (ResNet-50), input always 224×224. Scenario C: Training forward pass, model contains if x.sum() > 0: path_a() else: path_b() — a data-dependent branch. Scenario D: vLLM prefill phase, different requests have different prompt lengths. Solution: Scenario A: Yes, with some care ✓. Paged attention kernel parameters (page table) can be passed via a fixed buffer. In practice, SGLang/vLLM use CUDA Graphs for decode: pre-compile graphs for a set of batch sizes (e.g., bs=1,2,4,8,16,…) and pad to the nearest size. The growing seq_len doesn’t affect the per-step decode computation (each step processes only 1 token). Scenario B: Ideal use case ✓. Fixed input shapes, fixed model structure, no dynamic control flow — a textbook CUDA Graph application with significant speedup. Scenario C: No ✗. if x.sum() > 0 is data-dependent control flow. At capture time, only the branch actually taken gets recorded. If a different branch is taken during replay, the graph still executes the recorded path, producing wrong results. Scenario D: Not directly, but padding works ✓/✗. Prefill has variable seq_len across requests, so shapes are dynamic. Direct CUDA Graph use is not possible. However, like decode, you can pre-compile graphs for common seq_len buckets and pad shorter sequences. The trade-off: padding wastes compute, but saves launch overhead. For prefill, kernels are typically large enough that launch overhead is a small fraction — so the benefit is much less pronounced than in decode. Exercise 4: Shared Memory Tiling Design (design problem) You need to implement a GEMM kernel for C[M,N] = A[M,K] × B[K,N]: target GPU H100 (Shared Memory configurable up to 228 KB/SM); data type FP16 (2 bytes per element); block tile sizes BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=128, BLOCK_K=32. Questions: (1) How much Shared Memory does each block require? (2) What is the maximum number of blocks that can run concurrently on one SM? (3) If you change to BLOCK_K=64, what is the trade-off? Solution: Trade-off analysis (BLOCK_K=32 vs BLOCK_K=64): Metric BLOCK_K=32 BLOCK_K=64 Shared Mem / block 32 KB 64 KB Blocks / SM 7 3 Warps / SM 7×8=56 3×8=24 Occupancy 56/64 = 87.5% 24/64 = 37.5% K-loop iterations K/32 K/64 (halved) Compute per iteration 128×128×32 FLOPs 128×128×64 FLOPs (doubled) Why does occupancy matter? — The SM warp scheduling mechanism Key point: at any given moment, multiple warps are “in flight” on the same SM — not just one! The H100 has 4 warp schedulers per SM, each capable of issuing one instruction to one warp per cycle. So up to 4 warps execute simultaneously every cycle. Warp state Meaning Count Resident warps Resources (registers/smem) allocated; eligible to be selected any time up to 64/SM Eligible warps Not waiting for data or a barrier; can be issued next cycle varies dynamically Issuing warps Currently being dispatched by a scheduler up to 4/SM Of the 64 resident warps, 4 are selected each cycle. The rest are either waiting for HBM data (~400 cycles), waiting at __syncthreads(), or eligible but not yet picked. Key contrast with CPUs: Warp switching is zero overhead! Every resident warp’s registers remain in the Register File at all times (no save/restore needed). The scheduler simply advances its pointer to another warp’s PC — this is why GPUs can hide latency with many warps, while CPU context switches are expensive. Higher occupancy → more resident warps → even if many warps are stalled waiting for memory, the scheduler can still find eligible warps to keep the pipeline full. Lower occupancy → all warps may be waiting on data → all 4 schedulers sit idle → GPU utilization collapses. But higher occupancy is not always better: BLOCK_K=64 advantage: half the loop iterations → fewer __syncthreads() calls, less loop branch overhead, more MMA instructions per iteration (amortizes the fixed costs of the instruction pipeline). BLOCK_K=64 disadvantage: occupancy drops to 37% → if the kernel is latency-bound (interleaved compute and memory access without sufficient density), there aren’t enough warps to cover stall cycles. When is larger BLOCK_K better? When the kernel is compute-bound (Tensor Core utilization is already high and each warp produces enough MMA instructions to keep the pipeline fed); in that case occupancy is not the bottleneck, and reducing loop overhead pays off more. When is smaller BLOCK_K better? When K is small (few loop iterations to begin with) or the kernel has heavy non-compute work (e.g., epilogue stores and activation functions); then higher occupancy matters more. Practical guidance: In Triton/CUTLASS, BLOCK_K is typically auto-tuned across {32, 64, 128}. cuBLAS uses similar heuristics internally. No formula can directly predict the optimal value — real pipeline behavior depends on instruction mix, bank conflicts, register pressure, and other factors that are difficult to model analytically. Profile-guided tuning is the only reliable method. Coding Exercise A: Writing a Vector Add Kernel with Triton (programming) Implement an element-wise vector add kernel using Triton, including grid/block configuration and boundary masking. Benchmark it against PyTorch’s native implementation. Requirements: use the @triton.jit decorator; correctly handle non-aligned lengths (N not divisible by BLOCK_SIZE); show how to choose BLOCK_SIZE and compare performance; verify results are bit-identical to torch.add; use triton.testing.do_bench for benchmarking. Full solution: Expected output (on H100): Coding Exercise B: Measuring Kernel Time with torch.cuda.Event (programming) Correctly measure GPU kernel execution time (not CPU time!), including warmup, CUDA Event timing, and averaging over multiple runs. Compare GEMM execution time across matrix sizes, plot a TFLOPS curve, and identify which sizes are compute-bound versus launch-overhead-bound. Why can’t you use time.time()? The CPU and GPU execute asynchronously. time.time() only measures how long the CPU takes to dispatch the kernel, not the actual GPU computation time. You must use CUDA Events or pair wall-clock time with torch.cuda.synchronize(). Full solution: Expected output (on H100): Analysis summary: Small matrices (32–128): TFLOPS is very low because kernel launch overhead (~5–10 µs) far exceeds the actual compute time. The GPU’s thousands of cores sit mostly idle. Medium matrices (256–512): TFLOPS rises quickly as the GPU starts to be meaningfully utilized, but the tile still can’t fill all SMs. Large matrices (1024–4096): approaching peak TFLOPS — genuinely compute-bound. cuBLAS Tensor Core GEMM is most efficient at these sizes. Approaches for small matrices: Batched GEMM (pack multiple small matrices into one call), CUDA Graph (eliminate repeated launch overhead), kernel fusion (avoid writing intermediate results to HBM). Exercise 5: Roofline Model Analysis (interview question) Given: GPU NVIDIA H100 SXM; BF16 Tensor Core peak throughput 989 TFLOPS; HBM bandwidth 3.35 TB/s; Arithmetic Intensity (AI) = FLOPs / Bytes_accessed. Questions: (1) Where is the ridge point? (2) Classify the following kernels: GEMM [4096,4096]×[4096,4096] (AI=4096), LayerNorm [32, 2048, 4096] (AI≈5), Softmax [32, 32, 2048, 2048] (AI≈3), element-wise ReLU (AI=0.25); (3) What are the optimization strategies for memory-bound vs compute-bound kernels? Solution: Summary: Ridge point = 295 FLOPs/Byte; GEMM (AI=4096) is compute-bound; LayerNorm (AI≈5), Softmax (AI≈3), and ReLU (AI=0.25) are all memory-bound. In LLM inference, the vast majority of non-GEMM kernels are memory-bound — which is exactly why Flash Attention and kernel fusion are so impactful. Exercise 6: Shared Memory Bank Conflicts (interview question) Given: Shared Memory has 32 banks, each 4 bytes wide; 32 threads in a warp access Shared Memory simultaneously; multiple threads accessing different addresses in the same bank → bank conflict (serialized); multiple threads accessing the same address in the same bank → broadcast (no conflict). Questions: (1) Thread i accesses address i × 4 — how many bank conflicts? (2) Thread i accesses address i × 128 — how many bank conflicts? (3) Design a padding strategy to eliminate bank conflicts when accessing a 32×32 float matrix stored in Shared Memory by column. Solution: Interview key point: Bank conflicts are the biggest Shared Memory performance pitfall. In GEMM tiling, if the A tile is loaded row-by-row but accessed column-by-column (transposed access pattern), performance can drop several-fold without padding. Triton and CUTLASS both include built-in swizzle/padding mechanisms to handle this automatically. Exercise 7: CUDA Graph Applicability + Quantifying the Benefit (interview question) Given: an LLM decode step contains 200 small kernels; average compute time per kernel = 15 µs; kernel launch overhead without CUDA Graph = 5 µs per kernel. Questions: (1) Without CUDA Graph — what is the total time, and what fraction is launch overhead? (2) With CUDA Graph — what is the total time, and what is the speedup? (3) If some kernels have dynamic shapes, can CUDA Graph still be used? How do SGLang/vLLM handle this? Solution: Summary: Without graph 4 ms, launch overhead is 25%; with graph ~3 ms, 1.33× speedup; dynamic shapes are handled by pre-compiling multiple graphs + padding — standard practice in SGLang/vLLM. Interview follow-up: In the decode phase, individual kernels are very small (seq_len=1), so launch overhead makes up a larger fraction and CUDA Graph pays off more. This is why virtually every inference framework uses CUDA Graphs for decode but not for prefill (where kernels are large enough that launch overhead is negligible). Exercise 8: Occupancy vs. Performance (interview question) Given: a kernel uses 64 registers/thread and 48 KB shared memory/block; H100 SM resources: 65,536 registers/SM, 228 KB shared memory/SM, max 2,048 threads/SM, max 32 blocks/SM. Questions: (1) Considering only the register constraint, what is the maximum number of threads per SM? (2) Considering only the shared memory constraint, what is the maximum number of blocks per SM? (3) Assuming 256 threads/block, what is the actual occupancy? (4) Does higher occupancy always mean better performance? Give a counterexample. Solution: Summary: Register constraint allows at most 1,024 threads (4 blocks × 256); Shared Memory constraint also limits to 4 blocks; occupancy = 50%; higher occupancy does not always mean better performance! GEMM and other compute-bound kernels deliberately use large register files for data reuse, sacrificing occupancy to achieve higher actual throughput. Interview key point: NVIDIA’s official documentation explicitly states “higher occupancy does not always equate to higher performance.” In practice, use ncu (Nsight Compute) to profile and determine whether the bottleneck is latency hiding or instruction throughput. cuBLAS’s most optimized GEMM kernels typically run at only 25–50% occupancy. 2.8 Chapter SummaryKey Concepts Recap Topic Takeaway GPU architecture SM → Warp (32 threads) → SIMT execution; H100 has 132 SMs Memory hierarchy Registers are fastest but smallest; Shared Memory is the optimization lever; HBM bandwidth is the main bottleneck GEMM Multi-level tiling (Block → Warp → Tensor Core); maximize data reuse Tensor Cores 4×4 matrix FMA per cycle; FP16 input, FP32 accumulator; 16× faster than CUDA Cores CUDA Graph Capture → Instantiate → Replay; eliminates launch overhead; requires static shapes Profiling memory_snapshot locates fragmentation; Roofline identifies bottlenecks; expandable_segments mitigates OOM Further Reading CUDA C++ Programming Guide Triton Tutorials (OpenAI) PyTorch CUDA Semantics CUTLASS: CUDA Templates for Linear Algebra This post is Chapter 2 of the ML Systems series. The body is rendered as Markdown, with 6 interactive visualization components embedded as isolated iframes via custom {% anim %} tags, sourced from the Arkive tutorial.

title: GPU Anatomy and LLM Token Dataflow
content: To understand why LLM inference is slow and where the bottleneck actually is, you first need to see the complete path a single token takes through GPU hardware. This post starts from the full H100 die, goes through SM internals and the memory hierarchy, all the way to the dataflow from token input to output — with interactive diagrams throughout. Part 1: Full GPU die overviewThe H100 SXM is a massive 814mm² chip containing 132 SMs, 80 GB HBM3, and 3.35 TB/s of bandwidth. Below is an interactive GPU die diagram — click any component (HBM, Memory Controller, L2 Cache, Crossbar, SM, NVLink) to see a detailed description: Part 2: SM (Streaming Multiprocessor) internalsEach SM is the GPU’s fundamental compute unit, containing Tensor Cores, CUDA Cores, SRAM, and schedulers. Warp Scheduler × 4Each SM has 4 Warp schedulers, each managing multiple Warps (groups of 32 threads). When a Warp is waiting on memory, the scheduler instantly switches to another ready Warp (latency hiding). Each SM can manage up to 64 Warps simultaneously = 2048 threads. Tensor Cores × 4 (4th Gen)Hardware units designed specifically for matrix multiplication. Each Tensor Core can compute one 4×4 matrix FMA per cycle, supporting FP16, BF16, FP8, and INT8 formats. Nearly all Linear layers in LLMs are computed here. Inputs are read from the Register File; results are written back to registers. CUDA Cores (FP32) × 128General-purpose floating-point ALUs. Handle element-wise operations: addition, RMSNorm, GeLU/SiLU activation, softmax, RoPE positional encoding, etc. 1 FP32 FMA per cycle per core. Far more flexible than Tensor Cores but much slower (extremely inefficient for matrix multiplication). Shared Memory / L1 (SRAM) — 228 KBThe SM’s high-speed scratch space, explicitly managed by the programmer. The heart of Flash Attention: load K, V in tiles into SRAM, then complete + softmax + entirely in SRAM, avoiding writes back to HBM. Bandwidth ~30 TB/s (9× HBM), latency ~30 cycles. Size is the primary constraint — at only 228 KB, it can’t hold the entire KV Cache. Register File — 256 KBEach thread’s private ultra-fast storage. Tensor Cores and CUDA Cores read/write operands directly from here. Latency ~1 cycle, bandwidth ~60 TB/s. Each thread can use up to 255 32-bit registers. Register pressure: use too many → fewer Warps can run simultaneously → worse latency hiding. Load/Store Units × 32Responsible for all memory read/write operations. Every memory request goes through: (1) check L1/Shared Memory first; (2) miss → check L2 Cache; (3) miss → go to HBM. 32 LD/ST units means up to 32 memory transactions can be issued per cycle. During LLM decode, most time is spent waiting for these units to move weights from HBM. Three key intuitionsTensor Core vs CUDA Core: Tensor Cores are specialized for D = A×B + C matrix FMA — one 4×4 matrix per cycle. CUDA Cores do one scalar multiply-add per cycle. For a 4×4 matrix multiplication: Tensor Core takes 1 cycle; CUDA Cores need 64 multiplies + 48 adds. So LLM Linear layers all use Tensor Cores, and element-wise operations use CUDA Cores. Why SRAM matters so much: HBM is 80 GB but only 3.35 TB/s; SRAM is 228 KB per SM but ~30 TB/s. Flash Attention’s secret is keeping data in SRAM for computation as much as possible, avoiding round-trips to HBM. Naive Attention writes the result back to HBM, then reads it back to do softmax; Flash processes everything in tiles entirely within SRAM, reading K and V from HBM only once. Warps and latency hiding: HBM read latency is ~400 ns ≈ hundreds of clock cycles. If only 1 thread group is running, the GPU spends most of its time waiting on memory. The solution: put 64 Warps per SM — when one Warp waits on memory, the scheduler instantly switches to another ready Warp. This is the GPU’s core design philosophy — trade concurrency for latency. Part 3: Memory hierarchyFrom the farthest HBM to the nearest registers — the closer, the faster, but also the smaller: Level Capacity Bandwidth Latency Contents HBM3 (VRAM) 80 GB 3.35 TB/s ~400 ns Model weights + KV Cache + activations + optimizer state L2 Cache 50 MB ~12 TB/s ~150 ns Shared by all SMs; caches RoPE tables, small weights, frequently accessed KV Shared Memory / L1 (SRAM) 228 KB / SM ~30 TB/s ~30 ns SM-private, programmer-managed, Flash Attention workspace Register File 256 KB / SM ~60 TB/s ~1 ns Thread-private, direct operand source for compute units Tensor + CUDA Cores 989 TFLOPS FP16 / ~67 TFLOPS FP32 — — Read operands from registers → compute → write back to registers The fundamental tension: Tensor Cores need data fed at 989 TFLOPS, but HBM can only deliver 3.35 TB/s. This is H100’s arithmetic intensity roofline. LLM decode GEMV is only ~1–2 FLOPs/Byte — Tensor Cores are idle 99% of the time waiting on HBM! Part 4: Token dataflowThe interactive diagram below walks step by step through a single token’s complete journey through GPU hardware from input to output (LLaMA-70B decode). Each step highlights the active HBM regions, SMs, and caches, explaining where data comes from, where it goes, and what compute units it passes through: Key observations from the full flow: Steps 2 / 5 / 8 / 10 (various Projections) are all GEMVs: weights vastly outnumber activations, so weights are streamed from HBM → Tensor Cores for computation — this is the root cause of memory-bound behavior. Step 4 (Attention / Flash Decoding): the score matrix is never written back to HBM; K and V are read once, producing a single output vector. Step 7 (FFN Gate + Up) is the largest single weight read in the entire forward pass: W_gate + W_up = 896 MB. Total weight reads per layer: ~1.86 GB (Attention 512 MB + FFN 1.34 GB). For a 70B model with 80 layers, generating one token requires reading ~148 GB of weights + ~1.3 GB of KV Cache ≈ 150 GB. Theoretical time: In practice around 55–70 ms (various overheads). The final output is just 1 integer (next_token_id) — that’s the token you see appearing one character at a time. This token then re-enters Step 0 to begin the next decode iteration. This post renders as markdown with 2 interactive diagrams embedded via the custom {% anim %} tag in isolated iframes, sourced from the Arkive tutorial.

title: ML Systems Interview Question Bank: 60 High-Frequency Questions
content: A curated set of 60 high-frequency ML Systems interview questions spanning seven areas: Transformer, GPU & CUDA, Distributed Training, Inference Systems, RLHF, System Design, and Debugging. Below is an interactive question bank: filter by category or difficulty, search by keyword, and click any question to expand hints and answers. How to Use Category filter: Transformer / GPU & CUDA / Distributed Training / Inference Systems / RLHF / System Design / Debugging Difficulty filter: 🟢 Easy / 🟡 Medium / 🔴 Hard Search: type a keyword in the search box (e.g. Flash Attention, PagedAttention, GRPO) for live filtering Expand: click any question card to reveal hints and answers Questions are roughly distributed across Easy / Medium / Hard. Try answering each one yourself before expanding the solution. Knowledge MapQuick overview of key points by topic: Transformer (Questions 1–10)Attention numerical stability (dividing by to control dot-product variance), Multi-Head’s multi-subspace representation, GQA/MQA KV Cache savings, Flash Attention’s tiling + online softmax, KV Cache behavior during Prefill/Decode, RoPE relative positional encoding, Flash Attention 2’s parallelism dimension optimization, and the Arithmetic Intensity analysis of Prefill (compute-bound) vs. Decode (memory-bound). Core attention formula: Online softmax correction factor (updating the global max when processing a new block): GPU & CUDA (Questions 11–20)Warp divergence, the relationship between Shared Memory and L1 Cache, Roofline Model bottleneck identification, CUDA Graph three phases and limitations, Tensor Core MMA requirements, MFU calculation, Occupancy factors, memory snapshot OOM debugging, CUDA Stream synchronization, and GEMM three-level tiling (Thread Block → Warp → Thread) mapped to the memory hierarchy. Roofline ridge point: H100 SXM reference: FP16 peak 989 TFLOPS, HBM bandwidth 3.35 TB/s, ridge point ≈ FLOPs/byte. Distributed Training (Questions 21–30)Ring AllReduce communication volume of (independent of GPU count), ZeRO Stage 1/2/3 sharding strategies, Column/Row AllReduce requirements in Tensor Parallel, Pipeline bubble ratio, TP/PP/DP combined design, MoE Expert Parallel All-to-All overhead, communication backend selection, gradient accumulation, communication-computation overlap, and four-dimensional parallelism for giant MoE models. Pipeline bubble ratio ( = number of stages, = number of microbatches): Interleaved 1F1B further reduces it with virtual stages: . Inference Systems (Questions 31–40)Continuous Batching, PagedAttention, Radix Cache prefix sharing, Speculative Decoding speedup, FP8 E4M3/E5M2 format selection, 10K QPS serving design, TTFT and TPOT, Chunked Prefill, quantization calibration, and the Scheduler design differences between SGLang and vLLM. Speculative Decoding expected accepted token count ( = per-token acceptance rate, = draft length): When : tokens/step. RLHF Systems (Questions 41–50)GRPO vs PPO (GRPO uses group-level normalization, no Critic needed), GAE’s bias-variance tradeoff, Training-Inference Mismatch, Weight Sync strategies, PPO clip parameter effects, multi-turn tool calling RL system design, Reward Model and Bradley-Terry loss, veRL Hybrid Engine, Partial Rollout, and a comparison of veRL/SLIME/OpenRLHF frameworks.
