title: GPU Parallelism Strategies Explained: TP / PP / EP / SP
content: When training or running inference on large models, a single GPU’s memory and compute are nowhere near enough. This post systematically covers four mainstream parallelism strategies — Tensor Parallelism, Pipeline Parallelism, Expert Parallelism, and Sequence Parallelism — with interactive animations for the key mechanisms. Tensor Parallelism (TP)Split the weight matrix inside a single layer, have each GPU compute a portion, then AllReduce to merge the results. Column Parallel: Split the weight matrix by columnsTake the original weight matrix and split it in half by columns, one half per GPU: GPU 0 holds GPU 1 holds Each GPU multiplies the full input by its own half of the weights, producing different columns of the full result. Interactive animation: full MLP layer TP computation (Megatron-LM style)The essence of Megatron-LM is Column Parallel → GeLU (no communication) → Row Parallel → AllReduce — the entire MLP forward pass needs only 1 AllReduce. The animation below walks through the full computation flow on two GPUs step by step: Key takeaway: The entire MLP forward pass needs just 1 AllReduce! Why: Column Parallel outputs are different columns of the full result. GeLU is element-wise and doesn’t need the full vector. Row Parallel outputs have the same shape but different values — summing them gives the full result → AllReduce. Compared to the naive approach: If both Linear layers used Column Parallel, you’d need an AllGather in the middle to reassemble the full result before the second multiply. Megatron’s Column→Row combination cleverly skips that intermediate communication. Typical config: TP = 8 (8 GPUs on a single node over NVLink at 900 GB/s), 1 AllReduce per layer forward, 1 AllReduce per layer backward. Pipeline Parallelism (PP)Split the model by layers, with each GPU (or group of GPUs) responsible for a contiguous set of layers. Data flows through like an assembly line. Model split by layers across 4 stages Stage GPU Layers Stage 0 GPU 0 Layer 0-7 + Embedding Stage 1 GPU 1 Layer 8-15 Stage 2 GPU 2 Layer 16-23 Stage 3 GPU 3 Layer 24-31 + LM Head Interactive animation: 1F1B pipeline schedule1F1B (One Forward One Backward) scheduling has each stage alternately execute one forward and one backward micro-batch in steady state, maximizing GPU utilization. The animation below shows the forward/backward flow for 4 GPUs and 4 micro-batches (dark = Forward, light = Backward, blank = Pipeline Bubble): Key takeaway: PP splits by layer — each stage only stores the weights and activations for its own layers, and stages communicate activation tensors over the network. Communication volume: Only activation tensors are transmitted (much smaller than AllReduce), works across nodes. Downside: Pipeline bubbles (GPUs waiting idle); you need enough micro-batches to fill the pipeline. Typical config: PP = 4–16, cross-node via InfiniBand / RoCE. Expert Parallelism (EP)Exclusive to MoE models: each Expert lives on a different GPU, and the Router decides which Expert to send each token to. Interactive animation: token dispatch (Router → Expert routing)The animation below shows the full dispatch flow: tokens go through the Router to compute gating scores, get sent via All-to-All to the target Expert’s GPU, are computed, then sent back: EP vs TP in MoE layers Approach Sharding Communication Load TP=8 (shard inside each Expert) Each GPU holds 1/8 of every Expert AllReduce per layer (large) Balanced (same amount per GPU) EP=8 (each Expert on its own GPU) Each GPU holds 1 full Expert All-to-All (token dispatch) Potentially unbalanced (hot Experts get more traffic) Key takeaway: EP places different Experts on different GPUs and exchanges tokens via All-to-All. Advantage: Naturally matches the MoE structure — each GPU only needs to store weights and optimizer state for one Expert. Challenge: All-to-All volume depends on batch size and number of experts; some GPUs sit idle when load is unbalanced. Typical config: EP = number of Experts or a factor of it (EP=8 for 8 experts). Sequence Parallelism (SP)Split along the sequence dimension. Operations that TP can’t shard (LayerNorm, Dropout) are distributed by SP. The problem: TP can’t shard LayerNorm and DropoutOperations inside a Transformer layer fall into two categories: TP-shardable (split along the hidden dimension): Self-Attention, FFN / MLP Requires the full hidden dimension (TP can’t shard): LayerNorm, Dropout + Residual SP’s solution: shard these operations along the sequence dimensionThe input sequence [batch, seq_len, hidden_dim] is split along the seq_len dimension across two GPUs: GPU 0: first half of the sequence (e.g., first 4 tokens) → does LayerNorm / Dropout locally GPU 1: second half of the sequence (e.g., last 4 tokens) → does LayerNorm / Dropout locally Because LayerNorm / Dropout both operate independently per token along the hidden dimension, splitting by sequence doesn’t affect correctness at all. TP + SP together: one full layer’s flow Key insight: . SP splits these two steps apart, and they naturally complete the communication right at the TP↔SP boundary — total communication volume is unchanged! Key takeaway: SP is not an independent parallelism strategy — it’s a complement to TP. TP shards Attention/FFN; SP shards LayerNorm/Dropout. What it saves: Activation memory. Without SP, every GPU stores LayerNorm activations for the full sequence; with SP, each GPU only stores seq_len/TP worth of activations. Communication overhead: AllGather + ReduceScatter replaces the original AllReduce — same total volume, but activation memory is reduced to 1/TP. Typical config: SP = TP (always enabled together; this is Megatron-LM’s default behavior). Summary comparison Strategy Sharding dimension Communication type Volume Scope Typical value TP Hidden dimension AllReduce Large (2× per layer) Intra-node NVLink 2–8 PP Layer (depth) P2P (activations) Small (activations only) Cross-node 4–16 EP Expert index All-to-All Medium (token dispatch) MoE layers, cross-node 8–64 SP Sequence length AllGather + ReduceScatter = TP volume Paired with TP, intra-node = TP 1T MoE model: how to combine all four strategies This post renders as markdown with 3 interactive animations embedded via the custom {% anim %} tag in isolated iframes, sourced from the Arkive tutorial.

title: LLM Inference Systems: A Deep Dive into SGLang
content: A complete walkthrough of an LLM inference request from user input to final output: request lifecycle, continuous batching, KV cache management, scheduler design, quantization, speculative decoding, and more. The post body is markdown; key mechanisms are accompanied by interactive animations (click the buttons to see them in action). 4.1 Request LifecycleAn LLM inference request passes through several stages from user input to final output. In SGLang, this process is carefully designed as an efficient pipeline: TokenizerManager → Scheduler → TpModelWorker → DetokenizerManager. The animation below shows a request flowing through five stages: Tokenize → Schedule → Prefill → Decode → Detokenize. Stage Breakdown Stage Operation Bottleneck SGLang Optimization Tokenize Convert user input text to a sequence of token IDs CPU-intensive Async tokenization overlapped with GPU computation Schedule Assign requests to batch slots, manage priorities Scheduling latency Continuous batching + priority queue Prefill Process all prompt tokens in parallel, populate KV cache Compute-bound Chunked prefill, radix cache reuse Decode Autoregressive token-by-token generation Memory bandwidth PageAttention, efficient KV cache access Detokenize Convert generated token IDs back to text CPU-intensive Incremental detokenization + streaming The Essential Difference Between Prefill and DecodeThe prefill stage is compute-bound (high compute volume; GPU compute units are the bottleneck): all prompt tokens can compute attention in parallel, leading to dense matrix operations. The decode stage is memory-bandwidth-bound (frequent KV cache reads; HBM bandwidth is the bottleneck): only one token is generated per step, but the full KV cache must be read each time. Performance Metrics: TTFT and TPOT Metric Full Name Meaning Determining Factor TTFT Time To First Token Latency from request submission to the first output token Prefill speed + queuing time TPOT Time Per Output Token Generation interval for each subsequent token (the “typing speed” perceived by users) Decode speed User experience: 1000 / TPOT = tokens/sec. TPOT=50 ms → 20 tok/s (smooth), TPOT=200 ms → 5 tok/s (choppy). Prefill Speed Derivation: From GPU FLOPS to Tokens/secPrefill is compute-bound; speed is determined by GPU throughput / FLOPs per token: Quick-reference formula (H100 BF16, MFU≈60%): Decode Speed Derivation: Memory-Bandwidth BoundDuring decode, each weight is used by only one token per step; the bottleneck is the speed of reading data. Generating each token requires reading from HBM: Simplified case: short sequences + GQA (KV cache negligible): When is KV cache non-negligible? Scenario Model Size KV Cache KV Fraction TPOT Impact 70B + GQA + 4K seq 140 GB 1.3 GB 1% Negligible 7B + MHA + 4K seq 14 GB 2.1 GB 13% Minor 7B + MHA + 32K seq 14 GB 16.8 GB 55% TPOT doubles! 7B + MHA + 128K seq 14 GB 67 GB 83% Dominates entirely 70B + GQA + 128K seq 140 GB 41 GB 23% Non-negligible Takeaway: GQA/MLA not only saves memory — more importantly, it saves bandwidth — reducing the KV cache that must be read on every decode step, directly lowering TPOT. Empirical validation (theory vs. measured): Model GPU Theoretical TPOT Measured TPOT MBU Source LLaMA-7B (BF16) 1×A100 80GB 7.2 ms 9.3 ms (bs=4) ~77% HuggingFace TGI LLaMA-70B (BF16) 2×A100 80GB 36 ms 53.8 ms (bs=1) ~67% Cursor blog LLaMA-70B (BF16) H100 (estimated) 21 ms ~35 ms ~60% Databricks (H100 is ~36% faster than A100) MBU (Model Bandwidth Utilization) = theoretical TPOT / measured TPOT. A real-world 60–80% is normal, because kernel launch overhead, AllReduce (TP), and attention computation are all non-weight-read costs. Why does decode need batching? KV Cache Size EstimationDeriving KV cache per token from model config: Model Params Layers KV Heads Attention KV/token (BF16) LLaMA-7B 7B 32 32 (MHA) MHA 512 KB LLaMA-13B 13B 40 40 (MHA) MHA 800 KB LLaMA-70B 70B 80 8 (GQA) GQA 320 KB LLaMA-405B 405B 126 8 (GQA) GQA 504 KB DeepSeek-V3 671B 61 MLA MLA (512d) 122 KB Key observation: you cannot infer KV cache linearly from parameter count! Serving capacity estimation: How GPU Memory Is Actually AllocatedKV cache is not the only tenant — during inference, a GPU’s memory is divided among several “residents.” What exactly is that 10% reserved by vLLM’s gpu_memory_utilization=0.9? Enumerating every item makes it possible to calculate how many concurrent requests fit, and when OOM happens. Item Purpose Size (70B, TP=8, FP16, per GPU) Grows with concurrency / seq len? Weights Model parameters — Linear/Embedding/LayerNorm 140 GB / 8 = 17.5 GB ✗ Fixed KV cache K, V tensors for every past token, must be read during decode 0 — tens of GB ✓ The only item that grows linearly Activations (peak single layer) Intermediate results of current forward layer (QKV / attn out / MLP) ~100 MB (decode) — ~1 GB (long prefill) ✓ Only during prefill cuBLAS / cuDNN workspace GEMM kernel split-K / reduce staging buffers A few hundred MB per stream ✗ Allocated at startup NCCL / RCCL communication buffers Send/receive staging for TP all-reduce / all-gather 100 MB – 1 GB ✗ Allocated at startup CUDA graph memory vLLM captures one graph per batch size by default Hundreds of MB – 1+ GB ✗ Allocated at startup PyTorch caching allocator fragmentation Unreturned / uncoalesced blocks from past allocations 0.5 – 2 GB ✗ Accumulates over time CUDA driver / runtime baseline The baseline shown by nvidia-smi as soon as the process starts ~500 MB ✗ Fixed Total non-KV-cache overhead for 70B per GPU ≈ 17.5 (weights) + 2–3 (workspaces/graph/fragmentation) + 0.5 (driver) ≈ 20 GB. On an 80 GB GPU that leaves roughly ~60 GB for KV cache + prefill spikes — which is why gpu_memory_utilization=0.9 reserves 8 GB as a buffer. Key Caveats for Each ItemWeights — After TP sharding, each GPU holds only 1/TP, but embeddings are typically not sharded (the vocabulary is small enough that all-gathering after sharding would cost more). A 70B vocabulary of 32k × hidden 8192 × 2 bytes ≈ 0.5 GB — unsharded, not a problem. Activations — These are the dominant term in training (70B training activations alone reach 145 GB, as covered in the previous chapter); during inference they sit at ~100 MB. The reason: inference does not store gradients, so each layer can be discarded as soon as it finishes; FlashAttention avoids materializing the O(s²) attention scores. The two scenarios where this can blow up: Ultra-long prefill: a s=128k prompt requires 10·128k·8192/8 ≈ 1.3 GB per layer. Large prefill batch: doubling the batch doubles the activation footprint. vLLM’s --max-num-batched-tokens cap is specifically designed to bound this prefill peak. cuBLAS workspace — Running torch.cuda.memory_summary() often reveals several hundred MB of Allocated by CUDA libs. This is primarily cuBLAS’s GEMM split-K reduction buffer — large matrix multiplications partition the K dimension into chunks, compute each chunk independently, then reduce; the intermediate results need staging. Each CUDA stream allocates independently; multiple streams multiply this footprint. NCCL buffer — With TP=8, the staging memory for all-reduce per GPU ≈ hidden × bs × seq × 2 bytes × 2 (recv+send). NCCL expands this on demand; large batches cause more inflation. You can cap it with environment variables like NCCL_BUFFSIZE=8388608. CUDA graph — vLLM captures one graph for each common batch size (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ...) to eliminate kernel launch overhead. Each captured graph carries its own ~tens-of-MB workspace; the cumulative size is substantial. --enforce-eager disables this and saves 1–2 GB, at a cost of 10–20% decode throughput. Allocator fragmentation — PyTorch’s caching allocator carves large blocks for small requests and may not be able to coalesce freed blocks. Long-running serving processes typically use 1–2 GB more than they did at startup, invisibly. PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True can substantially mitigate this. Concrete Memory Budget: 70B on 8 × 80 GB H100 When Should You Lower gpu_memory_utilization? Symptom Real Cause Not Caused By OOM at startup weights + workspaces already exceed 90% Activation growth OOM during prefill burst Long prompts / large prefill batch causes activations to spike to GB scale temporarily KV cache growth (KV cache grows gradually, not instantly) OOM after long runtime Allocator fragmentation accumulates Weights / KV cache Lowering gpu_memory_utilization (e.g., 0.9 → 0.85) primarily provides headroom for workspaces + prefill spikes, and has little to do with steady-state activations. One-Line Intuition Training memory = (weights + grads + optimizer) (shardable with ZeRO) + activations (grow with batch×s², must be compressed with checkpointing + TP + SP) Inference memory = weights (static) + KV cache (grows linearly with concurrency, the only tunable pool) + workspace (allocated at startup) + activation spike (only during prefill) What gpu_memory_utilization is really reserving space for is workspace + spike, not steady-state activations. Smaller value → smaller KV cache pool → fewer concurrent requests fit; larger value → more likely to OOM during a prefill burst. Where Activations Actually Live in the TransformerThe table above vaguely says “intermediate results” for activations, but knowing exactly which tensors, and their shapes, determines how large a prefill spike will be and what FlashAttention saves. Walk through the forward pass of a pre-LN transformer block with every activation labeled: Each ★ is a large contributor; everything else is at the (b, s, h) scale. Grouping activations by order of magnitude: Scale Shape Which tensors Size per instance (70B, b=1, s=2048) O(b·s·h) (b, s, h) LN i/o, Q/K/V, attn_out, residual sum, LN2 i/o Each ≈ 34 MB O(b·s·4h) (b, s, 4h) MLP up output, GeLU output Each ≈ 134 MB (4× larger) O(b·n_h·s²) (b, n_h, s, s) Attention scores, softmax output Each ≈ 1.0 GB (s² explosion) At s=8192, a single attention score tensor is 17 GB per layer — it overwhelms everything else. This is why long-context training almost universally requires FlashAttention. What FlashAttention EliminatesFlashAttention’s core: scores and softmax outputs are never materialized to HBM, computed in SRAM tile-by-tile and fed directly to @ V. So with FA: ★ The two O(s²) items: disappear from the activation list (backward uses the same tiled recomputation — see FlashAttention backward) Everything else is unchanged Megatron’s Act per layer = 34·s·b·h + 5·a·s²·b formula has the 5·a·s²·b term eliminated by FA. This is why Megatron’s selective activation recomputation recomputes only attention scores by default — the single largest item, with the cheapest recompute cost (~10% extra FLOPs saves ~80% of activations). Two “Non-layer” Activations at the Boundaries Tensor Shape Size (70B, b=1, s=2048) Notes Input embedding output (b, s, h) 34 MB One copy; must be retained during training (needed for embedding backward) Output logits (b, s, vocab) LLaMA-2 vocab=32k: 130 MB; LLaMA-3 vocab=128k: 524 MB Larger than a single-layer activation; a common OOM hotspot Loss softmax intermediate (b, s, vocab) Same as above Commonly eliminated with fused CE kernels (Liger/Apex) The output logits tensor is the biggest single-point contributor — this is why fused cross-entropy is almost mandatory when training long-context + large-vocabulary models (the approach is identical to FlashAttention: avoid materializing the intermediate). Training vs. Inference: Which Activations Survive, Which Are Freed Training (backward needs them) Inference (no backward) LN i/o / Q / K / V / MLP intermediates Kept until backward completes Discarded as soon as a layer finishes; memory reused by the next layer Attention scores (O(s²)) Without FA: stored; with FA: not stored Without FA: temporary; with FA: not stored Output logits Kept until loss backward Discarded immediately (one token generated is enough) Total live activations simultaneously All layers × all items above (without checkpointing) Roughly only the current layer’s intermediates This is why training activations are ~150 GB/GPU (70B) while inference activations are ~100 MB/GPU — not because inference “saves” anything special, but because inference simply does not need to retain them all before backward begins. One-Line Intuition “Short” activations (O(b·s·h)): like hidden states passing through a pipeline stage by stage, one copy each, not huge but numerous. “Wide” activations (O(b·s·4h)): the MLP intermediate expands to 4×; these are the largest non-O(s²) items per layer and contribute the most to total activation memory. “Square” activations (O(b·n_h·s²)): the attention score matrix — explodes as soon as s grows. FlashAttention exists specifically to eliminate them. 4.2 Continuous Batching vs. Static BatchingTraditional static batching waits for every request in a batch to finish generating before starting on the next batch, causing severe GPU resource waste. Continuous batching dynamically adds and removes requests so that the GPU stays highly utilized at all times. The animation below compares GPU utilization between the two batching strategies (red = wasted slots): Core Implementation of Continuous Batching Key design points: Iteration-level scheduling: requests may join or leave after every decode iteration No padding required: requests of different lengths are handled efficiently via PageAttention Memory-aware scheduling: new requests are only admitted when the KV cache pool has sufficient space Priority support: shorter requests complete first, reducing average latency Performance Comparison Metric Static Batching Continuous Batching Improvement GPU utilization 30–50% 85–95% ~2× Throughput (tokens/s) Baseline 2–3× Significant Average latency High (waits for longest request) Low (timely release) 50–70%↓ Tail latency (P99) Very high Controllable Major improvement 4.3 KV Cache ManagementPageAttention: Virtual Memory for the KV CacheInspired by the OS paged memory model. PageAttention divides the KV cache into fixed-size pages (blocks) and uses a page table to implement non-contiguous physical memory mappings, solving the memory fragmentation problem in traditional approaches. Radix Cache: Prefix-Sharing TreeOne of SGLang’s core innovations. When multiple requests share the same system prompt or prefix, the radix cache shares KV cache via a tree structure, avoiding redundant computation. Below is an interactive radix tree: click the buttons to add requests and watch how shared prefixes are reused and how new requests match the longest cached prefix: Radix Cache Implementation Advantages of radix cache: Prefix sharing: requests with the same system prompt share KV cache, saving GPU memory Automatic matching: new requests automatically find the longest cached prefix, skipping already-cached prefill computation LRU eviction: reclaims infrequently used cache entries when memory is tight Multi-turn acceleration: KV from earlier turns in a multi-turn conversation is cached and reused 4.4 Scheduler DesignThe Scheduling Tension Between Prefill and DecodePrefill and decode have fundamentally different compute characteristics; efficiently scheduling both on the same GPU is a core challenge: Property Prefill Decode Compute profile Compute-bound (large matmul) Memory-bound (KV cache reads) Latency sensitivity Affects TTFT Affects TPOT Token count Hundreds to thousands 1 per step GPU utilization pattern High compute density High bandwidth demand SGLang’s scheduling strategy (overlap scheduling: overlapping CPU scheduling with GPU computation): Chunked Prefill: Why It Is Needed and How to Choose Chunk SizeProblem: long prefill blocks decode. Prefill and decode share the GPU’s SMs (compute units). A large prefill kernel, once submitted to the GPU, monopolizes all SMs until it finishes; subsequent decode kernels queue behind it: Note: Multiple CUDA streams do not solve this — if one kernel already occupies all SMs, a kernel on another stream, even if submitted, cannot get SM time. Chunked prefill interleaves at kernel boundaries; it is not true parallelism. Chunk size derivation: Scheduling policy: SJF (Shortest Job First) + memory-aware: Preemption: What to Do When Memory Runs OutWhen KV cache memory is insufficient to accommodate a new request, some running requests must be “evicted” to free space. Preemption strategies: Strategy Approach Recovery Speed Extra Cost Swap to CPU Move KV cache to CPU RAM Fast (PCIe copy back) Requires CPU memory + PCIe bandwidth Recompute Discard KV cache, re-prefill on recovery Slow (recompute) No extra memory, but wastes compute Kill Terminate the request entirely N/A Bad user experience Who should be preempted? Congestion control mechanism — analogous to TCP congestion control — when system load is high: Monitor waiting queue length and KV cache utilization When thresholds are exceeded, throttle new prefill admissions In extreme cases, trigger preemption (pause low-priority requests) Gradually restore admission rate as load decreases 4.5 Quantization OverviewQuantization reduces model memory footprint and compute overhead by lowering the numerical precision of weights and/or activations. For LLM inference, it is a key technology for deploying large models within constrained GPU memory budgets. Drag the slider below to switch precision levels and compare memory usage across FP32 / FP16 / FP8 / INT4: Common Quantization Strategies Method Weight Precision Activation Precision Characteristics W16A16 FP16 FP16 Baseline, lossless W8A8 (FP8) FP8 E4M3 FP8 E5M2 Natively supported on H100, nearly lossless W4A16 (GPTQ/AWQ) INT4 FP16 Weight-only quantization, activations at high precision W4A8 INT4 INT8 Aggressive compression, requires calibration FP8 quantization (natively supported by H100 Tensor Cores): Mixed precision strategy. Not all layers are well-suited for quantization. A typical approach: Attention QKV/O projections: suitable for FP8 quantization FFN layers: suitable for INT4 weight quantization (large parameter count) LayerNorm: keep at FP32 (precision-sensitive) First and last layers: typically kept at high precision 4.6 Speculative DecodingThe core idea of speculative decoding: use a small, fast draft model to generate multiple candidate tokens, then use the large target model to verify those tokens in parallel. Because verifying N tokens costs roughly the same as generating 1 token (both require one forward pass), sufficiently high acceptance rates yield significant speedups. The animation below shows the draft model generating 5 candidates, the target model verifying them in parallel, accepting 3 tokens plus 1 corrected token: Verification Algorithm Speedup AnalysisLet acceptance rate be , draft steps , and draft model speed be times that of the target: Closed-form formula for expected accepted tokens: 4.7 Constraint DecodingStructured Output GenerationIn practice we often need an LLM to produce output in a specific format (JSON, SQL, code, etc.). Constraint decoding guarantees that the output always conforms to a given grammar by dynamically masking illegal tokens during generation. Core approaches: CFG (Context-Free Grammar) guidance: define grammar rules; only legally next tokens are allowed during decoding JSON Schema constraints: dynamically compute a valid token mask from the JSON Schema Regex constraints: filter tokens using a regular-expression state machine FSM (Finite State Machine): compile the constraint into an FSM for efficient legal-token lookup Optimizations in SGLang: SGLang combines FSM state transitions with the radix cache — requests sharing the same constraint rule share FSM state and precomputed token masks, avoiding redundant compilation. Additionally, through jump-forward decoding, when the FSM determines that there is only one legal path ahead (e.g., the quotation marks around a JSON key), model inference can be skipped and the token emitted directly. 4.8 Model Loading PipelineThe Complete Flow from Disk to GPULoading a large model involves several steps: weight file parsing → weight mapping → tensor-parallel sharding → GPU memory allocation → quantization conversion. Key optimizations: Streaming load: load one shard file at a time to avoid CPU memory peaks Async H2D transfer: overlap CPU → GPU transfer with CPU loading of the next shard Safetensors format: zero-copy memory-mapped files, load specific tensors on demand Pre-computed sharding: TP plan determined upfront to avoid runtime allocations Exercises Exercise 1: Computing KV Cache Memory Given model parameters (Llama-70B, num_layers=80, num_kv_heads=8 GQA, head_dim=128, seq_len=4096, batch_size=32, FP16), compute KV cache memory. Questions: (a) KV cache size for a single request? (b) KV cache size for the entire batch? (c) With an 80 GB GPU and model weights of 140 GB (TP=2, 70 GB per GPU), how much remains for KV cache? What is the maximum batch size? Full Solution: Exercise 2: Scheduler Policy Design Scenario: H100 (80 GB) TP=1, 7B model (14 GB), KV cache pool with 50 GB remaining, running batch of 20 decode requests (average seq_len=2000), waiting queue of 5 prefill requests (prompt_len 100/500/2000/8000/32000), SLOs: TTFT < 2s, TPOT < 50 ms. (a) Prefill order? (b) Chunk size? (c) Is preemption necessary? Full Solution: Exercise 3: Speculative Decoding Speedup Analysis Target model 70B single forward 50 ms, draft model 7B single forward 8 ms, , . (a) Expected accepted tokens per round. (b) Total latency per round. (c) Speedup. (d) What if ? Full Solution: Exercise 4: Radix Cache Hit Rate Calculation A chatbot shares a system prompt (1000 tokens). 60% of requests share a prefix of 1200 tokens, 25% share 1150, and 15% share only 1000; average user query is 300 tokens. (a) Average cache hit token count. (b) Average newly computed prefill tokens. (c) How much is saved? Full Solution: Coding Exercise A: Implement a Simple Continuous Batching Scheduler Implement a continuous batching scheduler that supports dynamically inserting and completing requests; on each step, remove is_done requests and fill empty slots from the waiting queue. Coding Exercise B: Implement the Verification Logic for Speculative Decoding Given draft_probs and target_probs, implement token-by-token verification. Accept condition: rand() < min(1, target_p[x] / draft_p[x]); on rejection, sample from the normalized distribution max(0, target_p - draft_p). Theoretical per-token acceptance rate = . System Design Interview Questions (Anthropic/OpenAI Style)The following questions simulate system design and performance analysis questions from AI infrastructure interviews. Requirement: provide numerical derivations, not just qualitative answers. Interview Question 1: Capacity Planning — Serving Cluster for a 405B Model Deploy a 405B model (FP8, 405 GB), SLOs: P99 TPOT ≤ 100 ms / TTFT ≤ 2 s, QPS 200, average input 2000 / output 500, GPU H100 80 GB. Full Solution: Interview Question 2: What Is the Ceiling for Decode Batching? LLaMA-70B (BF16) on 1×H100 — derive the three upper bounds on batch size. Full Solution: Interview Question 3: Trade-offs of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation Mooncake/DistServe places prefill and decode on separate GPU clusters; analyze the KV cache transfer cost. Full Solution: Interview Question 4: Why Does Speculative Decoding Yield Diminishing Returns at High Batch Sizes? Full Solution: Interview Question 5: Design a KV Cache Strategy for Multi-turn Chat 70B GQA (KV per token 320 KB), 4×H100 (TP=4, 30 GB/GPU for KV), average 8 conversation turns, each turn: 200 user + 500 assistant tokens. Full Solution: Interview Question 6: Impact of Quantization on Serving Performance Compare BF16 / FP8 / INT4 deployment of LLaMA-70B. Full Solution: Interview Question 7: Graceful Degradation Under Traffic Spike Normal 100 QPS suddenly spikes to 500 QPS (5× spike) for 2 minutes, with no auto-scaling. Design a graceful degradation plan. Full Solution: This post is Chapter 4 of the ML Systems series. title: From Self-Attention to Flash Attention
content: From self-attention to Flash Attention — understanding the core computational principles behind modern LLMs. The body of this post is in Markdown; key mechanisms come with interactive animations (click the buttons to step through). 1.1 Self-AttentionThe core idea of self-attention is to let every token in the sequence “attend” to all other tokens. The formula is: The animation below uses small matrices (Q 2×2, K/V 3×2) to step through: QKᵀ → scale → softmax → weighted sum of V. Code: Scaled Dot-Product Attention 1.2 Multi-Head AttentionMulti-Head Attention (MHA) projects the input into multiple different subspaces; each “head” independently computes attention, then the results are concatenated and projected back to the original dimension. Why split into multiple heads? Diversity: different heads can learn to attend to different types of relationships (syntactic, semantic, positional, etc.) Computational efficiency: each head has dimension , so total computation is the same as a single large head Expressiveness: attention patterns across multiple subspaces are richer than those in a single space Typical configurations: GPT-3 uses 96 heads with , giving each head dimension 128. LLaMA-2-70B uses 64 query heads (plus 8 KV heads for GQA). The animation below shows how the tensor is split into multiple heads, computed in parallel, then concatenated and projected back: Grouped Query Attention (GQA)In standard MHA, every head has its own K and V projections. GQA lets multiple query heads share the same set of KV heads, significantly reducing the KV cache memory footprint: Method Query Heads KV Heads KV Cache Size MHA h h 1× GQA h h/g 1/g × MQA h 1 1/h × 1.3 Flash AttentionFlash Attention is an IO-aware exact attention algorithm. Its core motivation: GPU compute is far faster than memory bandwidth. The bottleneck in standard attention is not FLOPs — it’s the number of HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) reads and writes. Root Cause: HBM Access in Standard AttentionEvery step of standard attention requires HBM reads/writes. Tracking shapes and HBM access volume for a single head: Key bottleneck: The intermediate matrices S and P are both [N, N]. At N=4096, d=128: S[4096×4096] takes 32 MB, while Q/K/V each take only 1 MB — the intermediates are 32× larger than the inputs/outputs! We pay O(N²) extra memory and massive HBM traffic just to store temporary matrices. Flash Attention’s Solution: Tiling + Online SoftmaxCore idea: never write an N×N matrix to HBM. Tile Q, K, V into small blocks, and do all computation inside Shared Memory (programmer-controlled on-chip SRAM per SM; up to ~192 KB/SM on A100). Note this is distinct from L2 Cache (40 MB, hardware-managed) — Shared Memory is directly controllable. Let the Shared Memory capacity of a single SM be M elements. We need to simultaneously hold a K block, a V block, a Q block, an O block, and the intermediate score matrix: The animation below uses an example with N=8, d=4, to show the shape of each block matrix at every step, the computation, and how results accumulate into the final output O: IO Complexity Derivation (the key insight!)Standard Attention: HBM accesses total, extra memory. Flash Attention: the outer loop iterates over K,V blocks times; the inner loop iterates over Q blocks times: Substituting : Extra memory is only (a running max and running sum per row). Why is this so good? When (typically M=100K, d²=16K), . Example: N=4096, d=128, M=100K → standard ≈ 17.3M HBM accesses, Flash ≈ 2.75M (saving 84%!). Online Softmax AlgorithmStandard softmax requires two passes (pass 1 to find max; pass 2 to sum the exps), which demands that the full S matrix be materialized. Flash Attention uses an online algorithm that only needs a single pass. The animation below uses a 1×8 score vector (split into 4 blocks) to dynamically show how m, l, and O are updated block by block, and how old values are corrected by the correction factor α when a new block reveals a larger max: Mathematical intuition: the attention output is fundamentally just numerator / denominator: The online algorithm incrementally accumulates numerator and denominator, using a running max for numerical stability: Intuition: Relationship between O and l — l accumulates exp(score), O accumulates exp(score)×v, and at the end O/l is a softmax-weighted average; the update rules are perfectly symmetric. Why do we need α = exp(m_old − m_new)? — After encountering a larger score, all previous exp(s − m_old) values need to become exp(s − m_new). Since exp(s − m_new) = exp(s − m_old) × exp(m_old − m_new), multiplying old values by α does the job. What if the new block has no larger max? — m_new = m_old → α = 1 → old values stay unchanged, only new terms are added. Mathematical equivalence — this is not an approximation! After iterating over all blocks, O/l is strictly equal to softmax(QKᵀ)V. Full Pseudocode IO Complexity Summary Metric Standard Attention Flash Attention Advantage HBM read/write count Θ(Nd + N²) Θ(N²d²/M) reduced when M > d² Extra HBM memory O(N²) (stores S, P) O(N) (stores l, m) quadratic → linear! SRAM utilization unused O(M) (fully utilized) — Compute (FLOPs) O(N²d) O(N²d) (identical!) compute unchanged Numerical result exact exact (bit-identical) not an approximation! Flash Attention is not an approximate algorithm! It produces bit-identical results to standard attention. The only difference is in the IO pattern: it trades more compute for fewer memory accesses (because GPU compute is far faster than memory bandwidth). 1.4 Cross Attention vs Self-AttentionThe fundamental difference between self-attention and cross attention lies in where Q, K, V come from: Property Self-Attention Cross Attention Source of Q same sequence decoder sequence Source of K, V same sequence encoder output Typical use language modeling, BERT translation, vision-language Causal Mask used in decoder typically not used KV Cache grows each step fixed after encoding Applications: Self-Attention: GPT family (causal), BERT (bidirectional) Cross Attention: machine translation (encoder-decoder), multimodal models (image tokens attend to text tokens), Stable Diffusion (text→image conditioning) 1.5 KV CacheIn autoregressive generation, computing attention for each new token naively requires recomputing the keys and values for all previous tokens. KV cache avoids this redundancy by caching the already-computed K and V matrices. Why cache only K and V, not Q? Because during generation we only need the new token’s Q to attend over all previous K and V. The Q values of earlier tokens are no longer needed — their outputs are already determined: The animation below generates tokens one by one: the left side shows the attention matrix (only computing the new row), the right side shows the KV cache growing, and the bottom compares compute cost with and without caching: Memory footprint analysis: KV cache size = 2 (K+V) × num_layers × num_heads × head_dim × seq_len × dtype_size. Example: LLaMA-2-70B (80 layers, 64 heads, head_dim=128, FP16) at seq_len=4096: KV cache = 2 × 80 × 64 × 128 × 4096 × 2 bytes ≈ 10.7 GB per request. Code: KV Cache 1.6 Special Tokens and Chat TemplatesModern LLMs use special tokens to mark sequence structure and control generation behavior. These tokens are defined at training time, and the model learns their semantics. Token Purpose Example Models <BOS> / <s> beginning of sequence LLaMA, Mistral <EOS> / </s> end of sequence, stop generation LLaMA, Mistral <PAD> pad to fixed length BERT, T5 <UNK> unknown token (OOV handling) most models [INST]…[/INST] instruction markers LLaMA-2-Chat <|im_start|> / <|im_end|> chat message boundaries ChatML format Chat templates convert multi-turn conversations into token sequences the model can understand; the format varies across models: Important: an incorrect chat template can severely degrade model output quality. Every model has an expected format that must be followed exactly. Using tokenizer.apply_chat_template() is the safest approach. Role separation and attention masks: In a chat scenario, the system prompt is global context (all subsequent tokens can attend to it), the user turn is the user’s input, and the assistant turn is the model’s output. During SFT, cross-entropy loss is typically computed only on the assistant tokens; system and user tokens serve as context but do not contribute to the loss. Exercises Exercise 1: Manually Compute Scaled Dot-Product Attention Given matrices (): Q = [[1,0],[0,1]], K = [[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]], V = [[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]]. Compute Attention(Q, K, V) (no causal mask). Full solution: Exercise 2: Flash Attention IO Complexity Analysis Let N=4096, d=128, SRAM M=100KB (≈50K FP16 elements). Standard Attention HBM accesses: reads = 3Nd + 2N² ≈ 35.1M, writes = 2N² + Nd ≈ 34.1M, total 4N² + 4Nd ≈ 69.2M elements × 2 bytes ≈ 132 MB. Flash configuration: , take ; outer/inner loops each run times. Flash HBM accesses: ≈ N²d/B_c = 4096²×128/64 ≈ 33.5M elements, saving about 52% vs. standard. More importantly, no O(N²) extra memory is needed — standard requires 32 MB, Flash only needs O(N) ≈ a few KB. Exercise 3: Estimate KV Cache Memory (LLaMA-3-70B + GQA) Configuration: 80 layers, 64 query heads (GQA, KV heads=8), head_dim=128, FP16. batch=32, seq=8192. Conclusion: GQA (8 KV heads) reduces KV cache from 640 GB to 80 GB (87.5% saving); FP8 quantization further halves it to 40 GB. This is also why techniques like PagedAttention (vLLM) matter. Exercise 4 (Bonus): Why is Prefill Compute-Bound and Decode Memory-Bound? Arithmetic Intensity = FLOPs / Bytes Accessed. Prefill: N tokens are processed simultaneously, forming large GEMMs. QKV projection AI ≈ 3000 FLOPs/byte, Attention AI ≈ 2730 FLOPs/byte — both >> H100’s compute/bandwidth ratio (~295) → compute-bound. Decode: only 1 new token, but the entire KV cache must be read. FLOPs ≈ 67M, reads ≈ 64 MB → AI ≈ 1.05 FLOPs/byte << 295 → memory-bound; the GPU spends most of its time waiting for HBM to deliver the KV cache. The AI difference between the two phases is ~3000×! This is why LLM serving systems distinguish prefill from decode (continuous batching, chunked prefill). Coding Exercise A: Implement Multi-Head Attention from Scratch Requirements: implement Q/K/V projections → split heads → scaled dot-product attention → concat → output projection, with causal mask support, and verify against torch.nn.MultiheadAttention (max diff < 1e-5). Coding Exercise B: Implement Incremental Decode with KV Cache Requirements: implement prefill (process full prompt) + decode (one token at a time, reusing cached K/V), plus a no-cache baseline, verify that both produce bit-identical outputs, and demonstrate the speedup. Hint: during decode, only compute Q for the new token and attend over the full concatenated K/V; cache shape is (batch, num_heads, past_len, head_dim). title: RLHF Systems: From Theory to Production
content: From RL fundamentals through PPO and GRPO, to production frameworks like veRL / SLIME / OpenRLHF and Training-Inference Mismatch — a systems-level understanding of modern LLM alignment training. The body of this post is Markdown; key mechanisms are accompanied by interactive animations (step through them with the buttons). 1. RL Fundamentals ReviewMarkov Decision Process (MDP)In the RLHF setting we model the LLM generation process as an MDP: MDP element LLM counterpart Notes State Token sequence generated so far prompt + generated prefix Action Next token sampled from the vocabulary Policy LLM output distribution softmax over logits Reward Reward Model score typically given only at end of sequence Transition Deterministic concatenation Policy GradientThe core idea of Policy Gradient: increase the probability of good actions, decrease the probability of bad ones. Here is the Advantage Function (, measuring how much better a given action is than average), representing how much better action is in state relative to the average policy. Intuition behind the Advantage Function: : this action is better than average → increase its probability : this action is worse than average → decrease its probability : this action is on par with average → no change Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE)GAE balances bias and variance by taking an exponentially weighted average of multi-step TD errors: When this reduces to single-step TD (low variance, high bias); when it reduces to Monte Carlo (high variance, low bias). 2. PPO In DepthClipped Surrogate ObjectivePPO’s core innovation is using clipping to constrain the magnitude of policy updates, avoiding catastrophically large steps: When strays too far from 1 (i.e., the new and old policies diverge too much), the clip prevents further optimization. Drag the sliders below to change the parameters and observe how the clipped objective constrains policy updates: Full PPO LossThe total PPO loss consists of three terms: : policy update (described above) : Value Function loss = : entropy bonus, prevents the policy from collapsing too early 3. RLHF PipelineThree-Stage PipelineThe standard RLHF pipeline has three training stages. The animation below shows how data flows through SFT → Reward Model → PPO → Aligned Model: Stage 1: SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) Fine-tune the pretrained model on high-quality human demonstrations, teaching it to respond in the desired instruction-following format. Data: (prompt, ideal_response) pairs Objective: standard language modeling loss (next-token prediction) Output: SFT model Stage 2: Reward Model Training Train a scalar reward model to learn the human preference ranking. where is the human-preferred response and is the less-preferred one (Bradley-Terry model). Stage 3: PPO Training Use the RM as a reward signal and optimize the policy with PPO. A KL penalty is added to prevent drifting too far from the SFT model: 4. GRPO — Group Relative Policy OptimizationCore Idea: Eliminating the Critic NetworkGRPO (proposed by DeepSeek) is built around one key innovation: estimating the advantage via relative comparisons within a group of rollouts, with no separately trained value function (critic). For each prompt , generate responses , score each one, then normalize using the within-group mean and standard deviation. The animation below compares PPO (which requires a Critic network) with GRPO (which uses within-group relative comparisons): GRPO Advantages Property PPO GRPO Critic Network required (same scale) not required Memory footprint high (4 models) low (3 models) Advantage estimation GAE (temporal) group normalization Best suited for general use outcome-level reward Implementation complexity high lower GRPO algorithm: uses within-group relative rewards as the advantage, with no Critic model required. 5. Systems Design ChallengesTraining + Inference Co-designThe biggest engineering challenge in RLHF systems: the same model weights must serve both training (backward pass) and inference (rollout generation). The core tension: Training needs: parameter sharding (FSDP/DeepSpeed), activation storage, gradient computation Inference needs: Tensor Parallelism, KV Cache, continuous batching The two require completely different storage layouts and parallelism strategies! Common solutions: Strategy Pros Cons Colocate no network overhead memory contention, low utilization Separate deployment each side can be optimized independently requires weight sync Hybrid Engine dynamic switching complex to implement Toggle the tabs below to see the three Weight Sync strategies and play the NCCL broadcast animation: Training-Inference Mismatch: rollout and training use different kernels, leading to numerical discrepancies. 6. veRL ArchitectureDesign Philosophy: Single Controller + Hybrid EngineveRL (Volcano Engine RL) uses Ray as the distributed scheduling framework, with a single controller coordinating all components. Core components: Single Controller: one Python process manages the entire training loop Actor Workers: run the policy model (FSDP sharded) Rollout Workers: run the inference engine (vLLM/SGLang) Critic Workers: run the value model Reward Workers: run the reward model veRL Training Loop: Controller sends prompts to Rollout Workers Rollout Workers generate responses using the current policy Reward Workers compute reward scores Critic Workers compute value estimates Controller computes GAE advantages Actor Workers execute the PPO update Sync new weights to Rollout Workers → back to 1 Key to the Hybrid Engine: veRL’s Actor Workers and Rollout Workers can be colocated on the same set of GPUs: Training phase: GPUs do FSDP training Rollout phase: offload optimizer states, switch to inference mode Reduces the network overhead of weight synchronization 7. SLIME ArchitectureHigh-Throughput RLHF with SGLang + MegatronSLIME combines SGLang (a high-efficiency inference engine) with Megatron/FSDP (distributed training) to achieve high-throughput RLHF. Component Framework Characteristics Rollout Engine SGLang RadixAttention, continuous batching, chunked prefill Training Backend FSDP / Megatron ZeRO-3 / 3D parallelism Orchestration Ray flexible resource allocation Weight Sync NCCL / Shared Memory asynchronous updates Async Rollout Design: SLIME’s core optimization is overlapping training and rollout execution: SLIME full workflow: Ray orchestration + SGLang Rollout + Megatron/FSDP Training. 8. OpenRLHFOpen-Source RLHF FrameworkOpenRLHF is the most widely used open-source RLHF implementation in the community. It integrates vLLM/SGLang as the rollout engine and Ray for distributed scheduling. Design highlights: Modular design: Actor, Critic, Reward, and Reference models are deployed independently vLLM/SGLang integration: leverages the high-throughput characteristics of mature inference engines Ray orchestration: flexibly assigns GPUs to different roles Multiple algorithm support: PPO, DPO, GRPO, REINFORCE++ Typical deployment topology: GPU utilization optimization: OpenRLHF maximizes GPU utilization through packing and async scheduling: Rollout and training can overlap (near on-policy) Reward and Reference computations can run in parallel Dynamic batch size adapts to varying sequence lengths OpenRLHF training phase: vLLM/SGLang inference + DeepSpeed/Ray training orchestration. 9. Multi-turn RLRL in the Agent LoopModern LLM agents require multi-turn interaction: calling tools, observing results, continuing to reason. This poses new challenges for RL systems. Complexities of multi-turn rollouts: Variable-length trajectories: different queries may require anywhere from 1 to 10+ tool calls Asynchronous execution: tool call latency is unpredictable (API calls, code execution) Credit assignment: how should the reward be distributed across turns? Batching difficulties: different samples are at different stages, making naive batching impossible The animation below demonstrates a complete multi-turn interaction loop (Agent → Tool → Environment → Reward): Async Rollout Design Pattern: veRL Agent Loop: async multi-turn interaction architecture with tool calling and environment stepping. 10. Training-Inference MismatchOn-Policy vs Off-Policy Trade-offsIn the ideal case, PPO is an on-policy algorithm — rollouts must be generated by the current policy. In distributed systems, however, strict on-policy training carries enormous overhead. Truly On-Policy Near On-Policy (Importance Sampling) Re-rollout before every update Rollout and training overlap Data from the latest policy Data may come from an older (stale) policy Training and inference must alternate Requires importance sampling correction Low GPU utilization (mutual waiting) High GPU utilization KL divergence is exact Staleness can introduce bias Impact of staleness: suppose the rollout used at training step was generated at step (a lag of steps): When is large, the variance of grows dramatically → training becomes unstable. Practical solutions: Method Idea Trade-off Strict sync only train after rollout finishes low utilization but stable Bounded staleness allow at most steps of lag balances utilization and stability IS clipping clip importance weights biased but variance-controlled μ-PPO multi-step IS correction theoretically elegant but complex 11. Exercises Exercise 1: Manual GAE Computation Given the following sequence (episode length T=4): Rewards , Values , , , terminal state (). Compute the and at each time step. Full solution: Intuition: earlier time steps have higher advantage because the final positive reward propagates backward through GAE. Exercise 2: PPO Loss Computation Given (at a single token level): Old log prob , New log prob , Advantage , Clip . Compute (a) the probability ratio, (b) the unclipped objective, (c) the clipped objective, and (d) the final PPO loss. Full solution: Analysis: since (a good action), the policy increased the probability of this action (ratio > 1). But ratio = 1.65 is outside the [0.8, 1.2] range, so clipping kicks in and prevents an overly large update. This is exactly the conservative-update mechanism at the heart of PPO. Exercise 3: Designing a Weight Update Strategy GPU topology: 2 nodes, each with 8 × H100 (80 GB); intra-node NVLink (900 GB/s), inter-node InfiniBand (400 Gb/s); model has 70B parameters (FP16 ≈ 140 GB); requirement: Training (FSDP) + Inference (TP=4) deployed simultaneously. Design the optimal GPU allocation and weight sync strategy. Recommended approach: Rationale: Training owns Node 0 exclusively: with 70B FSDP across 8 GPUs, each card holds 17.5 GB of parameters plus optimizer states (70 GB/card), which fits within H100’s 80 GB. Intra-node NVLink ensures efficient AllGather. Inference on Node 1: two TP=4 instances process different rollout batches in parallel, increasing throughput. TP=4 communication is bottleneck-free over NVLink. Weight Sync: use NCCL broadcast (cross-node over InfiniBand). 70B FP16 ≈ 140 GB takes ~2.8 s over 400 Gb/s IB. Combined with double-buffering, the transfer can happen asynchronously while the next rollout batch begins. Utilization optimization: training and inference overlap — while the training update runs, inference continues rollout with the old weights; once the update finishes, NCCL broadcast pushes the new weights. Bounded staleness = 1. Exercise 4: Analyzing On-Policy vs Off-Policy Trade-offs Training a 7B model with RLHF, we observe the following metrics at different staleness levels: IS weight variance, KL divergence, reward improvement, and GPU utilization. Staleness IS Weight Variance KL Divergence Reward Improvement GPU Utilization 0 0 0.02 +0.15/step 35% 1 0.08 0.05 +0.13/step 55% 3 0.35 0.12 +0.10/step 75% 5 1.2 0.25 +0.05/step 85% 10 5.8 0.8 -0.02/step 92% Analyze: (a) What is the optimal staleness? (b) Why does reward actually drop at staleness=10? (c) How can we mitigate the problem without reducing staleness? (a) Optimal staleness analysis (wall-clock improvement ∝ reward_per_step × throughput; set base throughput = 1 at 35% util): Optimal staleness = 3, striking the best balance between per-step efficiency and throughput. (b) Why reward drops at staleness=10: IS weight variance = 5.8 means gradient estimates are extremely noisy; KL = 0.8 indicates the current policy has diverged significantly from the policy that generated the rollouts; this is equivalent to training on completely uncorrelated data — high variance causes the optimizer to “random-walk” rather than converge. (c) Mitigation (without reducing staleness): IS Clipping: clip importance weights to [0.5, 2.0], trading unbiasedness for stability Reduce PPO epochs: drop from 4 to 1-2, reducing per-step policy drift Increase KL penalty β: constrains the rate of policy change, reducing effective staleness Early stopping: monitor approx KL; discard the batch when it exceeds a threshold Partial refresh: use a mixed batch of 50% old data + 50% fresh rollouts Programming Exercise A: Implementing GAE Implement a complete GAE computation that correctly handles episode boundaries. Formula: , . Programming Exercise B: Implementing PPO Clip Loss Implement a complete PPO clip loss computation. Formula: , , . Key property: when and ratio > , is truncated (stops growing), preventing excessive policy drift; similarly truncated when and ratio < , preventing over-penalization of an action. Taking the min ensures conservative updates regardless of the sign of the advantage. Exercise C: PPO vs GRPO Memory Comparison Given a 70B parameter model for RL training. PPO maintains Actor + Critic + Reference + Reward (4 models); GRPO maintains Actor + Reference (2 models); Adam + BF16; each H100 has 80 GB. (a) Total memory requirements: a trainable model (Adam BF16) costs ~16 bytes/param (2B weights + 2B gradients + 4B+4B Adam states); a frozen inference-only model costs 2 bytes/param. (b) Minimum H100 count: PPO 2520/80 = 31.5 → at least 32 GPUs; GRPO 1260/80 = 15.75 → at least 16 GPUs. (c) GRPO sampling overhead: group_size=16 means sampling 16 responses per prompt (PPO typically uses 1), i.e., 16× the inference volume. But this is pure inference (no backward pass) and can be handled efficiently with vLLM batching. Key insight: inference cost is far lower than training a full Critic model — cheap inference substitutes for expensive Critic training. Exercise D: System Impact of On-Policy Training and Overlap Online RL requires rollouts from the current policy (on-policy), creating a “training-inference pipeline bubble.” If rollout takes 60% of wall time and training takes 40%: No overlap (sequential execution): training GPUs are idle during rollout → effective utilization is 40/(60+40) = 40%. With overlap (disaggregated + pipeline): separate the training and inference clusters. The training cluster trains on batch N while the inference cluster simultaneously generates batch N+1 with (slightly stale) weights. Both clusters run at close to ~90-95% utilization (with only a small bubble during weight sync). Exercise E: Weight Update Propagation Latency Analysis 70B parameters BF16 = 140 GB; InfiniBand 400 Gbps (= 50 GB/s); training step takes ~10 s. (a) Transfer time: s. (b) Can it keep up: → yes. There is 7.2 s of slack within a single step, enough to pipeline: asynchronously transfer step N’s weights while training step N+1. (c) Impact of stale weights: using stale weights for rollout introduces off-policy error. 1-step staleness causes negligible quality loss (adopted by most systems); N-step staleness grows roughly linearly in error, with noticeable quality degradation once KL exceeds the threshold. Design: async weight update — start rollout with slightly old weights, transfer new weights in the background, then switch on completion, hiding the 2.8 s latency inside computation. Exercise F: System-Level Detection of Reward Hacking During GRPO training the model may “hack” the reward model (achieving high RM scores while actual quality degrades). (a) Monitoring metrics: KL divergence trend: KL() — spikes sharply when hacking occurs Reward-KL correlation: in healthy training reward rises while KL stays flat; when hacking, reward rises but KL explodes Output diversity: unique n-gram ratio, distinct-N — hacking often causes output collapse Specific pattern detectors: repetition, format gaming (excessive bullets/markdown), abnormal length RM score vs ground truth: periodically sample human eval / LLM-as-judge to detect divergence (b) Pause trigger conditions: (c) Recovery strategies: roll back to the most recent “healthy” checkpoint; increase KL penalty β; update/retrain the Reward Model; add a diversity bonus to the reward function.
